Transport Layer Security (TLS) configuration
WHAT: Using legacy TLS protocols (SSLv2, SSLv3, TLS 1.0/1.1) or weak cipher suites (NULL, anonymous, EXPORT) exposes traffic to downgrade, decryption, and impersonation attacks.
WHY: Attackers can read or modify supposedly “secure” traffic, replay requests, or impersonate the server, breaking confidentiality, integrity, and authentication.
HOW: Configure servers to default to TLS 1.3 and support TLS 1.2 only if needed; disable SSLv2, SSLv3, TLS 1.0, and TLS 1.1; enable TLS_FALLBACK_SCSV to prevent downgrades; restrict cipher suites to strong options (e.g., GCM-based) and explicitly disable NULL, anonymous, and EXPORT ciphers.
EXAMPLE: In a web server config, set `ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3;` and `ssl_ciphers <strong-GCM-suites>;` while removing or disabling any `SSLv2`, `SSLv3`, `TLSv1`, `TLSv1.1`, `NULL`, `EXPORT`, or `anon` cipher entries.
TLS configuration and certificate hardening
WHAT: Insecure TLS configurations (weak/NULL/EXPORT ciphers, custom DH params in TLS ≤1.2, enabled compression, outdated crypto libraries, weak keys, weak hashes, or mismatched certificate domains) can lead to broken confidentiality, integrity, or authentication.
WHY: Attackers can decrypt or tamper with traffic (e.g., CRIME, Heartbleed-style issues), impersonate servers, or cause DoS by abusing bad parameters or vulnerable libraries.
HOW: Disable NULL/anonymous/EXPORT ciphers and TLS compression; for TLS 1.3, restrict Diffie-Hellman groups to standard secure groups (e.g., x25519, ffdhe2048+ via config); avoid custom DH params in TLS ≤1.2; keep TLS/crypto libraries fully patched; use ≥2048-bit private keys protected by strict filesystem permissions; use SHA-256 (not MD5/SHA-1) for certificate hashes; ensure certificate CN/SAN exactly match all served FQDNs; validate configuration with reputable TLS test tools.
EXAMPLE (Apache):
Before: `SSLCipherSuite ALL` / `SSLCompression on` / weak cert with SHA-1.
After: `SSLCipherSuite HIGH:!aNULL:!eNULL:!EXPORT` + `SSLOpenSSLConfCmd Groups x25519:secp256r1:ffdhe3072` + `SSLCompression off` + 2048-bit key, SHA-256 cert with correct CN/SAN.
TLS certificate domain scoping and wildcard usage
WHAT: Misconfigured TLS certificates (e.g., including non-qualified hostnames, IPs, internal domains on public certs, or over-broad wildcards shared across systems with different trust levels) expose private keys and services to misuse and compromise.
WHY: Overly broad or mixed-trust certificates increase the impact of key compromise, enable impersonation of multiple services, and leak internal infrastructure details to external clients.
HOW: Only include appropriate FQDNs (e.g., consider “www” explicitly; exclude IPs, non-qualified, and internal names on public certs); avoid wildcard certs unless strictly necessary; never share a wildcard across systems of different trust levels; prefer ACME per-host certificates or TLS-terminating reverse proxies; keep an inventory of all systems sharing a certificate and limit wildcard scope to specific subdomains.
EXAMPLE: Before: Public cert for `example.com` includes `example.com`, `www`, `10.0.0.5`, `internal.example.com`, and a wildcard `*.example.com` used by both `vpn.example.com` and `www.example.com`. After: Public certs only for `example.com` and `www.example.com`; internal names and IPs use separate internal PKI certs; VPN and public web server use distinct certs or a tightly scoped wildcard like `*.vpn.example.com` on a dedicated TLS-terminating proxy.
Use trusted CAs and enforce TLS for all application pages
WHAT: Certificates not signed by a trusted CA or pages served without TLS allow attackers to impersonate the site or intercept/modify traffic (e.g., stealing session tokens or injecting JavaScript).
WHY: Users and clients cannot reliably authenticate the server, enabling man-in-the-middle attacks, credential theft, and content tampering.
HOW: Obtain certificates only from CAs trusted by your users (public or internal), configure CAA DNS records to restrict which CAs may issue for your domains, and enforce HTTPS/TLS on every page (HSTS, redirects, and secure cookies).
EXAMPLE: Before: `http://example.com/login` and certificate from an untrusted CA. After: Redirect all `http://` to `https://example.com/...` with a certificate from a trusted CA and `Strict-Transport-Security` enabled.
Transport Layer Security and Sensitive Data Handling
WHAT: Failing to enforce TLS for all pages, mixing HTTPS pages with HTTP-loaded resources, omitting the Secure flag on cookies, or allowing caching of sensitive data can expose session tokens and confidential information to sniffing or injection attacks.
WHY: Attackers can steal cookies, hijack sessions, inject malicious JavaScript, or recover sensitive responses from browser/proxy caches or via man-in-the-middle on unencrypted HTTP.
HOW: Enforce HTTPS on all endpoints; redirect HTTP to HTTPS only where appropriate and use HSTS; for APIs, reject HTTP requests instead of redirecting; never load resources over HTTP on HTTPS pages; set the Secure attribute on all cookies; and disable caching of sensitive responses using headers like `Cache-Control: no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate`, `Pragma: no-cache`, and `Expires: 0`.
EXAMPLE: (HTTP headers)
Before: `Set-Cookie: session=abc123; Path=/` and no cache headers.
After: `Set-Cookie: session=abc123; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly` plus `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains`, `Cache-Control: no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate`, `Pragma: no-cache`, `Expires: 0`.
Mutual TLS and Certificate Pinning for Strong Client/Server Authentication
WHAT: The server does not verify the client’s identity, allowing attackers with a valid or trusted certificate to intercept and decrypt TLS traffic (e.g., via corporate TLS inspection or compromised CA).
WHY: Missing strong client authentication and server key verification enables man-in-the-middle attacks, credential theft, and data disclosure even over “HTTPS”.
HOW: For high-value or internal APIs, implement mutual TLS (mTLS) so clients present certificates that the server validates against an internal CA or allowlist; for mobile/thick clients or server-to-server calls, additionally implement certificate/public key pinning in the client, validating the server’s certificate or key against an embedded expected value and failing closed on mismatch.
EXAMPLE: Before (server): accept any TLS client that completes the handshake. After (server): configure TLS to `request_client_certificate` and verify it against a trusted client CA/CRL/OCSP; Before (mobile client): rely on default OS trust store. After (mobile client): compare the server certificate’s public key hash to a hard-coded expected hash and abort the connection if it does not match.
Abuse-case-driven security requirements
WHAT: Relying on vague, generic security requirements (e.g., “must be secure”, “defend against all attacks”) leads to missing concrete threats and unimplemented countermeasures in code and architecture.
WHY: Ambiguous requirements prevent accurate risk assessment, budgeting, and implementation of defenses, increasing the chance that high-impact attacks remain unaddressed.
HOW: For each feature, identify specific abuse cases and attacks relevant to the business/technical context, assess their risk, derive explicit security requirements and acceptance criteria, and define where countermeasures must live (network, infrastructure, code).
EXAMPLE: Before: “The API must be secure.” After: “For the payment API, identify abuse cases (e.g., replay of payment requests, parameter tampering), add user stories/acceptance tests for request signing and server-side validation, and implement the required checks in the payment service code.”
Abuse Case–Driven Security Requirements
WHAT: Failure to identify and document abuse/misuse cases for application features leads to missing security requirements and untested business-logic attack paths (e.g., abusing password reset to enumerate accounts or trading flows to game prices).
WHY: Unaddressed abuse cases enable attackers to exploit business logic and control weaknesses, causing revenue loss, data exposure, and degraded user experience.
HOW: For each feature/user story, perform threat modeling to ask “what can go wrong,” derive concrete abuse/misuse cases, and turn them into explicit security requirements, acceptance criteria, and targeted security tests; ensure countermeasures are designed and implemented in the appropriate layer (network, infrastructure, or code) and budgeted into the sprint/project.
EXAMPLE: Before: User story for password reset has no abuse cases or security tests. After: Add abuse case “attacker enumerates accounts via reset flow,” requirement “rate-limit and generic responses for reset requests,” and tests that verify enumeration is not possible.
Abuse case–driven security requirements
WHAT: Missing or undocumented abuse cases for each business feature leads to unimplemented security requirements and unhandled attack paths.
WHY: Uncaptured attacks (e.g., XSS in comments, arbitrary price changes) can bypass controls, causing data compromise, fraud, or financial loss.
HOW: For every feature/User Story, run a structured workshop with business, risk, technical, QA, and security roles to enumerate technical and business abuse cases, assign risk ratings, and turn selected abuse cases into explicit security requirements or acceptance criteria with unique IDs for tracking.
EXAMPLE: Before: User Story “As a customer, I can update the cart price” with no security criteria. After: Add acceptance criteria “AC-Sec-ABUSE_CASE_001: Cart price must be server-calculated and immutable from client input; attempts to modify client-side price are rejected and logged.”
File upload validation for malicious content
WHAT: User-controlled file uploads (e.g., Office documents) are accepted without validating their content, allowing files with embedded malicious macros or payloads to be stored or processed.
WHY: Malicious files can lead to malware execution on client or server systems, data compromise, or further compromise of the application environment.
HOW: For every uploaded file, validate type and content server-side using a robust parser, restrict allowed formats and features (e.g., disable macros), and follow OWASP File Upload Cheat Sheet guidance; reject or sanitize files that fail validation.
EXAMPLE: Before: accept and store any uploaded file based solely on extension; After: check MIME type and size, load the file with a secure parsing library, verify it matches the expected safe format, and reject files containing active content such as macros.
Abuse-case-driven security tracking and validation
WHAT: Failure to systematically track and validate implementation of defined abuse cases can lead to missing, incomplete, or accidentally removed security countermeasures in code, design, or infrastructure.
WHY: Untracked or unvalidated abuse-case handling allows known attack paths to remain exploitable or become reintroduced, undermining security requirements and exposing the application to regression vulnerabilities.
HOW: For each abuse case, record where it is handled (design, infrastructure, network, code) via documentation, schemas, or explicit code annotations/comments; then enforce automated (SAST/DAST rules, security-focused unit/integration/functional tests, CI jobs) and manual checks (peer security reviews, pentests against the abuse-case list) to ensure all abuse cases are correctly and completely implemented and remain in place over time.
EXAMPLE: In code, annotate handling logic, e.g., `@AbuseCase(ids={"ABUSE_CASE_001","ABUSE_CASE_002"})` on classes/modules that implement specific countermeasures, and add CI tests that fail the build if these abuse cases are not covered or if related tests start failing.
Injection and Access Control Security
WHAT: Untrusted input reaching interpreters (SQL/LDAP/NoSQL/OS commands/XML/ORM, etc.) or access-control decisions (IDs, tokens, sessions, CORS) without strict validation and enforcement, allowing attackers to execute arbitrary operations or access other users’ data.
WHY: Leads to data theft or modification, account takeover, privilege escalation, remote code execution, denial of service, and unauthorized API or system access.
HOW: Treat all external data as untrusted; use parameterized queries and safe APIs; disable XML external entities and dangerous parser features; enforce server-side authorization on every request using user-bound identifiers; validate and normalize IDs and tokens; implement secure session handling and rate limiting; configure CORS with strict allowlists.
EXAMPLE: Before (SQL): `query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id=" + req.param("id");` After: `PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?"); ps.setInt(1, req.getIntParam("id"));`
Access control, crypto, configuration, XSS, and deserialization hardening
WHAT: Missing or weak access controls, insecure token/session handling (JWT, cookies, hidden fields), CORS misconfigurations, default/weak/unchanging crypto keys, disabled certificate validation, insecure server/framework settings, missing security headers, verbose error messages, XSS sinks, and unsafe deserialization allow privilege escalation, unauthorized access, and code execution.
WHY: These issues let attackers act as other users/admins, access or modify protected data, call unauthorized APIs, execute arbitrary code in the browser or server, and pivot deeper into the system.
HOW: Enforce server-side authorization on every endpoint and method; validate and sign tokens, prevent replay, and implement revocation/expiration; configure strict CORS allowlists; use strong, rotated, non-default crypto keys and verify TLS certificates; harden server/framework configs, disable unnecessary features/accounts, and send secure headers; avoid detailed error messages in production; validate/encode all untrusted output to prevent XSS; and avoid deserializing untrusted data or use safe, allowlisted serialization formats and types.
EXAMPLE: Before (web): API trusts role from client JWT without verification, allows `POST/PUT/DELETE` without checking user’s permissions, uses default framework error pages and no CSP/X-Frame-Options headers, and deserializes arbitrary objects from request bodies. After: Server verifies JWT signature/claims and checks role/ownership per request, enforces method-level authorization, enables hardened framework and server security settings with strict security headers, returns generic errors, and replaces arbitrary object deserialization with validated, schema-bound DTOs or safe data formats.
Using Components with Known Vulnerabilities
WHAT: Using third-party components (libraries, frameworks, services) with publicly known security vulnerabilities in deployed code.
WHY: Attackers can reliably exploit these known flaws to gain unauthorized access, execute code, or compromise data and systems.
HOW: Maintain an inventory of all dependencies; use automated tools (e.g., SCA) to detect known CVEs; regularly update/patch components; remove unused dependencies; avoid components without security maintenance.
EXAMPLE: Before: app depends on `libX` v1.2 with a known RCE CVE and no version constraints. After: upgrade to `libX` v1.4 with the fix and pin the version in the dependency manifest.
Vulnerability Disclosure Process for Software Projects
WHAT: Inadequate or unclear vulnerability disclosure processes (e.g., no secure reporting channel, undefined scope, or failure to respond/publish fixes) can leave exploitable bugs unreported, unpatched, or silently abused.
WHY: Poor disclosure handling increases window of exposure, enables attackers to exploit known but unpatched issues, damages trust with researchers, and can delay or prevent users from applying critical security updates.
HOW: Define and publish a vulnerability disclosure policy that includes: a secure reporting channel (e.g., security@ email with PGP, web form), clear scope/terms for testing and any bug bounty, expected response timelines, commitment not to threaten good-faith researchers, a process to request CVEs, and a practice of issuing public advisories and changelogs when security bugs are fixed.
EXAMPLE: Before: No documented way to report security bugs; security fixes silently merged in code without advisories. After: Add SECURITY.md describing how to report vulnerabilities, scope and timelines; configure security@yourdomain with PGP; on each security fix, publish an advisory and changelog entry and, where appropriate, request a CVE.
Secure vulnerability reporting practices
WHAT: Risk of leaking sensitive information or personal data when reporting vulnerabilities, especially if sent over insecure channels or to inappropriate contacts.
WHY: Unprotected or misdirected reports can expose user data, aid attackers in exploiting the vulnerability, or create legal/privacy violations.
HOW: Use encrypted channels (e.g., PGP) when supported; send details only to verified security contacts; include only the minimum necessary technical data and redact all personal data before sharing.
EXAMPLE: Before: Sending full HTTP logs with unredacted user identifiers and session cookies over plain email to a generic contact. After: Redact user identifiers and cookies, verify a security@ contact or security.txt entry, and encrypt the email with the published PGP key before sending.
Security reporting and mitigation guidance
WHAT: When reporting a vulnerability, provide enough technical detail (e.g., HTTP requests/responses, HTML snippets, proof-of-concept code) for developers to reliably understand, reproduce, and verify the issue and its impact.
WHY: Clear, reproducible reports enable accurate triage, correct fixes, and reduce the risk that a real vulnerability is dismissed, misfixed, or left exploitable.
HOW: Include concrete reproduction steps, affected endpoints/parameters, environment assumptions, and impact description; redact personal data; when unsure of specific fixes, reference vetted guidance (e.g., OWASP cheat sheets) instead of speculative remediation advice.
EXAMPLE: Report structure: (1) Summary and impact, (2) Step-by-step reproduction with exact requests/responses, (3) Minimal proof-of-concept code, (4) References to relevant secure-coding guidance for the affected technology.
Vulnerability Disclosure and Proof-of-Concept Handling
WHAT: Mishandling vulnerability disclosure and proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit code (e.g., publishing full working exploits without coordination) can expose users to unpatched attacks and damage trust with vendors and platforms.
WHY: Premature or uncoordinated disclosure increases the window of exploitation for attackers, can lead to legal or contractual issues (e.g., NDA, bug bounty rules), and may harm affected users and systems.
HOW: Coordinate disclosure timelines with vendors; always notify vendors before publishing and share the final advisory link; include impact, affected/fixed versions, mitigations, and timelines; carefully assess whether to publish PoC/functional exploit code; comply with bug bounty and NDA rules; seek legal advice when disclosure is disputed.
EXAMPLE: Before: Immediately posting full exploit code and technical details to a public repository without notifying the vendor. After: First reporting the vulnerability to the vendor, agreeing on a disclosure timeline, then publishing a write-up with mitigations and (if appropriate) a limited PoC only after a patch is available.
Vulnerability disclosure and bug bounty program process
WHAT: Poorly defined or unmanaged vulnerability disclosure and bug bounty processes (unclear contacts, no triage, insecure communication, no timelines) can cause missed or mishandled security reports and unresolved vulnerabilities.
WHY: This leads to exploitable issues remaining in production, legal and reputational risk, and breakdown of cooperation with security researchers.
HOW: Publish clear security contact points (e.g., security@, /.well-known/security.txt, bug tracker instructions), define internal triage and escalation workflows, request structured report data, support encrypted channels (e.g., PGP), set and honor response/triage/fix timelines, and document scope and safe-harbor terms before running a bug bounty.
EXAMPLE: Before: No documented security contact, ad-hoc handling of emailed reports by support staff. After: Public security.txt with security@company.com, PGP key, reporting template and scope; internal runbook routing all security reports to a dedicated triage team with defined SLAs for acknowledgment, triage, fix, and retest.
Vulnerability Disclosure and Advisory Process
WHAT: Inadequate handling and disclosure of security vulnerabilities (e.g., no clear triage, fix timeline, or advisory) can leave users running vulnerable versions without awareness or guidance.
WHY: Poor disclosure and communication increase the window of exposure, hinder patch adoption, and erode trust in the software’s security.
HOW: Establish a formal process: acknowledge reports, triage and confirm issues, define and communicate fix timelines, publish security advisories listing affected/patch versions, conditions of vulnerability, mitigations, and CVE, and keep researchers and users updated throughout.
EXAMPLE: Before: Fix vulnerabilities silently with no public notice or version list. After: For each confirmed vulnerability, publish an advisory (e.g., on a “Security Advisories” page and mailing list) detailing impact, affected versions, patched versions, mitigations, and CVE, and reference it in release notes.
Security advisory disclosure timing
WHAT: Risk of attackers exploiting newly disclosed vulnerabilities if full technical details and exploit code are published before users can apply patches.
WHY: Early public release of exploit-ready details increases the window of exposure, enabling widespread compromise before systems are updated.
HOW: Coordinate disclosure timelines with researchers; request delayed publication of full technical details until after patches are widely available; ensure advisories are promptly published and easy to find so administrators can patch quickly.
EXAMPLE: N/A
Cookie theft detection for session hijacking
WHAT: Session cookies can be stolen and reused from a different environment (IP, device, locale, time), allowing attackers to hijack active user sessions until they expire.
WHY: A valid stolen session cookie effectively bypasses authentication and 2FA, enabling full account takeover and unauthorized actions under the victim’s identity.
HOW: On session creation, persist server-side metadata (IP address, User-Agent, Accept-Language, timestamp, and optionally Accept, Accept-Encoding, Sec-Fetch-*, sec-ch-* headers) and, on each request, compare for significant changes; when anomalies are detected, trigger risk-based responses (step-up auth, re-login, out-of-band confirmation, or session invalidation).
EXAMPLE: Before: On login, issue a session cookie and trust it for all subsequent requests without tracking environment changes. After: On login, store IP/User-Agent/Accept-Language/Date with the session; on each request, if IP region or device fingerprint changes beyond an allowed threshold, mark the session high-risk and require re-authentication or invalidate the session.
Session hijacking detection and mitigation for bearer session cookies
WHAT: Session cookies are accepted solely by value; if a stolen cookie is reused from a different device (IP/UA/headers), the server may treat the attacker as the user.
WHY: An attacker with a valid session cookie can fully impersonate the user, access confidential data, and perform sensitive actions.
HOW: On each request to sensitive endpoints, compare stored session metadata (e.g., IP/GeoIP range, User-Agent, selected headers) with current request values; on significant deviation, trigger additional verification (CAPTCHA for low‑risk, full re-authentication and new session cookie for high‑risk) and invalidate or rotate the session.
EXAMPLE: Before: `app.post("/users/delete", handler)` (no session checks). After: `app.post("/users/delete", cookieTheftDetectionMiddleware, handler)` where `cookieTheftDetectionMiddleware` checks IP/UA consistency and, on mismatch, forces re-login or CAPTCHA before proceeding.
Handling Malformed XML Documents
WHAT: Applications that accept or process malformed XML (e.g., missing end tags, invalid characters, invalid structure) or use parsers in “recovery” mode may continue processing instead of failing fast, leading to unexpected behavior, data integrity issues, and excessive CPU usage that can be abused for DoS.
WHY: Attackers can send specially crafted malformed XML to trigger asymmetric resource consumption (DoS), bypass expected structure checks, or corrupt/alter interpreted data when parsers attempt to “fix” invalid documents.
HOW: Use XML parsers that strictly follow W3C specifications, disable recovery/lenient modes, reject malformed XML with a fatal error, validate each element’s content and structure against a schema, and benchmark malformed vs well‑formed processing time to detect and mitigate expensive failure paths (e.g., rate limit or size/time bound XML processing).
XML schema validation and structure enforcement
WHAT: Failure to strictly validate XML documents (missing or overly permissive schemas, unbounded nesting, acceptance of extra elements/values) allows malformed or attacker-crafted XML to be parsed and processed as if it were legitimate input.
WHY: This can lead to denial of service (e.g., stack overflow from deeply nested tags), logic manipulation (e.g., altered prices or IDs), crashes, and potentially code execution when parsers mishandle invalid structures.
HOW: Define and enforce a precise XML Schema (XSD, not DTD) for every XML document type; restrict allowed elements, attributes, value ranges, and nesting depth; reject documents that do not fully conform; use only local or trusted schema repositories with integrity checks and secure transport when remote; configure parsers to fail fast on invalid or excessively nested XML.
EXAMPLE: Before: Application parses any incoming `<buy>` XML and uses the first `<id>` and `<price>` elements found without schema validation. After: Application validates against a strict XSD that allows exactly one `<id>` and one `<price>` with constrained types/ranges, rejects documents containing additional or malformed elements, and enforces parser limits on maximum depth and size.
Insecure XML schema definitions
WHAT: XML schemas that use overly generic types (e.g., unconstrained strings or integers) or lack length/range and character-set restrictions allow arbitrarily large or malformed values (e.g., a one‑million‑digit age or base64 fields with trailing arbitrary data) to be accepted as valid input.
WHY: Such improperly validated XML data can cause resource exhaustion (availability issues), integrity problems, and unintended processing of embedded or malformed content, potentially exposing internal errors or bypassing security checks.
HOW: For each XML element, choose the most specific built‑in type (e.g., base64Binary, nonNegativeInteger) and add explicit constraints (maxLength, pattern, minInclusive/maxInclusive). Reject or truncate values exceeding defined limits and ensure parsers validate against the strict schema before application processing.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): `<xs:element name="age" type="xs:string"/>` — accepts any length/content. After (secure): `<xs:element name="age" type="xs:nonNegativeInteger"><xs:simpleType><xs:restriction base="xs:nonNegativeInteger"><xs:maxInclusive value="150"/></xs:restriction></xs:simpleType></xs:element>`.
XML schema data validation for untrusted numeric input
WHAT: User-controlled XML values (e.g., quantity, denominators, prices) may be accepted with overly broad numeric types (integer, float, double), allowing negative, zero, Infinity, or NaN where only positive, finite values are valid.
WHY: This can cause logical vulnerabilities (negative balances), divide-by-zero crashes, or application failures that attackers can exploit to corrupt data or disrupt service.
HOW: Define strict XML Schema types for each element: use xs:positiveInteger where zero/negatives are invalid (e.g., quantity, denominators), use xs:decimal instead of float/double when Infinity/NaN are not allowed, and add xs:restriction/xs:enumeration to allow only specific valid values.
EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe): `<xs:element name="quantity" type="xs:integer"/>` / `<xs:element name="denominator" type="xs:integer"/>` / `<xs:element name="price" type="xs:double"/>`
EXAMPLE: After (safer): `<xs:element name="quantity" type="xs:positiveInteger"/>` / `<xs:restriction base="xs:positiveInteger"/>` for denominator / `<xs:element name="price" type="xs:decimal"/>`
XML schema input validation
WHAT: Failure to constrain XML element/attribute values (allowed values, length, patterns, numeric ranges, and occurrence counts) can let malformed or extreme data reach application logic, causing overflows, divide-by-zero, or resource exhaustion.
WHY: Unvalidated or weakly validated XML input can lead to crashes, logic errors, data corruption, and denial of service when the application processes unexpected or excessive values.
HOW: Use XML Schema restrictions: enumerations for fixed sets, minLength/maxLength/length for size bounds, pattern for syntax rules, assertions to exclude dangerous values (e.g., zero denominators), and minOccurs/maxOccurs to cap collection sizes; reject documents that fail schema validation before further processing.
EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe): accept any string for `<month>` and any integer for `<denominator>` and any number of `<buy>` elements; After (safer): define `<month>` with `<xs:enumeration>` of valid month names, `<denominator>` with `<xs:assertion test="$value != 0"/>`, and `<buy>` with a reasonable `maxOccurs` limit.
XML jumbo payload and unbounded elements handling
WHAT: Unbounded XML constructs (e.g., maxOccurs="unbounded", excessive depth/width, many attributes) can cause the application to process extremely large or numerous XML documents, exhausting CPU, memory, or network resources.
WHY: Uncontrolled resource consumption enables denial-of-service attacks, making the service slow or unavailable to legitimate users.
HOW: Define strict upper bounds on occurrences, depth, and attribute counts in XML schemas; configure parsers with limits on document size, nesting depth, and entity expansion; and reject or throttle requests that exceed these limits, logging such events.
EXAMPLE: Before (schema): `<xs:element name="buy" maxOccurs="unbounded">` → After: `<xs:element name="buy" maxOccurs="1000">` and configure the XML parser with maximum document size and depth constraints.
Schema Poisoning in XML Schemas
WHAT: XML processing that accepts embedded, local, or remote schemas without integrity checks or proper file permissions can be schema-poisoned, allowing attackers to alter validation rules or inject malicious DTDs (e.g., enabling external entity expansion).
WHY: Poisoned schemas can lead to file disclosure, denial of service, internal port scanning, brute-force attacks, or arbitrary data being accepted and processed by the server.
HOW: Disable or strictly limit DTD/XXE processing; do not trust embedded schemas; store local schemas with restrictive filesystem permissions (e.g., rw-r--r--, owned by a dedicated service account); pin and validate remote schemas via HTTPS with certificate validation and integrity checks; avoid fetching schemas over plain HTTP or from untrusted locations.
EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe, remote HTTP DTD): `<!DOCTYPE note SYSTEM "http://example.com/note.dtd">` → After (safer, local locked-down DTD over HTTPS or bundled resource): `<!DOCTYPE note SYSTEM "https://schemas.example.com/note.dtd">` with the file stored read-only for non-privileged users and XXE disabled in the XML parser.
XML external entities and remote schemas
WHAT: XML parsers that load external DTDs/schemas or resolve external entities (local or remote) can be tricked into fetching attacker-controlled resources, expanding entities excessively, or reading local files.
WHY: This enables confidentiality breaches (local file disclosure), integrity issues (tampered schemas), availability attacks (parser/resource exhaustion), and content redirection via DNS or HTTP tampering.
HOW: Disable DTDs and external entity resolution by default; if absolutely required, restrict to a strict allowlist of trusted, pinned hosts over HTTPS, validate DNS/hostnames, set hard limits on entity expansion, and never allow schemas/entities to reference arbitrary local files or untrusted remote URLs.
EXAMPLE (Java, before): `DocumentBuilderFactory dbf = DocumentBuilderFactory.newInstance(); dbf.setNamespaceAware(true);`
EXAMPLE (Java, after): `dbf.setFeature("http://apache.org/xml/features/disallow-doctype-decl", true); dbf.setFeature("http://xml.org/sax/features/external-general-entities", false); dbf.setFeature("http://xml.org/sax/features/external-parameter-entities", false);`
XML External Entity (XXE) in XML parsers
WHAT: XML is parsed with external entities enabled, allowing XML input to reference local files (e.g., `<!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "/etc/passwd">`) that are then read and processed by the application.
WHY: Attackers can read sensitive local files, perform SSRF, or cause denial of service by supplying malicious XML with external entities.
HOW: Disable DTDs and external entities in all XML parsers; in Java, set secure processing features (e.g., `factory.setFeature("http://apache.org/xml/features/disallow-doctype-decl", true)` and disable external general/parameter entities) before parsing untrusted XML.
EXAMPLE: Before (vulnerable): `DocumentBuilderFactory factory = DocumentBuilderFactory.newInstance(); DocumentBuilder builder = factory.newDocumentBuilder(); builder.parse("contacts.xml");` After (safer): configure `factory` with features to disallow DOCTYPE and external entities before calling `newDocumentBuilder()` and `parse()`.
XML External Entity (XXE) and Entity Expansion Attacks in Java XML Parsers
WHAT: XML parsers (e.g., SAXParserFactory, XMLInputFactory) process user-controlled XML with DTDs and entity expansion enabled, allowing external entities, recursive entities, quadratic blowup, or “billion laughs” payloads to be resolved.
WHY: Malicious entities can exfiltrate local files (e.g., /etc/passwd), perform SSRF, or exhaust CPU and memory, causing denial of service or crashes, even in contexts like SOAP where DTDs should be rejected.
HOW: For all untrusted XML, disable DTDs and external entities and limit entity expansion; in Java, configure factories before parsing (e.g., disallow DOCTYPE declarations, external general/parameter entities, and enable secure processing), and ensure SOAP processors reject any message containing a DTD.
EXAMPLE:
Before (unsafe): `SAXParserFactory f = SAXParserFactory.newInstance(); SAXParser p = f.newSAXParser(); p.parse("contacts.xml", handler);`
After (safer): `SAXParserFactory f = SAXParserFactory.newInstance(); f.setFeature("http://apache.org/xml/features/disallow-doctype-decl", true); f.setFeature("http://xml.org/sax/features/external-general-entities", false); f.setFeature("http://xml.org/sax/features/external-parameter-entities", false); f.setFeature("http://javax.xml.XMLConstants/feature/secure-processing", true); SAXParser p = f.newSAXParser(); p.parse(inputStreamFromUntrustedSource, handler);`
XML External Entity and SSRF Protection
WHAT: Untrusted XML input that allows external or parameter entity resolution can cause XXE, enabling local file retrieval, SSRF to internal/remote services, and forced DNS lookups.
WHY: Attackers can exfiltrate sensitive files (e.g., /etc/passwd), scan internal networks, abuse internal services, or leak information via DNS/HTTP requests.
HOW: Disable external and parameter entity resolution and DTD processing in XML parsers; reject or strip DOCTYPE/ENTITY declarations; use safe parser configurations/libraries designed to be XXE-safe; never fetch remote DTDs or schemas based on user-controlled input.
EXAMPLE: Before (Java): `DocumentBuilderFactory dbf = DocumentBuilderFactory.newInstance();`
After (Java): `dbf.setFeature("http://apache.org/xml/features/disallow-doctype-decl", true); dbf.setFeature("http://xml.org/sax/features/external-general-entities", false); dbf.setFeature("http://xml.org/sax/features/external-parameter-entities", false);`
XML External Entity (XXE) and External Connection Handling
WHAT: Improperly allowing XML external entities and external parameter entities to load local files or remote DTDs can exfiltrate sensitive data and be abused for port scanning and brute-force attacks via crafted URLs.
WHY: Attackers can retrieve local files, send their contents to remote servers, map internal networks, and brute-force services, leading to data breaches and infrastructure compromise.
HOW: Disable external entity resolution and DTD processing in XML parsers; block network access from XML resolution code; if external entities are required, strictly allowlist safe URLs and disallow file:// and internal addresses; sanitize and log errors without leaking connection details.
EXAMPLE: In Java, configure the parser: `factory.setFeature("http://apache.org/xml/features/disallow-doctype-decl", true); factory.setFeature("http://xml.org/sax/features/external-general-entities", false); factory.setFeature("http://xml.org/sax/features/external-parameter-entities", false);`
Set request size limits
WHAT: Failing to set a maximum size for HTTP request bodies allows unbounded buffering/parsing, leading to resource exhaustion.
WHY: Attackers can send very large request bodies to exhaust server memory or disk, causing denial of service.
HOW: Configure a strict maximum request body size for all endpoints (and per-route overrides if needed) using framework or middleware options (e.g., raw-body `limit`), and reject or terminate requests exceeding this limit.
EXAMPLE:
Before (no limit): `app.use(express.json());`
After (with limit): `app.use(express.json({ limit: '1mb' }));`
Request size limits and non-blocking order-dependent operations
WHAT: Unbounded or improperly enforced request body sizes can exhaust memory/disk, and blocking or misordered asynchronous operations (e.g., auth in a callback, privileged action outside) can create race conditions and security flaws.
WHY: Attackers can send oversized or mis-labeled payloads to cause denial of service, or exploit race conditions to perform actions before validation/authentication completes.
HOW: Set strict per–content-type request size limits (e.g., separate limits for JSON vs multipart), validate that the actual body format matches the declared Content-Type (at least for risky types or large requests), and ensure all order-dependent or security-critical operations (e.g., auth, file operations) are grouped in a single non-blocking callback chain or async flow rather than mixing async callbacks with synchronous calls.
EXAMPLE: JavaScript (request limits): `app.use(express.json({ limit: "1kb" })); app.use(express.urlencoded({ extended: true, limit: "1kb" }));` plus middleware that inspects and validates the body format against `req.headers['content-type']` before further processing.
Input validation and output escaping in Node.js
WHAT: Failure to properly validate and sanitize user-controlled input (e.g., query parameters, body data) and to escape output before rendering HTML/JavaScript can lead to injection flaws (SQLi, XSS, command injection, file inclusion, LDAP injection, DoS, directory traversal, etc.).
WHY: Untrusted input that is directly used in queries, commands, file paths, or rendered pages allows attackers to execute arbitrary code, access or modify sensitive data, disrupt service, or take over the application.
HOW: Validate all external input using an allowlist of accepted values where possible; otherwise enforce strict schemas (type, length, pattern, structure) and reject or escape dangerous characters; normalize and consistently parse inputs (e.g., Express query parsing quirks); always perform context-appropriate output escaping for any data reflected in HTML/JS (e.g., using escape-html or node-esapi); use vetted libraries like validator and express-mongo-sanitize to centralize and standardize validation.
EXAMPLE: Before (Node.js/Express): `res.send('<div>'+req.query.foo+'</div>');` After: validate `req.query.foo` with `validator` (e.g., `isAlphanumeric`, length checks) and then send `res.send('<div>'+escapeHtml(req.query.foo)+'</div>');`
Prevent brute-force attacks and CSRF, and remove unused routes
WHAT: Login and other sensitive endpoints can be brute-forced, forged via CSRF, or exposed through automatically generated/unused routes, leading to unauthorized access or expanded attack surface.
WHY: Successful brute-force or CSRF attacks can compromise accounts and perform unauthorized state changes; unused or auto-generated routes can leak data or enable arbitrary actions.
HOW: Implement rate limiting, request throttling, CAPTCHAs, and account lockout on login and authentication routes; use a maintained CSRF protection middleware instead of deprecated packages like `csurf`; audit frameworks for auto-generated routes and explicitly remove or disable any unused or unnecessary endpoints.
EXAMPLE: In Node.js/Express, apply a rate limiter or bouncer middleware on `/login` and `/auth` routes, integrate a supported CSRF middleware on all state-changing POST/PUT/DELETE routes, and configure Sails/Feathers to disable or restrict auto-generated REST endpoints that are not explicitly required.
Prevent HTTP Parameter Pollution in Express applications
WHAT: Attackers can send multiple HTTP parameters with the same name, causing Express to interpret them as arrays and potentially bypass validation or alter logic.
WHY: Uncontrolled multiple values can lead to authorization bypass, unexpected behavior, or injection when only a single, trusted value was assumed.
HOW: For routes handling user-controlled query/body parameters, normalize inputs to a single value; in Express, use the `hpp` middleware early in the middleware chain to keep only the last value for each parameter.
EXAMPLE: Before: `app.use(express.json());` (parameters may be arrays). After: `const hpp = require('hpp'); app.use(hpp()); app.use(express.json());`
Symlink handling and error management in Node.js
WHAT: Symbolic links inside “allowed” paths may point outside restricted directories, and unhandled or improperly handled errors (uncaughtException, EventEmitter errors, async callback errors) can crash the app or leak sensitive information (e.g., stack traces) to users.
WHY: Following unvalidated symlinks can bypass path restrictions and expose unintended files; unhandled/incorrectly resumed exceptions leave the process in an unknown state, enabling denial of service, inconsistent behavior, or information disclosure.
HOW: Exclude relative symlinks from allowed paths or resolve and validate real paths before access; in Node.js, always attach listeners to 'error' events on EventEmitters, use error-first callbacks for async APIs, bind to process.on('uncaughtException') only to log, clean up resources, and then terminate the process; never show detailed stack traces to end users—log them server-side and return generic error messages.
EXAMPLE:
Before (unsafe symlink use):
fs.readFile(userPath, ...); // userPath may be a symlink escaping allowed dir
After (safe symlink use):
const real = fs.realpathSync(userPath);
if (!real.startsWith(allowedDir)) throw new Error('Forbidden path');
fs.readFile(real, ...);
Use secure cookies and HTTP security headers in Express apps
WHAT: Session cookies and HTTP responses may be insecure if cookies lack flags (secure, httpOnly, sameSite, scoped path) and security headers are not set.
WHY: Insecure cookies and missing headers increase risk of session hijacking, XSS, CSRF, clickjacking, and other common web attacks.
HOW: Configure express-session with secure, httpOnly, sameSite, and a restricted path for cookies; then enable helmet to set standard security headers on all responses.
EXAMPLE:
Before: app.use(session({ secret: 'key' }));
After: app.use(session({ secret: 'key', cookie: { secure: true, httpOnly: true, sameSite: true, path: '/user' } })); app.use(helmet());
HTTP Security Headers Configuration for Web Applications
WHAT: Missing or misconfigured HTTP security headers (HSTS, X-Frame-Options, CSP, X-Content-Type-Options, cache control, X-Download-Options, X-Powered-By) can allow downgrade attacks, XSS, clickjacking, MIME sniffing, sensitive data caching, file execution in browser context, and information leakage.
WHY: Improper headers can let attackers intercept or modify traffic, steal credentials or data, frame your pages for clickjacking, execute injected scripts, or gain information useful for further attacks.
HOW: In server middleware, explicitly set secure defaults: enforce HTTPS with HSTS; restrict framing with X-Frame-Options or CSP frame-ancestors; define a strict Content-Security-Policy; disable MIME sniffing with X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff; disable caching only on sensitive responses; prevent IE download execution with X-Download-Options: noopen; and remove X-Powered-By.
EXAMPLE: In an Express.js app, use Helmet and nocache: `app.use(helmet.hsts()); app.use(helmet.frameguard()); app.use(helmet.contentSecurityPolicy({directives:{defaultSrc:["'self'"],scriptSrc:["'self'"],frameAncestors:["'none'"]}})); app.use(helmet.noSniff()); const nocache=require("nocache"); app.use(nocache()); app.use(helmet.ieNoOpen()); app.disable("x-powered-by");`
Stay away from dangerous dynamic code and regex patterns
WHAT: Using dangerous JavaScript functions (e.g., eval, child_process.exec, unsafe fs/vm usage) or “evil” regular expressions with user-controlled input can lead to remote code execution, file inclusion/directory traversal, or Regular Expression Denial of Service (ReDoS).
WHY: Attackers can execute arbitrary system commands, read/write arbitrary files, or craft inputs that cause regex evaluation to take exponential time, hanging or crashing the application.
HOW: Avoid eval and child_process.exec with any user-controlled data; prefer safer APIs (e.g., JSON.parse, child_process.execFile/spawn with argument arrays and strict validation). Strictly validate and sanitize all paths passed to fs and isolate vm usage in a hardened sandbox. Design regexes to avoid catastrophic backtracking (no nested quantifiers or overlapping alternations) and use tools like vuln-regex-detector to analyze patterns before deployment.
EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe): const out = eval(userInput); const res = exec(`grep ${userArg} file`); fs.readFile(userPath); /(([a-z])+.)+A-Z+/.test(str); After (safer): const obj = JSON.parse(userJson); const res = execFile('grep', ['--', safeArg]); fs.readFile(validatedPath); use a rewritten, linear-time regex verified by a ReDoS scanner.
Use security linters and strict mode in JavaScript
WHAT: Failing to use SAST security linters and JavaScript strict mode allows insecure patterns and dangerous legacy features (e.g., implicit globals) to slip into the codebase unnoticed.
WHY: Undetected insecure patterns can lead to vulnerabilities and hard-to-debug runtime issues that may be exploitable in production.
HOW: Integrate SAST-capable linters (e.g., ESLint, JSHint) into CI, enable and periodically review security-focused rules (including custom rules for risky patterns), and always enable strict mode (e.g., via `"use strict";` or transpiler config) for all JavaScript modules.
EXAMPLE:
Before:
```javascript
func(); function func() { y = 3.14; } // no linter, no strict mode, silent global
```
After:
```javascript
"use strict";
func();
function func() {
let y = 3.14; // linter enforces no-undef, strict mode throws on missing declaration
}
```
Error Handling and Information Disclosure
WHAT: Unhandled or improperly handled errors that return stack traces, SQL errors, file paths, or technology/version details to clients, instead of a generic error response.
WHY: Such detailed error messages aid attackers in reconnaissance, help identify injection points, and expose internal implementation details that increase exploitability.
HOW: Configure a global error handler to catch unexpected exceptions, log full details only on the server, and return a generic, implementation-agnostic error response (e.g., HTTP 5xx with RFC 7807-compliant body) that reveals no stack traces, queries, or paths.
EXAMPLE: Before (Java web.xml): no `<error-page>` mapping, default container error pages show stack traces. After: add `<error-page><exception-type>java.lang.Exception</exception-type><location>/error.jsp</location></error-page>` and implement `error.jsp` to log the exception server-side and return a generic error message to the client.
Generic error handling in web APIs
WHAT: Avoid returning raw exception messages or stack traces to clients; instead send a generic, non-sensitive error response for unexpected server errors (e.g., when catching java.lang.Exception in a global handler).
WHY: Detailed error messages can leak implementation details, internal paths, or sensitive data, aiding attackers in reconnaissance or exploitation.
HOW: Implement a global error handler (e.g., @RestControllerAdvice/@ExceptionHandler in Spring) that logs full exception details server-side but always returns a generic message and appropriate HTTP status (5xx for server errors, 4xx for client misuse) with a safe content type (e.g., application/problem+json).
EXAMPLE:
Before: return ResponseEntity.status(500).body(e.getMessage());
After: log.error("Unexpected error", e); return ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR, "An error occur, please retry");
Centralized error handling in ASP.NET Core APIs
WHAT: Unhandled exceptions in ASP.NET Core APIs can leak internal details or produce inconsistent error responses if not routed through a centralized, generic error handler.
WHY: Exposing stack traces or internal messages can reveal implementation details useful to attackers and make client behavior unpredictable.
HOW: Configure `UseExceptionHandler("/api/error")` in non-development environments; implement a dedicated error controller that logs the exception server-side and returns only a generic, consistent error payload and appropriate HTTP status code (e.g., 500), without including exception details.
EXAMPLE:
Before (no global handler): exceptions bubble up and may show detailed error pages in production.
After (global handler): `app.UseExceptionHandler("/api/error");` and in `ErrorController.Handle()`, log `HttpContext.Features.Get<IExceptionHandlerFeature>()?.Error` and return a fixed JSON message with `StatusCode = 500`.
Centralized generic error handling and logging in ASP.NET Web API
WHAT: Unhandled exceptions in ASP.NET Web API can leak internal error details to clients or return inconsistent responses if not centrally logged and mapped to a generic error response.
WHY: Exposing stack traces or internal messages can reveal implementation details useful for attackers; inconsistent error formats complicate secure client handling and monitoring.
HOW: Implement a global ExceptionLogger to log all unhandled exceptions, and a global ExceptionHandler that always returns a generic, non-sensitive error body (e.g., fixed message) with appropriate HTTP status codes; register them via config.Services.Replace and enable customErrors in Web.config to hide detailed errors from remote clients.
EXAMPLE: Before (no global handler): exceptions bubble up and ASP.NET returns detailed error pages or raw messages. After: register GlobalErrorLogger and GlobalErrorHandler in WebApiConfig, have Handle() set context.Result to an IHttpActionResult that returns a fixed JSON message and 500/4xx code, and configure `<customErrors mode="RemoteOnly" defaultRedirect="~/ErrorPages/Oops.aspx" />`.
Secure HTTP Error Handling in ASP.NET Web API
WHAT: Returning detailed error messages or incorrect HTTP status codes can leak implementation details and obscure real server-side failures.
WHY: Information leakage helps attackers understand your stack and vulnerabilities; unmonitored 5xx errors can hide exploitable bugs and instability.
HOW: Return generic error messages without stack traces or internal details; use 4xx codes for client-caused errors and 5xx for unexpected server failures; log full details server-side and monitor/alert on 5xx trends.
EXAMPLE: Before (in controller): `return InternalServerError(ex); // returns stack trace in response`. After: `Log(ex); return StatusCode(HttpStatusCode.InternalServerError); // generic message to client`.
Java Bean Validation for Input Sanitization and Consistency
WHAT: Missing or inconsistent use of Java Bean Validation constraints (e.g., @Pattern, @Digits, @Min, @Max, @Size, @Email, @URL) on model fields, parameters, and return values can allow invalid or malicious input to propagate through application layers.
WHY: Unvalidated or weakly validated input can lead to injection, data integrity issues, and unexpected behavior across controllers, services, and persistence layers.
HOW: Define appropriate Bean Validation constraints on all externally influenced fields in your domain models and enable validation with @Valid at every boundary (controllers, service methods, constructors); centralize constraints on the model so they are enforced uniformly across all tiers.
EXAMPLE:
Before (no validation on title): public class Article { private String articleTitle; }
After (validated title): public class Article { @Pattern(regexp = "[a-zA-Z0-9 ]") private String articleTitle; }
Validation error handling in controllers
WHAT: Returning raw validation error messages directly in HTTP responses exposes internal validation details and potentially sensitive data to clients.
WHY: Attackers can use detailed error messages to infer validation rules, enumerate fields, or harvest sensitive information, aiding input tampering and other attacks.
HOW: Map validation errors to generic, user-safe messages; avoid returning framework/internal messages; log detailed errors server-side only; use structured error responses with sanitized text.
EXAMPLE:
Before: `return errorMessage += "ERROR: " + e.getDefaultMessage();`
After: `log.error("Validation failed: {}", e.getDefaultMessage()); return "Invalid input. Please correct the highlighted fields.";`
Input validation with bean validation constraints
WHAT: Failure to validate user-controlled input (e.g., review ratings, titles, nested bean fields) can allow out-of-range values or malformed data to be processed or stored.
WHY: Unvalidated or improperly validated input can lead to data integrity issues, logic bypass, and can contribute to injection or other downstream vulnerabilities.
HOW: Use bean validation annotations (@Min, @Max, @Pattern, @Email, etc.) on all user-controlled fields, enable cascading validation with @Valid on nested beans, and avoid deprecated/unsafe constraints such as @SafeHtml; ensure controllers check BindingResult for errors and reject invalid requests with appropriate HTTP status codes.
EXAMPLE: Before (no validation): `public class Review { private int reviewRating; }` / After: `public class Review { @Min(1) @Max(5) private int reviewRating; }` and in controller: `public String postReview(@Valid Review review, BindingResult result, HttpServletResponse response) { if (result.hasErrors()) { response.setStatus(HttpServletResponse.SC_BAD_REQUEST); return "Validation error"; } }`
Network segmentation between service tiers
WHAT: Failing to segment FRONTEND, MIDDLEWARE, and BACKEND networks and to restrict interservice access allows direct cross-tier and cross-service communication (e.g., FRONTEND of one system talking to MIDDLEWARE/BACKEND of another, or MIDDLEWARE directly reaching foreign databases).
WHY: Lack of segmentation and strict firewall rules enables lateral movement, unauthorized data access, and bypass of application-layer controls, increasing impact of any single compromise.
HOW: Place components into separate security zones (FRONTEND, MIDDLEWARE, BACKEND) and VLANs; configure firewalls so that: (1) FRONTEND ↔ MIDDLEWARE is only allowed within the same system; (2) MIDDLEWARE → BACKEND is only allowed to its own BACKEND; (3) direct access to BACKEND from FRONTEND or from other services’ segments is denied by default.
EXAMPLE: Before: firewall allows any FRONTEND → any DB on port 5432. After: firewall rule allows FRONTEND_A → MIDDLEWARE_A only, and MIDDLEWARE_A → DB_A only; all other cross-zone or cross-service DB access is denied.
Secure logging and log integrity
WHAT: Logs of applications and infrastructure must be transmitted to a separate logging server in an append‑only manner so that compromised systems cannot modify or delete existing log entries.
WHY: Prevents attackers who gain access to an application or host from erasing or tampering with evidence, hindering incident detection, investigation, and forensics.
HOW: Configure applications and services to send logs to a remote log collector (e.g., via syslog or similar protocols) that only accepts new log events and disallows remote modification or deletion; restrict direct write access to log storage to the logging service account only.
EXAMPLE: Before: application writes logs only to local files on the same host that it runs on; After: application writes to local logs and simultaneously forwards all log events to a hardened remote syslog server with append‑only permissions and no remote log-edit capability.
Unsafe Deserialization of Untrusted Data
WHAT: Deserializing untrusted or user-controlled data using native object deserialization mechanisms (e.g., PHP unserialize(), Python pickle/PyYAML/jsonpickle, Java Serializable/ObjectInputStream/XMLDecoder/XStream) can allow attackers to instantiate arbitrary classes or trigger dangerous behaviors.
WHY: Unsafe deserialization can lead to remote code execution, denial of service, access control bypass, data leakage, or clobbering of trusted fields.
HOW: Avoid native object deserialization for untrusted data; instead use safe data formats (e.g., JSON via json_encode/json_decode in PHP). In Java, restrict deserialization by overriding ObjectInputStream.resolveClass() to allow only an explicit allowlist of classes and use safer readObject replacements that validate input size and object count; mark sensitive fields in Serializable classes as private transient so they are never serialized or controlled by users.
EXAMPLE: Java before: `ObjectInputStream ois = new ObjectInputStream(in); MyObj o = (MyObj) ois.readObject();` After: subclass ObjectInputStream, override resolveClass() to check the requested class against an allowlist, and use that stream instead; declare `private transient double profit;` so it is not serialized.
Prevent unsafe Java object deserialization
WHAT: Unrestricted deserialization of Java domain objects (e.g., via java.io.ObjectInputStream) can allow construction of arbitrary object graphs, enabling gadget chains and remote code execution when untrusted data is deserialized.
WHY: Attackers can send crafted serialized streams that instantiate dangerous classes or invoke unexpected behavior, leading to RCE, data exfiltration, or application takeover.
HOW: For classes that must implement Serializable but must never be deserialized, declare a private final readObject(ObjectInputStream) that always throws; for allowed deserialization, subclass ObjectInputStream and override resolveClass to allow only a strict allowlist of expected types; where you cannot change code, use a javaagent or similar mechanism to harden ObjectInputStream globally (e.g., denylist known gadget classes) and avoid accepting serialized objects from untrusted sources.
EXAMPLE:
Before (unsafe): `ObjectInputStream ois = new ObjectInputStream(in); Object obj = ois.readObject();`
After (safer): `class SafeOIS extends ObjectInputStream { protected Class<?> resolveClass(ObjectStreamClass desc) throws IOException, ClassNotFoundException { if (!ALLOWED.contains(desc.getName())) throw new InvalidClassException("Unauthorized", desc.getName()); return super.resolveClass(desc); } }`
Unsafe deserialization of untrusted data in JSON, XML, YAML, and custom formats
WHAT: Deserialization libraries (fastjson, jackson-databind, Kryo, YamlBeans, XStream, SnakeYAML, json-io, XMLDecoder, Castor, .NET serializers) can deserialize attacker-controlled types or arbitrary classes when unsafe options are enabled (e.g., autotype, polymorphism, disabled class registration, UnsafeYamlConfig, relaxed allowlists, unsafe constructors, @type/type metadata).
WHY: Unsafe deserialization of untrusted input can lead to remote code execution, data exfiltration, or other critical compromise via gadget chains in the application or its dependencies.
HOW: Use only maintained, patched versions; disable features that allow arbitrary type resolution (autotype, polymorphic typing, @type, unsafe configs); require explicit class registration or allowlists; use safe constructors (e.g., SafeConstructor in SnakeYAML); never deserialize untrusted data into arbitrary types; in .NET, avoid TypeNameHandling/JavaScriptTypeResolver with user-controlled type names and audit any serializer where the type comes from user input.
EXAMPLE (Java, fastjson2): // UNSAFE: parserConfig.setAutoTypeSupport(true); JSON.parseObject(userJson, Object.class, parserConfig);
// SAFE: parserConfig.setAutoTypeSupport(false); JSON.parseObject(userJson, SafeDto.class, parserConfig);
Insecure .NET deserialization and attacker-controlled type resolution
WHAT: In .NET code that deserializes untrusted data, avoid BinaryFormatter and any deserialization where the target type or TypeNameHandling/JavaScriptTypeResolver is influenced by user-controlled or external data, as this can instantiate arbitrary or dangerous types during deserialization.
WHY: Insecure deserialization can lead to remote code execution, denial of service (e.g., modifying file attributes), or misuse of gadget types (e.g., ObjectDataProvider, PSObject) even before you can inspect the deserialized object.
HOW: Do not use BinaryFormatter; prefer DataContractSerializer or XmlSerializer and never let untrusted data select the type (no dynamic Type.GetType from external sources). For JSON.Net, set TypeNameHandling = None and, if type names must be used, enforce a strict allowlist via a custom SerializationBinder; do not use JavaScriptSerializer with JavaScriptTypeResolver. Restrict deserializable types to a minimal, audited allowlist and keep gadget-creating code separate from internet-facing deserialization code.
EXAMPLE: // Unsafe: attacker controls type
// var typeName = GetTransactionTypeFromDatabase();
// var s = new DataContractJsonSerializer(Type.GetType(typeName));
// Safe (pattern): use a fixed, known type or map an external key to a hardcoded allowlisted Type, and for JSON.Net always configure: settings.TypeNameHandling = TypeNameHandling.None.
Safe Deserialization Practices
WHAT: Insecure deserialization occurs when untrusted or unauthenticated data is deserialized into native objects, allowing attacker-controlled objects or custom deserialization logic to execute.
WHY: Malicious payloads can trigger arbitrary code execution, privilege escalation, or data tampering during or after deserialization.
HOW: Prefer pure data formats (e.g., JSON, XML) instead of native object serialization; use dedicated DTOs for data transfer; only deserialize data that is cryptographically signed and authenticated; reject any unsigned or tampered messages before deserialization.
EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe): deserialize arbitrary binary-serialized objects received over the network; After (safer): accept only JSON data, validate its schema, verify a digital signature or MAC on the message, then map the parsed data into simple DTO structures.
Microservices edge and service-level authorization
WHAT: Relying solely on edge-level (API gateway) authorization can allow direct, anonymous access to internal microservices if the gateway is bypassed, and creates a single point of failure for access control decisions.
WHY: An attacker who reaches internal services without passing through the gateway can invoke privileged operations, leading to data exposure, unauthorized actions, and violation of defense-in-depth.
HOW: Enforce mutual authentication (e.g., mTLS) between all clients and internal services, require valid access tokens on every service-to-service call, and implement authorization checks both at the API gateway (coarse-grained) and within each microservice (fine-grained).
EXAMPLE: Before: Internal service trusts any request from the internal network without token or client certificate checks. After: Internal service validates mTLS client cert and verifies/scopes an access token on every request, even when called from the API gateway.
Authorization policy freshness in centralized embedded PDP
WHAT: Risk of applying outdated authorization rules when microservices cache authorization decisions or hard-code authorization logic that must be changed in source code.
WHY: Stale or inconsistent policies can cause unauthorized access or denial of legitimate access across microservices.
HOW: Centralize policy definition; distribute and evaluate policies via an embedded PDP on the same host; cache only policies/attributes (not final decisions); ensure timely policy synchronization and avoid long-lived decision caches.
EXAMPLE: Before (risky): microservice caches allow/deny decisions per user/resource for long periods; After (safer): microservice uses an embedded PDP library that periodically refreshes policies from a central PAP and evaluates each request against the latest in-memory policy without caching final decisions.
Centralized, layered authorization and policy management
WHAT: Failing to centralize and externalize authorization policies (and instead hardcoding them in microservice code) leads to inconsistent, incomplete, and hard-to-maintain access control enforcement.
WHY: Inconsistent or ad-hoc authorization increases the risk of privilege escalation, bypassed checks, and policy drift across services, especially at scale.
HOW: Use a centralized, platform-level authorization solution with an embedded PDP and shared libraries; externalize policies in a dedicated policy language; enforce defense in depth (gateway/proxy, shared microservice libraries, and business-code checks); and establish formal procedures for policy development, approval, and rollout.
EXAMPLE: Before (bad): each microservice implements its own hardcoded role checks and custom middleware; policies differ between services. After (good): all services call a shared authorization library that queries a central policy repository, with policies versioned and managed by a dedicated platform security team.
Secure identity propagation in microservices
WHAT: Avoid propagating external access tokens directly to internal microservices; instead, propagate a separate, signed internal identity structure so internal services never accept or depend on external tokens.
WHY: Direct reuse of external tokens increases attack surface (e.g., token leakage, unintended exposure of internal services) and lets compromised or malicious services forge identities and bypass access control.
HOW: At the edge, authenticate the request, extract user identity (ID, roles, permissions), and issue a signed or encrypted internal token/structure using a secret from a key management system; configure internal services to accept only this internal format and validate its signature on every call.
EXAMPLE: Before: InternalService receives and validates the same JWT/cookie OAuth2 token used by external clients. After: EdgeService validates the external token, builds an internal “passport” object with userId and roles, signs it with HMAC using a KMS-managed key, and passes only this signed passport to InternalService, which verifies the signature and enforces authorization.
Secure identity propagation and logging in microservices
WHAT: Failure to securely propagate identity and logs in microservices can expose internal identity structures, allow token misuse, or cause loss of audit logs during outages or attacks.
WHY: Leaked internal identity representations or weak token validation can lead to impersonation and privilege abuse; lost or incomplete logs undermine accountability, traceability, and incident investigation.
HOW: Use an internal, signed identity representation (separate from external access tokens), verified and issued at the edge, propagated only between services, and never exposed to clients; choose online token validation for critical requests and offline validation only for non‑critical ones; perform service‑to‑service auth via mTLS or signed tokens over TLS; have each microservice log only to local stdout/stderr files and use a separate logging agent to ship logs to a central service to avoid data loss on logging subsystem failure.
EXAMPLE: Edge service verifies external token → issues signed internal identity object → passes it via headers to downstream services over TLS; each service logs locally (stdout/stderr) while a sidecar/agent tails the file and publishes to Kafka/NATS for centralized processing.
Secure Logging Architecture for Microservices
WHAT: Risk of data loss, spoofing, privilege escalation, and data exposure if microservices log directly over the network without authentication, access control, or sanitization.
WHY: Logging service or network failures and DoS can cause log loss; unprotected channels enable spoofing and traffic injection; unsanitized logs can leak sensitive data.
HOW: Write logs to a local file; use a same-host logging agent to ship logs asynchronously via a message broker; enforce mutual TLS between agent and broker; configure strict access control and least privilege on the broker; sanitize logs to remove sensitive data; include correlation IDs and structured/contextual fields.
EXAMPLE: Before: microservice → (HTTP) → central logger with raw request/response bodies. After: microservice → local file; logging agent (on same host) → mutual TLS → message broker with ACLs → central logger, with PII stripped and correlation_id added.
LDAP Injection Prevention
WHAT: LDAP queries are constructed by concatenating unsanitized user input into LDAP filters or DN strings, allowing attackers to alter the query logic and access or modify unintended directory data.
WHY: Successful LDAP injection can bypass authentication, escalate privileges, or read/modify sensitive directory entries, leading to unauthorized access and data compromise.
HOW: Never concatenate raw user input into LDAP queries; instead, use parameterized/typed LDAP APIs or frameworks that automatically escape input, apply correct LDAP encoding/escaping for all user-controlled values, enforce least-privilege LDAP credentials for the application, and validate user input with strict allow-lists.
EXAMPLE: Before (Java): `String filter = "(uid=" + userInput + ")"; ctx.search(base, filter, controls);` After: `String safeUid = LdapEncoder.filterEncode(userInput); String filter = "(uid=" + safeUid + ")"; ctx.search(base, filter, controls);`
LDAP query construction and escaping
WHAT: Untrusted input is directly concatenated into LDAP DNs or search filters without proper LDAP-specific escaping, allowing LDAP injection or malformed queries.
WHY: Attackers can alter LDAP queries to bypass authentication, escalate privileges, or access/modify unauthorized directory data.
HOW: Treat all LDAP-bound data as untrusted; normalize input, then validate with strict allowlists per field; use LDAP-specific escaping/encoding APIs (e.g., encodeForLDAP/encodeForDN, Encoder.LdapFilterEncode/LdapDistinguishedNameEncode) appropriate to context (search filter vs DN); disallow or escape LDAP/JNDI metacharacters (\ # + < > , ; " = and leading/trailing spaces in DNs; * ( ) \ NUL in filters) unless safely encoded.
EXAMPLE: In Java, do not build `String filter = "(&(sn=" + userSN + ")(userPassword=" + userPassword + "))";` directly; instead validate `userSN`/`userPassword` with allowlists and pass them through `encodeForLDAP` before concatenation.
Prevent LDAP injection in .NET and Java code by correctly encoding untrusted input before it is used in LDAP filters or distinguished names.
WHAT: Unvalidated or unencoded user-controlled data placed into LDAP filters or DNs can alter the query structure and lead to LDAP injection.
WHY: LDAP injection can expose or modify directory data, bypass authentication/authorization, or escalate privileges.
HOW: For Java, use OWASP ESAPI’s encodeForLDAP(String) and encodeForDN(String) on all untrusted input before inserting it into LDAP queries; for .NET, use Encoder.LdapFilterEncode(string) for filters and Encoder.LdapDistinguishedNameEncode(string[, bool, bool]) for DNs, or use frameworks like LINQ to LDAP that automatically encode inputs.
EXAMPLE (C#): // Before: filter = "(uid=" + userInput + ")";  // After: filter = "(uid=" + Encoder.LdapFilterEncode(userInput) + ")";
LDAP Injection Hardening for LDAP Clients
WHAT: LDAP queries are constructed or executed in a way that allows attacker-controlled input to alter the query, especially when using overly privileged bind accounts or allowing anonymous/unauthenticated binds.
WHY: Successful LDAP injection can expose or modify directory data, escalate privileges, or bypass authentication and authorization controls.
HOW: Use least-privilege LDAP bind accounts (no write or admin rights for query-only operations), disable or strictly restrict anonymous/unauthenticated binds, require bind authentication for all operations, and apply strict allow-list input validation on all user-controlled data before including it in LDAP queries.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): bind as a directory admin and allow anonymous binds for some operations; After (more secure): bind with a read-only service account, disable anonymous/unauthenticated binds, and validate all filter components against a strict allow-list before constructing LDAP filters.
gRPC Service Security Guideline
WHAT: gRPC services may be exposed to eavesdropping, impersonation, and unauthorized access if TLS, authentication, and authorization are not correctly implemented (e.g., plaintext transport, missing token checks, or no method-level permission checks).
WHY: Lack of transport encryption and strong authz/authn can lead to credential theft, data disclosure, service impersonation, and privilege escalation across microservices.
HOW: Always enable TLS (v1.2+) with strong ciphers in production, disable weak protocols, and use mTLS for service-to-service calls with short-lived, auto-rotated certificates; enforce authentication on every protected method using validated, short-lived tokens or API keys in metadata headers (not in method parameters); and implement least-privilege, method-level authorization based on roles/permissions.
EXAMPLE:
Before (insecure server): `s := grpc.NewServer()` with no interceptors.
After (secure server):
```go
creds, _ := credentials.NewServerTLSFromFile(certFile, keyFile)
s := grpc.NewServer(
grpc.Creds(creds),
grpc.UnaryInterceptor(authInterceptor), // validates JWT/API key + roles
)
```
Input validation and resource protection for gRPC services
WHAT: Missing or weak validation of Protocol Buffer messages and user inputs, unbounded message sizes, and lack of rate limiting/timeouts can lead to injection, memory exhaustion, and denial-of-service.
WHY: Attackers can exploit unvalidated data to perform SQL injection or send oversized/frequent requests that exhaust CPU, memory, or connections, causing outages and data compromise.
HOW: Validate all protobuf fields server-side (e.g., protoc-gen-validate, allowlists for strings), always use prepared statements for database access, enforce MaxRecvMsgSize/MaxSendMsgSize, implement per-client rate limiting, and configure strict request timeouts.
EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe SQL): `db.Query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '" + email + "'")`; After (safe): `db.QueryRow("SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = ?", email)` with prior `isValidEmail(email)` and gRPC server created with `grpc.MaxRecvMsgSize(...)` and a rate-limiting interceptor.
Secure error handling and logging for gRPC services
WHAT: Detailed error responses or logs that include sensitive data (e.g., stack traces, internal IDs, tokens) can expose system internals to attackers.
WHY: Exposed internals help attackers enumerate APIs, bypass controls, or reuse sensitive data, increasing the risk of compromise and data leakage.
HOW: Return generic, client-safe error messages mapped to appropriate gRPC status codes, while logging detailed errors server-side with structured, security-focused logs that exclude secrets and include correlation IDs.
EXAMPLE:
Before (insecure): return nil, status.Error(codes.Internal, fmt.Sprintf("db error: %v", err))
After (secure): log.Printf("db error for user %s: %v", getUserID(ctx), err); return nil, status.Error(codes.Internal, "internal server error")
gRPC service security testing and configuration
WHAT: Missing or misconfigured authentication, authorization, input validation, rate limiting, TLS, or error handling in gRPC services can allow unauthorized access, injection, resource exhaustion, or information disclosure.
WHY: These weaknesses enable attackers to bypass access controls, tamper with data, exhaust resources, or gain sensitive information, compromising confidentiality, integrity, and availability.
HOW: Require and verify auth on every gRPC method; enforce authorization boundaries; validate all message fields; implement and test rate limiting and message size limits; configure and verify TLS/ALPN and certificate handling; centralize security via interceptors/context; use framework security features and secure credential storage; avoid verbose error messages in production.
EXAMPLE: Before (Go): `grpc.NewServer()` with handlers doing no auth, no validation, and running over plaintext. After: create interceptors that check auth tokens from context, enforce per-method authorization, validate request fields, apply rate limiting, configure `grpc.Creds(credentials.NewTLS(tlsConfig))`, and ensure errors return generic messages without internal details.
Software Supply Chain Component Hardening
WHAT: Using vulnerable, misconfigured, or untrusted supply-chain components (e.g., VCS, CI/CD, build tools, package managers, third‑party libraries) can introduce malicious code, compromised builds, or unauthorized binaries into your software.
WHY: A single compromised component can undermine the integrity, confidentiality, or availability of the entire software system and all downstream consumers.
HOW: Inventory all SSC components; restrict and audit access to VCS/CI/CD/build systems; enforce branch protection and signed commits; pin and regularly scan dependencies; use trusted registries; require reproducible builds and signed artifacts; and monitor for unauthorized configuration or source changes.
EXAMPLE: Before: Build from any branch with unpinned dependencies from public registries and no access controls on CI. After: Build only from protected main/release branches, require code review and signed commits, pin dependency versions from vetted registries, and restrict CI credentials with least privilege.
Strong access control for software supply chain systems
WHAT: Inadequate access control for build, development, CI/CD, and version-control systems allows compromised or over-privileged accounts to inject malicious code, manipulate pipelines, or replace legitimate artifacts.
