HOW: Require MFA for all authentication mechanisms (web, API, mobile) and for high‑risk actions; implement risk‑based MFA prompts (e.g., new/high‑risk device/location); use strong factors such as FIDO2 passkeys; on failed MFA, offer alternate registered factors and notify the user with time/agent/location; design recovery with strong verification (e.g., pre‑issued one‑time recovery codes, multiple independent factors, verified postal delivery, or rigorously verified support workflows) and ensure no recovery path is weaker than normal MFA.
EXAMPLE: Before (web only): `POST /login` requires MFA, but `POST /api/login` accepts password only and support can disable MFA after a simple email request. After: both `/login` and `/api/login` require MFA; high‑risk actions trigger additional MFA; recovery uses pre‑generated one‑time codes or multiple pre‑registered factors plus strict identity checks, never a password‑only or email‑only path.
Multi-factor Authentication (MFA) and Account Recovery Hardening
WHAT: Weak or poorly designed MFA and account recovery flows (e.g., single weak factor, insecure recovery options, unvetted third-party MFA) can let attackers bypass authentication, especially if recovery is easier to compromise than normal login.
WHY: Compromise of MFA or recovery can lead to full account takeover across all relying applications, even if passwords are strong.
HOW: Provide multiple independent MFA factors and single-use recovery codes; avoid security questions as a factor; secure recovery via verified channels (postal mail, support with strong identity verification, or trusted-user vouching); and, when using third-party MFA, assess its security, isolation, and compromise impact before integrating.
EXAMPLE: Before: Allow password + weak security questions for both login and recovery. After: Require password + TOTP/hardware token for login; issue single-use recovery codes at MFA setup; disable security questions; and route account lockout recovery through verified postal codes or a documented high-assurance support process.
Multi-factor authentication implementation
WHAT: Insecure MFA implementations can introduce new vulnerabilities, such as backend servers becoming single points of failure, stolen tokens being usable without a PIN/device lock, insecure storage of backup seeds, or client certificates being reused across accounts or stolen from compromised workstations.
WHY: These weaknesses allow attackers to bypass MFA, impersonate users, or cause large-scale outages if central components fail.
HOW: Use standards-based TOTP/U2F protocols; require device/PIN protection for physical tokens; ensure TOTP seeds and backup codes are stored and backed up securely; avoid custom token variants; harden and redundantly deploy backend MFA services; bind client certificates to individual accounts and protect certificate stores on endpoints.
EXAMPLE: Before: Accept any valid client certificate for any account and allow login if certificate is present. After: On enrollment, bind a specific certificate fingerprint to a single user ID and, on login, verify both the password and that the presented certificate fingerprint matches the stored one for that user.
Multi-factor authentication (MFA) method selection and implementation
WHAT: Choosing weak or inappropriate MFA factors (e.g., SMS, phone calls, or unsecured email) for applications handling PII or financial data, or storing authentication certificates insecurely on user workstations, can allow attackers to bypass authentication via phishing, SIM swapping, device compromise, or email account takeover.
WHY: Compromised or spoofed MFA factors can lead to full account takeover, exposure of PII, financial fraud, and long-term identity theft, especially when biometric or certificate data is stolen and cannot be easily changed.
HOW: For applications with PII or financial risk, avoid SMS/phone-based MFA and unauthenticated email links/codes; prefer phishing-resistant methods such as smartcards, hardware tokens, or well-managed client certificates backed by a secure PKI. Ensure certificates and private keys are stored in secure hardware (e.g., smartcards/TPM), enforce MFA on email accounts used for verification, rate-limit and monitor OTP/message requests, and design biometric storage and matching to use secure, encrypted, and revocable templates.
EXAMPLE: Before (weak MFA): `sendSmsCode(user.phone); // used to protect banking login`
After (stronger MFA): `redirectToWebAuthnAssertion(user.id); // use FIDO2/WebAuthn with hardware-backed keys for banking login`
Biometric and Location-Based Authentication Configuration
WHAT: Risk of weak or privacy-invasive MFA implementations when using biometrics, IP/geolocation, geofencing, or behavioral profiling (e.g., over-trusted IP allowlists, poorly protected biometric data, or inaccurate behavior models).
WHY: Can lead to account takeover, insider abuse, privacy violations, and irreversible compromise of biometric identifiers if data or trust boundaries are breached.
HOW: Treat biometrics and behavioral data as highly sensitive; encrypt at rest and in transit; avoid using them as the sole factor; restrict and regularly review trusted IP ranges and geofences; require additional factors for high-risk locations; account for VPN/relay obfuscation; tune and monitor behavioral systems to minimize false positives and adapt to user changes.
EXAMPLE: When implementing IP-based conditional access, only allow authentication from a small, audited set of corporate CIDR ranges and always require a second factor (e.g., hardware token) even from trusted IPs, instead of granting full access based solely on source IP.
Adaptive or Risk-Based Authentication Hardening
WHAT: Risk-based authentication can be bypassed if risk signals (e.g., IP, device fingerprint, behavioral biometrics) are spoofable or if fallback flows are weaker than the primary MFA, allowing attackers to gain access during high-risk events.
WHY: Weak or spoofable risk evaluation and fallback mechanisms enable account takeover, especially during anomalous logins, account recovery, or suspicious activity, undermining the entire authentication scheme.
HOW: Use multiple independent, hard-to-spoof risk signals; treat high-risk events by enforcing strong MFA or denying access; ensure fallback methods (e.g., SMS, email recovery) are at least as strong as primary MFA; regularly review and tune risk rules against real attack patterns.
EXAMPLE: Before: On high-risk login, allow password reset via email link without MFA. After: On high-risk login, require strong MFA (e.g., FIDO2 key or app-based OTP) and block password reset or account recovery unless the same strong factor is successfully verified.
Avoid leaking secrets when publishing npm packages
WHAT: Secrets (API keys, passwords, .env files) may be unintentionally included in published npm tarballs due to misconfigured .gitignore/.npmignore or missing allowlists.
WHY: Exposed secrets in public packages enable account takeover, data theft, or abuse of external services.
HOW: Ensure all secret-bearing files are excluded via .npmignore (not only .gitignore), or preferably use the package.json "files" allowlist to include only safe files; review the publish contents with npm publish --dry-run before actual publication.
EXAMPLE: Before: relying only on .gitignore and forgetting to update .npmignore, causing .env to be published. After: add .env to .npmignore and/or configure "files": ["dist", "index.js"] in package.json and verify with npm publish --dry-run.
Minimize npm script-based supply-chain attacks
WHAT: Malicious npm packages can execute arbitrary commands via lifecycle run-scripts (e.g., postinstall) during installation, compromising systems that install them.
WHY: Attackers can steal tokens, exfiltrate data, or run arbitrary code in your CI/CD or developer machines via these scripts.
HOW: Always vet third-party modules (author, downloads, repo, issues); delay adopting brand-new releases; review changelogs before upgrading; install with `--ignore-scripts` for untrusted packages; set `ignore-scripts=true` in project or global `.npmrc` where feasible.
EXAMPLE: Before: `npm install some-package` (runs its install scripts). After: `npm install some-package --ignore-scripts` and configure `.npmrc` with `ignore-scripts=true` for environments that must not execute third-party scripts.
Use a local npm proxy
WHAT: Relying directly on the public npm registry for all installs can expose you to supply-chain attacks, unavailable dependencies, and unvetted package access.
WHY: A compromised or unavailable upstream registry, or a malicious package/version, can lead to code execution in your build/CI, data exfiltration, or production compromise.
HOW: Configure npm to use a private/local registry proxy (e.g., Verdaccio) with authentication, access control, and scoped routing to upstream registries; cache tarballs locally and restrict which external registries and packages are allowed.
EXAMPLE: (shell)
Before: npm install
After: npm set registry http://localhost:4873 && npm install
npm 2FA, token management, and typosquatting defenses
WHAT: Accounts and CI systems can be compromised if npm logins lack 2FA, if author tokens are overly privileged or widely exposed, or if malicious typosquatted packages are installed and execute install scripts.
WHY: Attackers can steal credentials or tokens, publish or alter packages, access private modules, exfiltrate environment variables (e.g., secrets in process.env), or run arbitrary code during install.
HOW: Enable npm 2FA (auth-only or auth-and-writes) via the UI or `npm profile enable-2fa`, store emergency codes securely, create least-privilege tokens (e.g., `--read-only`, `--cidr`), regularly list/revoke tokens, stay logged out by default on shared machines, verify package names/metadata before installing, and use `--ignore-scripts` when installing untrusted packages.
EXAMPLE: `npm profile enable-2fa auth-and-writes` to protect login and write actions; `npm token create --read-only --cidr=192.0.2.0/24` for a restricted CI token; `npm info <pkg>` to inspect a package; `npm install some-package --ignore-scripts` to avoid running install scripts from untrusted modules.
OAuth 2.0 Client and Authorization Server Security
WHAT: Do not expose open redirectors (URLs that forward to arbitrary URIs from query parameters), and prevent authorization code interception and CSRF in OAuth 2.0 flows.
WHY: Open redirects and missing CSRF/PKCE protections can let attackers exfiltrate authorization codes/tokens, impersonate users, or redeem stolen codes.
HOW: Validate redirect URIs against a strict allowlist (no dynamic domains/paths), use PKCE for all public clients, use nonce or state-bound CSRF tokens, and avoid forwarding/redirecting any request that may contain user credentials.
EXAMPLE: Before: /redirect?next={user_url} → blindly redirect to next. After: /redirect?next={id} → map id to a fixed, server-side allowlisted URL; enable PKCE on the client and require code_verifier at the token endpoint.
OAuth2/OIDC Token Replay and Privilege Control
WHAT: Authorization and resource servers may allow replay or misuse of authorization codes, tokens, or refresh tokens if PKCE, nonce, sender-constraining, and least-privilege scopes/audiences are not correctly enforced.
WHY: Replay or misuse of tokens can let attackers impersonate users, escalate privileges, or access unintended resources, even without knowing user credentials.
HOW: Use PKCE with a transaction-specific, non-exposed code_challenge and enforce matching code_verifier; use OIDC nonce bound to client/user agent; reject token requests with code_verifier if no prior code_challenge; avoid implicit and password grants; sender-constrain access and refresh tokens (e.g., mTLS, DPoP, rotation); restrict tokens by audience, scope, and actions, and verify these on every resource server request.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): client uses implicit grant, no PKCE, broad "scope=read write", access token valid for multiple APIs and accepted without audience/scope checks. After (more secure): client uses authorization code + PKCE (S256), includes nonce, AS issues sender-constrained tokens with "scope=read:orders" and "aud=orders-api", and the orders API rejects any token whose aud/scope do not match the requested operation.
OAuth 2.0 Authorization Server and Client Security
WHAT: Insecure OAuth configurations such as using the Resource Owner Password Credentials grant, allowing client-controlled identifiers/claims, weak client authentication, or non-TLS/HTTP redirect URIs expose user credentials and tokens to attackers.
WHY: These issues can lead to credential theft, impersonation of resource owners or clients, token leakage, and mix-up attacks, compromising accounts and protected resources.
HOW: Do not use the Resource Owner Password Credentials grant; enforce strong client authentication with asymmetric methods (e.g., mTLS, private_key_jwt); prevent clients from setting or influencing client_id, sub, or similar identity claims; require end-to-end TLS and reject authorization responses and redirect URIs over plain HTTP (except loopback for native apps).
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): allow grant_type=password and register redirect_uri="http://example.com/callback" with client-chosen client_id. After (secure): disable grant_type=password, require mTLS or private_key_jwt, server-generated client_id and sub, and only accept redirect_uri values with https scheme (or loopback HTTP for native apps).
Prototype Pollution Prevention in JavaScript
WHAT: Prototype pollution occurs when attacker-controlled input can modify object prototypes (e.g., via __proto__, constructor.prototype), leading to unexpected properties or behavior across the application.
WHY: Polluted prototypes can cause unauthorized data access, privilege escalation, logic corruption, or even remote code execution when polluted properties are later trusted.
HOW: Prefer Map/Set over plain objects for key/value storage; when objects are required, create them with Object.create(null) or {__proto__: null}; consider Object.freeze()/Object.seal() on built-in prototypes (after verifying libraries don’t rely on extending them); in Node.js, use --disable-proto=delete to remove __proto__ as a defense-in-depth measure.
EXAMPLE: Before (vulnerable): const opts = {}; opts[userInputKey] = userInputVal;
After (safer): const opts = Object.create(null); opts[userInputKey] = userInputVal;
Least-Privilege Authorization Design
WHAT: Failing to enforce least privilege allows users or services to access resources or perform actions beyond what their role or task requires.
WHY: Excessive privileges enable horizontal or vertical privilege abuse, leading to unauthorized data access, modification, or destructive operations with potentially severe business impact.
HOW: Define fine-grained roles/permissions per business function; assign each user/service only the minimal permissions needed; regularly review and revoke unused or unnecessary privileges; separate duties so peer roles cannot access each other’s sensitive data by default.
EXAMPLE: N/A
Least privilege enforcement in application design
WHAT: Failure to enforce least privilege in an application (e.g., granting components or users broader access rights than required) exposes sensitive resources.
WHY: Excessive privileges increase the blast radius of any compromise, enabling unauthorized access, data exfiltration, or abuse of critical operations.
HOW: During architecture, design, and throughout the SDLC, explicitly define minimal required permissions for each component/user, implement role-based or attribute-based access control, and regularly review and reduce granted privileges to match actual needs.
EXAMPLE: (no language specified; define roles like “read-only-reporting” vs. “admin” and ensure code paths use the least-privileged role needed for each operation).
Access Control Design and Enforcement
WHAT: Missing or inconsistent authorization rules (e.g., no rule, wrong rule, or skipped check) allow users to perform operations or access resources beyond their intended permissions.
WHY: Leads to privilege escalation, data disclosure, or unauthorized modification when any request bypasses or misapplies access control.
HOW: Define clear trust boundaries and least-privilege permissions per user/role/attribute and resource/operation; configure deny-by-default for unmatched requests; centralize and enforce permission checks on every request using framework-level filters/middleware; regularly test and review permissions to detect privilege creep.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): `if (user.isLoggedIn()) { return getAccount(request.accountId); }` After (secure): `if (acl.canRead(user, request.accountId)) { return getAccount(request.accountId); } else { return AccessDenied; }`
Framework and Third-Party Authorization Configuration
WHAT: Risk of broken authorization when relying on third‑party frameworks/libraries (e.g., filters/middleware) with default, missing, or misunderstood authorization configuration, or with vulnerable components.
WHY: Misconfiguration or latent vulnerabilities can let attackers bypass intended access controls, leading to unauthorized data access or operations.
HOW: Define authorization requirements first, then select and configure frameworks to meet them; avoid default configs, add custom authorization logic where needed, and test configuration behavior in your environment; continuously monitor dependencies (e.g., via Dependency Check, vendor/NVD feeds) and update or replace vulnerable components.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): relying solely on a framework’s default authorization middleware with no custom rules or tests; After (secure): explicitly configuring authorization policies/routes, adding custom checks for app-specific rules, and including dependency vulnerability scanning in the CI/CD pipeline.
OWASP C7: Enforce Access Controls
WHAT: Missing or improperly performed role checks in RBAC (especially without role hierarchies and with chained role checks) can grant users too much or too little access.
WHY: Incorrect access control decisions can expose sensitive data or functions to unauthorized users or block legitimate users, violating least privilege.
HOW: Prefer ABAC or ReBAC for fine-grained, object-level, and multi-factor access decisions; centralize and standardize access checks; avoid ad-hoc chained role checks and ensure every protected action is guarded by a single, well-defined policy.
EXAMPLE: Before (RBAC): `if (user.hasAnyRole("SUPERUSER","ADMIN","ACCT_MANAGER")) { deleteAccount(id); }` After (ABAC/ReBAC): `if (policyEngine.allows(user, "delete", account)) { deleteAccount(id); }`
Role-based access control checks in large systems
WHAT: Missing, incomplete, or ad-hoc role checks (e.g., chaining multiple `hasRole`/`hasAnyRole` calls without a clear policy) can grant users too much or too little access.
WHY: Incorrect access control enables privilege escalation, data exposure, or denial of legitimate operations, undermining system security and compliance.
HOW: Centralize authorization logic; define and enforce access-control policies in a single layer (e.g., policy engine or middleware) instead of scattered inline checks; avoid role explosion by using structured policies (e.g., ABAC/ReBAC) and retrieving roles/attributes server-side rather than trusting client-sent roles.
EXAMPLE: Before (bad): `if (user.hasAnyRole("SUPERUSER","ADMIN","ACCT_MANAGER")) { deleteAccount(id); }` → After (better): `if (policyEngine.isAllowed(user, "account:delete", id)) { deleteAccount(id); }`
CWE-639: Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key
WHAT: Failure to enforce authorization on object lookups when identifiers (e.g., account IDs, primary keys) are user-controlled and guessable, allowing access to other users’ resources.
WHY: Attackers can tamper with IDs to perform IDOR attacks, causing horizontal or vertical privilege escalation and unauthorized data access.
HOW: Avoid exposing direct identifiers when possible; use authenticated user context (e.g., securely implemented JWT or server-side session) or user/session-specific indirect references; always perform per-request authorization checks on the specific object being accessed, not just on the object type.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): GET /accountTransactions?acct_id=523 → server returns any account 523 data if it exists. After (secure): server derives account ID from the authenticated session/JWT and/or verifies that the requesting user is authorized to access acct_id=523 before returning data.
CWE-280: Improper Handling of Insufficient Permissions or Privileges
WHAT: Authorization failures and exceptions are not consistently handled, leaving the application in an unstable or unpredictable state and potentially exposing sensitive error details.
WHY: Unhandled or mis-handled authorization failures can lead to authorization bypass, information disclosure (e.g., logs, stack traces), and broader compromise of the application.
HOW: Centralize server-side authorization checks and failure handling; always catch and handle access-control-related exceptions; on failure, return only appropriate HTTP status codes and generic messages; verify that no failure path leaves partial actions applied or exposes sensitive data.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): `if (!user.canAccess(resource)) { throw e; }` where `e` propagates to a default error page showing stack traces or logs. After (secure): `if (!user.canAccess(resource)) { logger.warn("Unauthorized access attempt"); return Response.status(403).body("Access denied."); }`
CWE-778 and CWE-779: Insufficient and Excessive Logging
WHAT: Logging too little misses security-relevant events; logging too much records unnecessary or sensitive data and strains resources.
WHY: Insufficient logging hides attacks and hinders incident response; excessive logging can leak sensitive information and cause operational issues.
HOW: Define per-application logging requirements; log security-relevant events with consistent, parseable formats; exclude secrets/PII unless strictly required; periodically review logs and configuration.
EXAMPLE: Before: logging full request bodies and session tokens for all requests. After: logging only event type, timestamp, user ID, and request metadata, explicitly redacting tokens and sensitive fields.
XSS filter evasion and incomplete input filtering
WHAT: Relying solely on input filtering to block Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) allows attackers to bypass filters with crafted payloads and still inject executable script into rendered pages.
WHY: Successful XSS lets attackers run arbitrary JavaScript in victims’ browsers, leading to session theft, account takeover, data exfiltration, and UI redressing.
HOW: Do not depend on input filters alone; use context-aware output encoding, safe templating, Content Security Policy (CSP), and, where possible, avoid rendering user-controlled HTML/JS entirely.
EXAMPLE: Before (vulnerable): server stores user input and outputs it directly into HTML. After (safer): server stores raw input but encodes it for HTML/attribute/JS context on output and enforces a restrictive CSP.
Cross-Site Scripting via HTML/JS Injection and Obfuscated Payloads
WHAT: User-controlled data is injected into HTML attributes, event handlers, URLs (e.g., javascript:), or script contexts without proper encoding/validation, allowing execution of arbitrary JavaScript, including via malformed tags, missing quotes, character references, or split keywords.
WHY: An attacker can run arbitrary code in the victim’s browser, steal cookies or tokens, perform actions as the user, deface content, or pivot to further attacks.
HOW: Treat all user input as untrusted; contextually encode output (HTML, attribute, JS, URL) using a vetted library; disallow javascript: URLs and inline event handlers for user-controlled data; enforce a strict allowlist for attributes and protocols; normalize and decode input before filtering; use CSP to block inline scripts where possible.
EXAMPLE: Before (vulnerable): `<a onmouseover=alert(document.cookie)>link</a>` with `title` from user. After (safe): `<a href="/profile" title="{{ html_attr_escape(user_title) }}">link</a>` and reject/strip any `javascript:` or event-handler attributes from user input.
XSS filter evasion via encoded control characters and non-alphanumeric separators in HTML/JS
WHAT: User-controlled HTML attributes (e.g., href, onload, src) can execute JavaScript even when “javascript:” or event handlers are filtered, by inserting control chars (TAB, LF, CR, NULL), spaces, or non-alphanumeric symbols between tokens (e.g., `jav	ascript:`, `java\0script:`, `onload!#$...=alert()`).
WHY: Incomplete or pattern-based filtering can be bypassed, leading to stored or reflected XSS, allowing session theft, account takeover, or arbitrary actions in the user’s browser.
HOW: Do not attempt to “clean” or pattern-filter HTML/JS; instead, strictly encode untrusted data into text-only contexts (HTML-escape, attribute-escape, JS-escape as appropriate), disallow `javascript:` URLs and inline event handlers entirely for user input, and use a vetted HTML sanitizer or templating system that enforces an allowlist of tags/attributes and normalizes/decodes before checking.
EXAMPLE: Before (vulnerable): `<a href="{{ user_url }}">Click</a>` where `user_url` is only regex-filtered for `javascript:`. After (safer): validate `user_url` as an absolute/relative HTTP(S) URL on the server, reject any non-HTTP(S) schemes, and HTML-escape it before insertion, or render only server-generated URLs and place user input in text nodes, not in href/src/event attributes.
XSS handling in HTML/JavaScript output
WHAT: User-controlled data is injected into HTML or JavaScript contexts without strict context-aware encoding and tag/attribute validation, allowing XSS via malformed tags, missing closing tags, protocol-based URLs (e.g., javascript:), event handlers, or escaping tricks that bypass naive filters (e.g., bracket-counting, regex-only checks).
WHY: Attackers can execute arbitrary script in the victim’s browser, leading to session theft, account takeover, data exfiltration, CSRF, and full UI compromise.
HOW: Use a vetted, context-aware encoding library for every sink (HTML body, attribute, URL, JS string); disallow javascript:/vbscript:/data: URLs and inline event handlers; never concatenate untrusted data into <script>, <style>, or tag/attribute names; implement allowlists for tags/attributes/URL schemes; and use modern CSP (no inline script, no unsafe-eval).
EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe): `<script>var a = "{{userInput}}";</script>` and `<img src="{{userUrl}}">`
After (safe): `<script>var a = "{{encodeForJS(userInput)}}";</script>` and `<img src="{{encodeForHTMLAttr(userUrl)}}" />` with server-side checks rejecting non-HTTP(S) schemes.
Event handler abuse in web applications
WHAT: Untrusted script or HTML bound to DOM event handlers (e.g., onClick, onFocus, onKeyDown, onBeforeCopy, onDrop) can execute when user actions or programmatic triggers (execCommand, print, drag/drop, focus changes) fire those events, leading to unintended code execution.
WHY: This enables cross-site scripting (XSS), data exfiltration, clipboard or file abuse, and UI redressing by running attacker-controlled code in the user’s browser with the application’s privileges.
HOW: Never insert untrusted data into event handler attributes or inline JavaScript; use safe DOM APIs and frameworks that auto-escape; prefer addEventListener with static handler functions; validate and sanitize any dynamic HTML; disable or restrict dangerous commands (e.g., execCommand, window.print) where possible and enforce Content Security Policy (CSP) to block inline event handlers.
EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe): `<div onClick="doSearch('<?= $_GET['q'] ?>')">Search</div>`; After (safer, JS): `const q = sanitize(input); document.getElementById('btn').addEventListener('click', () => doSearch(q));`
Event handler XSS via DOM events
WHAT: Untrusted data is bound directly to DOM event handler attributes (e.g., onLoad, onClick, onKeyDown, onPaste), allowing attacker-controlled JavaScript to execute when the corresponding event fires.
WHY: This enables cross-site scripting (XSS), letting attackers run arbitrary code in the user’s browser, steal data, hijack sessions, or perform actions as the user.
HOW: Never concatenate or assign user-controlled strings into event handler attributes or properties; instead, keep HTML static and attach handlers via addEventListener to trusted functions, and strictly validate/encode any data that influences event-driven behavior.
EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe): `<img src="?q=...${userInput}..." onload="${userInput}">` → After (safer): `<img id="avatar" src="/img/default.png">` and in JS: `document.getElementById('avatar').addEventListener('load', safeOnLoadHandler);`
Event-driven script execution risks in web handlers
WHAT: Event handlers like `onSelect`, `onSubmit`, `onUnload`, `onStorage`, and media/timing events can be programmatically triggered by attackers to execute attached scripts without explicit user intent.
WHY: Malicious triggering of these events can lead to unauthorized actions (e.g., auto-submission, navigation, media control), data leakage, or XSS-like behavior when handlers process untrusted data.
HOW: Treat all event-triggered input as untrusted; avoid side effects directly in handlers, require explicit user confirmation for sensitive actions, validate and sanitize any data used in handlers, and disable or ignore events that can be auto-fired by script when not strictly needed.
EXAMPLE: Before: `element.onselect = () => form.submit();` After: `element.onselect = () => showConfirmDialog(() => form.submit());`
Cross-Site Scripting via Styles, Meta, Frames, and Encodings
WHAT: Application reflects or stores untrusted HTML/CSS/attributes (e.g., STYLE tags/attributes, background URLs, CSS expressions, META refresh, IFRAME/FRAME/TABLE/TD/DIV tags, US-ASCII–encoded payloads) without proper sanitization, allowing injected JavaScript execution (XSS).
WHY: Attackers can run arbitrary script in the victim’s browser, leading to session theft, account takeover, CSRF, data exfiltration, defacement, and drive‑by attacks.
HOW: Treat all user-controlled content as untrusted; HTML-encode by default, and when HTML is required, sanitize with a robust, actively maintained library that removes scripts, event handlers, javascript: URLs, CSS expressions, META refresh, and dangerous tags/attributes; enforce a restrictive Content Security Policy (disallow inline script, javascript: URLs, and unsafe CSS features); avoid US-ASCII or unusual encodings for user input, and normalize/validate before output.
EXAMPLE (HTML/JS):
// Vulnerable: directly inserting user HTML/CSS
element.innerHTML = userInput;
// Safe: encode or sanitize first
element.textContent = userInput; // or: element.innerHTML = DOMPurify.sanitize(userInput);
Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) via HTML/Script Injection
WHAT: User-controlled input is inserted into HTML, attributes, URLs, CSS, XML, or SSI/PHP contexts without proper encoding or filtering, allowing attackers to inject script or HTML that executes in the victim’s browser (e.g., via DIV styles, BASE/OBJECT/IMG tags, XML islands, SSI/PHP, or renamed .js files).
WHY: Malicious scripts can run with the user’s privileges, enabling credential theft, session hijacking, unauthorized actions (e.g., admin commands via IMG requests), data exfiltration, or malware delivery.
HOW: Treat all user input as untrusted; for each output context (HTML body, attribute, URL, CSS, JS, XML, SSI, etc.) apply strict allowlists and context-appropriate escaping/encoding; disable or strip dangerous constructs (e.g., `javascript:`, `expression`, event handlers, `OBJECT/APPLET/EMBED` where not needed); avoid reflecting raw input into SSI/PHP or file paths; use a vetted XSS protection library or framework output-encoding APIs.
EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe, HTML context): `echo "<div>" . $_GET['name'] . "</div>";` After (PHP with HTML encoding): `echo "<div>" . htmlspecialchars($_GET['name'], ENT_QUOTES | ENT_SUBSTITUTE, 'UTF-8') . "</div>";`
XSS filter and URL validation evasion
WHAT: Application blocks or rewrites specific URLs (e.g., `http://www.google.com/`) or patterns using naive string/regex checks, allowing attackers to bypass filters via alternate encodings (IP, DWORD, hex, octal, Base64, mixed encodings), protocol shortcuts (`//`), CNAME changes, or content-replace side effects (e.g., `java&\#x09;script:` → `javascript:`).
WHY: Attackers can still load malicious external resources or execute JavaScript (XSS), despite apparent URL restrictions, leading to account compromise, data theft, or full session hijacking.
HOW: Do not rely on blacklist string/regex filters; instead, fully normalize and decode URLs (all encodings, protocol shorthands, host variants) using a robust URL parser, then enforce an allowlist of schemes and hosts; never transform attacker-controlled strings in ways that can create dangerous tokens (e.g., turning `java&\#x09;script:` into `javascript:`); prefer server-side mapping of IDs to trusted URLs over passing raw URLs from users.
EXAMPLE: Before (vulnerable): `if (url.indexOf("http://www.google.com/") !== -1) reject();` After (safer): `const u = new URL(normalize(url)); if (!["https:"].includes(u.protocol)) reject(); if (!["www.google.com"].includes(u.hostname)) reject();`
Cross-Site Scripting and Unvalidated Redirect Parameters
WHAT: Application trusts user-controlled parameters (e.g., content_type, param) in links, HTML, JavaScript, and redirects without strict validation or proper context-specific encoding, enabling reflected or stored XSS and open-redirect-based XSS.
WHY: Attackers can execute arbitrary JavaScript in victims’ browsers, steal cookies or sensitive data, perform actions as the user, or redirect users to malicious sites.
HOW: Treat all query/path parameters as untrusted; validate them with strict allowlists (e.g., numeric IDs, fixed enums, known URLs), reject or sanitize unexpected values, and always apply context-appropriate encoding (HTML, HTML attribute, JS, URL) before output; never concatenate raw user input into header('Location...') or client-side redirects.
EXAMPLE: Before (PHP redirect): `header('Location: '.$_GET['param']);` → After: `if (!in_array($_GET['param'], $allowedPaths, true)) { http_response_code(400); exit; } header('Location: '.$allowedPaths[$_GET['param']]);`
GraphQL Input Validation and Injection/DoS Prevention
WHAT: User-controlled GraphQL inputs are passed into HTTP requests, database queries, or other interpreters without strict validation, allowing injection (SQL/NoSQL/OS/LDAP/XML) or overly expensive queries that cause DoS.
WHY: Unvalidated or improperly handled input can lead to data theft, data corruption, remote command execution, request smuggling, or API unavailability through resource exhaustion.
HOW: Validate all incoming data with allowlists and strict GraphQL types (scalars, enums, custom validators, schemas for mutation inputs); use a single internal character encoding; reject invalid input without leaking details; for interpreter-bound data, use safe APIs (parameterized queries, correctly used ORMs/ODMs) or robust escaping/encoding libraries; avoid using user input to control hosts/resources unless absolutely required.
EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe): `db.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + args.name + "'");` After (safer): `db.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = $1", [args.name]);`
GraphQL DoS Mitigation via Query Limiting, Timeouts, and Cost Controls
WHAT: Unbounded GraphQL query depth, object counts, and execution time allow attackers to craft expensive queries (e.g., deeply nested or requesting huge lists) that exhaust CPU/memory and cause Denial of Service.
WHY: Excessive resource consumption from a single or few requests can make the API unresponsive, impacting availability and potentially other co‑hosted services.
HOW: Enforce maximum query depth and per-field item counts, add application-level timeouts for query/resolver execution, perform query cost analysis with a maximum allowed cost, and add rate limiting, batching, caching, and pagination; use framework tools such as MaxQueryDepthInstrumentation (graphql-java) or graphql-depth-limit / graphql-input-number (JavaScript).
EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe): allow any query depth and `posts(first: 99999999)` with no timeout or cost checks. After (safer): configure depth/amount limiters, reject queries exceeding thresholds, and wrap resolvers with a 10-second timeout that aborts execution and logs a timeout error.
GraphQL API Access Control and Resource Limiting
WHAT: Missing or weak access control, query complexity limits, rate limiting, and resource limits in a GraphQL API can allow attackers to enumerate data, perform IDOR/BOLA/BFLA attacks, or cause DoS via expensive queries or high request volume.
WHY: Without these controls, unauthorized users may read/modify other users’ data and a single client can exhaust CPU, memory, or backend capacity, degrading or taking down the service.
HOW: Enforce authorization on every resolver (both edges and nodes) using RBAC or similar; disable introspection and GraphiQL in production/public environments; configure query cost/complexity limits (e.g., MaxQueryComplexityInstrumentation, graphql-cost-analysis, graphql-validation-complexity); apply rate limiting per IP/user via WAF/API gateway/web server; and set OS/container-level CPU/memory limits (e.g., cgroups, ulimits, Docker resource limits).
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure resolver): `user(id: $id) { return db.findUserById(id); }` with introspection and no rate limiting. After (secure resolver): `user(id: $id, ctx) { requireAuth(ctx); requireRole(ctx, 'user'); assertOwnResource(ctx.userId, id); enforceQueryCost(ctx); return db.findUserById(id); }` with introspection disabled, gateway rate limiting, and container CPU/memory caps.
Broken object and field-level access control in GraphQL
WHAT: Failing to enforce authorization when accessing objects or fields by ID (including unintended `node`/`nodes` query fields) or when fetching/mutating data allows callers to read or modify resources they should not access, and batching many such operations in a single request can amplify abuse.
WHY: This leads to Broken Object Level Authorization/IDOR, data leakage, unauthorized data modification, enumeration of sensitive objects (users, emails, IDs), brute forcing of secrets, and application-level DoS that may evade traditional rate limits and security tooling.
HOW: For every resolver that reads or writes data (including ID-based lookups and mutations), perform explicit per-object and per-field authorization checks based on the authenticated user and intended access level; remove or disable unintended generic accessors like `node`/`nodes` or wrap them with strict auth; and enforce server-side limits on GraphQL complexity, depth, number of operations, and number of objects per request so that batching cannot exceed safe thresholds.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure resolver): `droid(id) { return db.droids.findById(id); }` — After (secure resolver): `droid(id, ctx) { const d = db.droids.findById(id); if (!canViewDroid(ctx.user, d)) throw new ForbiddenError(); return d; }` and configure the GraphQL server to reject requests whose total cost (fields × objects × operations) exceeds a defined limit.
Mitigating GraphQL Batching and Insecure Defaults
WHAT: Unrestricted GraphQL batching and insecure default configurations (verbose errors, unrestricted introspection/GraphiQL) allow brute-force, enumeration, and denial-of-service attacks by letting attackers batch many sensitive operations or discover schema details.
WHY: Attackers can brute-force usernames/emails/tokens, overwhelm the backend with large batched queries, and map internal schema and fields, increasing the impact and ease of exploitation.
HOW: Implement code-level per-request limits on number of objects/operations; disallow batching for sensitive objects (usernames, emails, passwords, OTPs, session tokens); cap concurrent/batched operations; disable stack traces and debug error messages in production; and disable or tightly restrict introspection and GraphiQL to trusted environments or authenticated/admin users only.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): GraphQL server with no per-request limits, batching allowed for all types, debug errors enabled, and public introspection/GraphiQL. After (secure): Enforce max N objects/operations per request, reject batched queries for auth-related types, cap concurrent executions, return generic error messages without stack traces, and restrict introspection/GraphiQL to internal/admin-only endpoints.
GraphQL introspection and error exposure hardening
WHAT: GraphQL APIs often expose introspection, GraphiQL, and detailed error messages (stack traces, debug mode) to unauthenticated users, leaking schema details and internal implementation data.
WHY: Exposed schema and verbose errors help attackers map your API, discover hidden or deprecated/private fields, and identify vulnerabilities, increasing the risk of abuse and targeted attacks.
HOW: Disable or strictly restrict introspection and GraphiQL to authenticated/authorized roles only (or system-wide for internal APIs); if supported, also disable “did you mean?” field-suggestion hints when introspection is off. In production, turn off debug mode and stack-trace/error detail in responses, logging full errors only to internal systems.
EXAMPLE: In JavaScript (Apollo Server), set `debug: false` and `NODE_ENV='production'`; when using `express-graphql`, configure `validationRules: [NoIntrospection]` and `graphiql: process.env.NODE_ENV === 'development'` so that introspection and GraphiQL are not available in production to unauthenticated users.
Injection Flaw Prevention
WHAT: Injection flaws occur when untrusted data is sent to an interpreter (e.g., SQL, LDAP, XPath, OS commands) and is concatenated into queries or commands, allowing attackers to alter their behavior.
WHY: Successful injection can expose or modify sensitive data, bypass access controls, execute administrative or OS-level commands, and compromise entire systems.
HOW: Never build queries/commands by concatenating user input; instead use parameterized queries/prepared statements or safe APIs, validate and sanitize all untrusted input with strict allowlists, and refactor legacy code where possible or apply virtual patching when source changes are not feasible.
EXAMPLE: Before (SQL, vulnerable): `query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = " + userInput;` After (safe): `query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?"; stmt = conn.prepareStatement(query); stmt.setInt(1, userId);`
SQL Injection Prevention in Database Access
WHAT: Risk of SQL injection when building dynamic SQL queries (including stored procedures) using unsanitized or unparameterized user-controlled input, especially with functions like sp_execute, execute, or exec.
WHY: Attackers can modify query structure, access or modify unauthorized data, execute arbitrary SQL commands, or compromise the entire database server.
HOW: Use prepared statements/parameterized queries for all user input; avoid unsafe dynamic SQL in stored procedures; where parameters cannot be used (e.g., table/column names), use strict allow-list mapping from user input to predefined identifiers; otherwise redesign the query.
EXAMPLE:
Before (vulnerable): `query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = " + userInput;`
After (safe): use a prepared statement with a bound parameter for `userInput`, and never concatenate raw user input into the SQL string.
Preventing injection when building queries from user input
WHAT: Building SQL/LDAP queries using unvalidated user-controlled values for table/column names or query parameters can lead to SQL/LDAP injection and unauthorized data access or modification.
WHY: Attackers can alter queries to read/modify sensitive data, escalate privileges, or corrupt directory contents.
HOW: Never concatenate raw user input into queries; map user-supplied identifiers to a fixed allowlist of legal table/column names, validate all parameters, and use parameterized queries or stored procedures; only use escaping as a last-resort retrofit for legacy code.
EXAMPLE: Before (Java, vulnerable): `String q = "SELECT * FROM " + request.getParameter("tbl") + " WHERE user_name='" + custname + "'";` After (Java, safer): `String tbl = mapToAllowedTable(request.getParameter("tbl")); String q = "SELECT account_balance FROM " + tbl + " WHERE user_name = ?"; PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement(q); ps.setString(1, custname);`
LDAP query construction and escaping
WHAT: Untrusted data is concatenated into LDAP DNs or search filters without proper LDAP-specific escaping, allowing LDAP injection or malformed queries.
WHY: Attackers can alter LDAP queries to bypass authentication, escalate privileges, or access/modify unauthorized directory entries.
HOW: For every user-controlled value inserted into an LDAP DN or search filter, apply the correct LDAP escaping routine (DN-encoding for DNs, search-filter encoding for filters); never build LDAP queries via raw string concatenation without escaping.
EXAMPLE: Before (Java, vulnerable): `String filter = "(&(uid=" + userInput + ")(objectClass=person))";` After (Java, safer): `String filter = "(&(uid=" + escapeSearchFilter(userInput) + ")(objectClass=person))";`
OS Command Injection in Web Applications
WHAT: Unvalidated user input is passed to OS command execution APIs (e.g., system calls), allowing attackers to inject additional commands (e.g., via `;` in query parameters).
WHY: Successful injection lets attackers execute arbitrary commands on the server, upload malicious programs, or read sensitive files such as `/etc/passwd`.
HOW: Avoid building shell commands with user input; use safe, parameterized APIs that do not invoke a shell; if absolutely unavoidable, strictly validate and allowlist acceptable input values and characters, and reject or escape command separators like `;`, `&`, `|`.
EXAMPLE: Before (vulnerable): `system("ls " . $_GET['dir']);` After (safer): use a library/API that lists directories directly (e.g., `scandir($_GET['dir'])`) after validating `dir` against an allowlist of known-safe paths.
Command and Input Injection Prevention
WHAT: Risk of command or protocol injection when user-controlled data is concatenated into commands or network protocol streams (e.g., building a single command string with arguments or embedding unvalidated input in SMTP/FTP/IMAP conversations).
WHY: Attackers can execute arbitrary commands, alter protocol behavior, or abuse established sessions, leading to data compromise, remote code execution, or service misuse.
HOW: Use parameterized or structured APIs that separate commands from arguments; validate commands against an explicit allowlist; validate arguments with positive/allowlist rules and canonicalization; constrain input via regular expressions that define allowed characters and maximum length, excluding metacharacters like & | ; $ > < \ ! ` and whitespace; if no parameterized API exists, apply context-appropriate escaping for the target interpreter.
EXAMPLE: (Java) Insecure: new ProcessBuilder("C:\\DoStuff.exe -arg1 -arg2");  // single, concatenated command string.
Secure: new ProcessBuilder("TrustedCmd", "TrustedArg1", "TrustedArg2");  // command and each argument passed separately and validated beforehand.
RESTful Web Service Attack Surface Identification
WHAT: Failing to identify all REST endpoints and non-standard parameters (URL segments, headers, JSON/XML fields) leads to incomplete security testing and untested attack surface.
WHY: Undiscovered endpoints and parameters may contain exploitable vulnerabilities (e.g., auth bypass, injection) that remain undetected and can be abused in production.
HOW: During development and testing, maintain and share formal or semi-formal API documentation; use proxies to capture full HTTP requests (including headers and bodies); systematically enumerate URL patterns, header-based parameters, and structured JSON/XML fields, and ensure all are included in security tests.
EXAMPLE: Before: Only test `/api/users?name=` from UI flows. After: Use proxy logs and docs to also test `/api/users/1234/roles`, custom headers like `X-Auth-Token`, and nested JSON fields such as `{"profile":{"email":...}}`.
REST API parameter fuzzing and authentication handling
WHAT: Failing to correctly identify and fuzz URL and structured parameters (JSON, XML, non-standard segments) and to emulate authentication can leave hidden authorization and input-validation flaws undiscovered.
WHY: Undetected flaws in parameter handling can allow attackers to bypass access controls, escalate privileges, or trigger injection and logic vulnerabilities in production.
HOW: Treat extension-less or highly varying URL segments as potential parameters; distinguish path vs. parameter by sending invalid values and observing 404 vs. app-level errors; focus fuzzing on near-boundary invalid values and sequences that exceed the current user’s expected range; always reproduce the real authentication mechanism during fuzzing.
EXAMPLE: (HTTP) Before: Fuzz only query string (?id=) while ignoring /svc/Grid.asmx/GetRelatedListItems and /src/XXXX/page segments and sending requests without auth headers. After: Systematically test /GetRelatedListItems and /src/{id}/page as parameters with boundary values while including the same cookies/tokens/headers used by real clients.
Secure defaults and fail-safe design
WHAT: Insecure product designs that lack secure defaults, have an unnecessarily large attack surface, or do not fail safely to well-defined states.
WHY: Increases the chance that a single bug or misconfiguration leads to compromise, data exposure, or persistent insecure states.
HOW: Define and implement secure-by-default configurations, minimize exposed interfaces and features, and ensure all error/exception paths revert to known safe defaults that are documented and tested.

Security principles for application design and implementation
WHAT: Failing to apply least privilege, separation of duties, defense-in-depth, zero trust, and secure development practices leads to excessive access, single points of failure, and fragile security controls.
WHY: Over-privileged components or users, missing layered controls, and implicit trust paths increase the likelihood and impact of data breaches, fraud, and unauthorized system access.
HOW: Design roles, services, and components to have only the minimal permissions needed; separate critical duties across independent components; implement multiple, independent security layers (network, application, data); require explicit authentication/authorization for every request regardless of network location; and integrate secure coding, vulnerability testing, and security reviews into the development lifecycle.
EXAMPLE: Before (violation of least privilege): a web app’s DB user has full admin rights to all schemas. After (least privilege): create a dedicated DB role with only SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE on the specific tables the app needs, and no DDL or cross-database access.
Secure component and connection design
WHAT: Risk of insecure libraries, services, and connections if components are chosen or wired together without security review, leading to weak points in the application’s architecture.
WHY: Insecure or poorly isolated components and connections can expose sensitive data, enable lateral movement, or break tenant isolation, causing severe business and security impact.
HOW: Select components from an approved “Golden Path/Paved Road” catalog of secure patterns; verify licensing and maintenance status; perform threat modeling on all components and connections; enforce tier and environment segregation based on required product security level and tenant needs.

Secure application design and configuration
WHAT: Insecure input handling, weak auth, poor cryptography, over-privileged components, insecure error handling, hardcoded secrets, unsafe memory use, and misconfiguration can lead to issues like SQL injection, buffer overflows, data exposure, and unauthorized access.
WHY: These failures enable attackers to read/modify sensitive data, escalate privileges, execute arbitrary code, disrupt service, or bypass controls across different tiers of the application.
HOW: Validate and type-check all inputs; implement strong authN/Z; use approved cryptography for data in transit/at rest; apply least privilege; avoid hardcoded secrets by using secure secret stores; handle errors without leaking sensitive info; use safe languages or rigorously manage memory; enforce secure-by-default configuration, defense-in-depth, secure communications, and fail-secure behavior; keep dependencies/images patched; and continuously test, review, and threat-model the system.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure input): `query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = " + userInput;`
After (validated & parameterized): `id = parseInt(userInput, 10); query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?"; stmt.executeQuery(query, id);`
Zero Trust Access Control for Applications
WHAT: Treat every application resource (APIs, services, databases) as untrusted by default and require per-request authentication and authorization instead of relying on “internal network” trust or long-lived permissions.
WHY: Network perimeter bypass (e.g., VPN compromise, lateral movement) can give attackers broad access to internal apps and data if access is not continuously validated.
HOW: Implement short-lived, strongly authenticated sessions (e.g., OAuth2/OIDC tokens), enforce authorization at every service/API boundary, use TLS 1.3+ for all service-to-service and client-to-service traffic, and dynamically evaluate access policy using user identity, device posture, location, time, and behavior.
EXAMPLE: Before: Internal microservice trusts any request from 10.0.0.0/8 without auth. After: Each request must present a valid JWT access token over TLS; the service verifies signature, audience, expiry, and scopes/claims before executing the operation.
Zero Trust API Access Controls
WHAT: Failing to enforce strict authentication, authorization, and validation on every API call allows attackers to abuse stolen credentials, compromised devices, or malformed requests to access or exfiltrate data.
WHY: Leads to unauthorized access, lateral movement, data exfiltration, and abuse of privileged accounts even when credentials or VPN access appear valid.
HOW: Require strong authZ/authN on every request, bind tokens to device and session, use short-lived tokens, validate request schemas, enforce least privilege and micro-segmentation, monitor behavior continuously, and revoke or step-up auth on anomalous activity.
EXAMPLE: Before: API accepts bearer token and executes request without schema checks or device/risk evaluation. After: API verifies token freshness and device binding, checks user and resource policy, validates request body against a strict schema, and denies or challenges if risk score or behavior is abnormal.
Identity and access management with Zero Trust
WHAT: Failing to enforce strong, adaptive access controls (e.g., unrestricted device access, long-lived broad permissions, unmonitored access to code/data) exposes systems and source code to unauthorized use and data exfiltration.
WHY: Weak access management can lead to account/device compromise, lateral movement, code theft, and loss of sensitive technical and business information.
HOW: Enforce Zero Trust principles: require MFA for all identities; restrict access to least privilege and time-bound approvals; route untrusted devices through isolated environments; block direct data downloads; and log, monitor, and review all sensitive access.
EXAMPLE: Before: Users with permanent, broad access to repositories and documents from any device, without MFA or detailed logging. After: Users get only project-specific, temporary access via MFA; untrusted devices use an isolated workspace; all actions are recorded and periodically reviewed.
Multi-factor Authentication and Access Control
WHAT: Weak or phishing-prone authentication (e.g., SMS-based MFA) and overly broad, persistent privileges expose accounts, devices, and applications to takeover and lateral movement.
WHY: Attackers can bypass weak MFA, abuse long-lived admin rights, or use compromised devices and networks to access sensitive data and critical systems.
HOW: Use phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2/WebAuthn, smart cards), avoid SMS-based MFA, enforce least privilege and just-in-time access, separate admin accounts, authenticate devices with certificates, encrypt data in transit and at rest, and protect applications with WAFs and API gateways.
EXAMPLE: Before: User logs in with password + SMS code and has permanent admin role. After: User logs in with FIDO2 security key; admin role is granted just-in-time via an approval workflow and automatically revoked after task completion.
Legacy system authentication hardening
WHAT: Legacy applications that only support basic username/password authentication without multi-factor authentication (MFA) create a security gap, especially when they protect sensitive data or critical functions.
WHY: Weak, single-factor authentication is easily compromised (phishing, credential stuffing, password reuse), allowing attackers to gain direct access to high-value legacy systems.
HOW: Front legacy apps with modern identity providers or proxies that enforce MFA, require strong password policies, and support modern protocols; if integration is impossible, prioritize refactoring or replacing the system and strictly limit network and account access in the interim.
EXAMPLE: Before: Legacy app directly exposed, accepting only username/password. After: Legacy app accessible only via an identity-aware proxy that authenticates users with SSO + MFA, then forwards authenticated sessions to the legacy backend.
Securing Legacy Systems in Zero Trust Architectures
WHAT: Legacy systems often use weak or outdated authentication, unencrypted protocols, flat/trusted network assumptions, and minimal logging, creating exploitable gaps when integrated into modern environments.
WHY: Attackers target these systems to bypass strong controls elsewhere, leading to credential theft, data exposure in transit, lateral movement across networks, and undetected compromise.
HOW: Place legacy apps behind security proxies/wrappers that enforce strong auth and MFA; isolate them in tightly controlled, monitored network zones; use protocol translation gateways to bridge modern auth (e.g., SAML/OAuth) to legacy mechanisms; and deploy network-based monitoring to compensate for poor native logging.
EXAMPLE: Before: App is directly exposed on the internal network using basic auth over HTTP with broad network access and no central logging. After: App is only reachable via an identity-aware proxy that requires MFA, terminates TLS, restricts network paths to a dedicated segment, and sends detailed access logs to a central SIEM.
Multi-cloud and container security configuration
WHAT: Misconfigured or inconsistent security across clouds and containers (e.g., unencrypted inter-cloud traffic, unrestricted container-to-container communication, unscanned images, missing runtime checks).
WHY: Leads to data exposure, lateral movement between services, exploitation of known vulnerabilities, and undetected malicious activity.
HOW: Enforce unified identity and access management across clouds; require encryption for all inter-cloud and inter-service traffic; define strict network policies for container communication; integrate image vulnerability scanning into CI/CD; enable runtime monitoring and anomaly detection for containers.
EXAMPLE: Before: Containers communicate freely on the default network with no TLS and images are pulled and run directly from a registry. After: Apply Kubernetes NetworkPolicies to restrict pod egress/ingress, use a service mesh with mTLS for all service calls, and gate deployments on passing image vulnerability scans.
Zero Trust Logging and Monitoring
WHAT: Insufficient logging and analysis of Zero Trust security events, leading to undetected threats and inability to tune access policies or prove compliance.
WHY: Poor visibility allows attacks to go unnoticed, weakens incident response, and can cause compliance failures due to missing or incomplete audit trails.
HOW: Implement comprehensive, centralized logging for all authentication, authorization, and access decisions; forward logs to a SIEM or analytics platform that can handle expected volume; regularly review alerts, tune rules, and validate that all critical services emit structured, timestamped logs.

Web application security and IAM integration
WHAT: Failing to protect web applications, APIs, and authentication flows against common attacks (e.g., OWASP Top 10) and weak access control decisions.
WHY: Leads to account takeover, data exfiltration, privilege escalation, and compromise of application and backend services.
HOW: Implement strong authentication (MFA) using open standards (e.g., SAML, OAuth, FIDO2), enforce risk-based access decisions, and follow OWASP ASVS/OWASP Top 10 controls for input validation, session management, and access control on every API and application endpoint.
EXAMPLE: Before: Custom username/password form with homegrown session cookies and no MFA or input validation. After: Use standards-based SSO (SAML/OAuth) with MFA, framework-provided session handling, centralized authorization checks on each API route, and validation/sanitization aligned with OWASP ASVS.
Secure security-event logging vocabulary
WHAT: Failure to use a consistent, structured vocabulary and format for security-event logs makes it hard to detect, correlate, and respond to attacks across applications.
WHY: Inconsistent or missing security-event logs increase mean time to detect and contain breaches, raising incident impact and cost.
HOW: Define and adopt a standard JSON log schema (timestamp in ISO 8601 with UTC offset, app ID, event type keyword, level, description, network/request metadata); ensure all security-relevant code paths trap errors and emit events using this vocabulary; coordinate with SRE/IR teams so their tooling ingests and alerts on these standardized fields.
EXAMPLE: Before: application prints free-form error strings or stack traces to stdout with no event type. After: on authentication success/failure, emit a structured JSON object including `datetime`, `appid`, `event` (e.g., `AUTHN_login_success:username`), `level`, `description`, and relevant request metadata.
Authentication and Authorization Security Event Logging
WHAT: Missing or incomplete logging of authentication and token events (logins, failures, locks, password changes, impossible travel, token creation/revocation) prevents reliable detection and investigation of account abuse.
WHY: Without these logs, brute-force attacks, account takeovers, misuse of tokens, and policy violations may go undetected and cannot be forensically analyzed or correlated with other security signals.
HOW: Implement structured, timestamped logging for all authn events: login success/fail/success-after-fail, max-fail reached, account lock with reason, password change and failure, impossible-travel detections, and token creation/revocation (including user ID and relevant metadata), and ensure logs are sent to a centralized, tamper-resistant log store.
EXAMPLE: On login failure, emit a WARN log with fields {datetime, appid, event:"authn_login_fail:<userid>", description}; on password change success, emit INFO with event:"authn_password_change:<userid>"; on impossible travel detection, emit CRITICAL with event:"authn_impossible_travel:<userid,region1,region2>".
Security event logging for auth, crypto, and resource access
WHAT: Missing or inconsistent logging of authentication token revocation/reuse/deletion, authorization failures/changes/admin actions, crypto failures, rate-limit exceedance, and file uploads can prevent detection and investigation of security incidents.
WHY: Without these logs, you may miss token abuse, privilege escalation, data access violations, cryptographic misuse, abuse of service, or malicious uploads, hindering incident response and compliance.
HOW: Implement structured, centralized logging for each listed event type with user ID, resource/target, timestamp, and outcome; avoid logging secrets (tokens/keys) in full; ensure logs are immutable, access-controlled, and monitored with alerts for CRITICAL/WARN events.
EXAMPLE: Before: no log on token reuse or authz failure. After: on revoked-token use or unauthorized resource access, write a structured log entry `{datetime, appid, event: "authn_token_reuse:<userid>,<tokenid>", level: "CRITICAL", description: "...", ...}` to your central logging system and trigger an alert.
Secure file upload and input handling
WHAT: Unvalidated or weakly validated file uploads and server-side inputs can allow malicious files (wrong type, containing malware) or unexpected parameters to be stored, served, or processed, and can expose original filenames to users.
WHY: This can lead to malware distribution, data exfiltration, path traversal, forced browsing, or logic abuse via unexpected fields or parameters.
HOW: Always validate uploaded files for type and safety (e.g., virus scan), rename/move them to internal identifiers and never expose original filenames in download URLs, enforce strict server-side validation/allowlists for all inputs, and reject or log and block requests containing unexpected fields or excessive 404 probing.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): store and serve `/uploads/${userFilename}` directly with no scanning or type checks; accept any JSON fields and ignore unknown ones. After (secure): scan file, verify MIME/type, store as `/data/${generatedId}`, serve by `fileId` only, and validate request body against a strict schema that rejects unknown or malformed fields.
Security logging for attacks, privilege changes, and sensitive data access
WHAT: Log detected attack tools (e.g., by user-agent), blocked illegal cross-origin requests, failed direct-object access attempts, privilege/permission changes on protected objects, and creation/read of sensitive data.
WHY: These events indicate active attacks, privilege escalation attempts, or potential data exfiltration and provide an audit trail for detection, forensics, and incident response.
HOW: Implement centralized, tamper-resistant logging that records timestamp, user or IP, user agent, target object/path, old/new privilege levels, and event description; ensure CORS checks block unauthorized origins while still logging them; enforce access control for direct object references and log all denied attempts; tag sensitive data locations and log create/read operations.
EXAMPLE: Pseudocode pattern: `if isAttackTool(ua) or isIllegalCors(req) or isUnauthorizedObjectAccess(req) or isPrivilegeChange(obj) or isSensitiveDataAccess(obj): logSecurityEvent(userId, ip, ua, obj, action, details)`
Sensitive data access and session event logging
WHAT: Missing or incomplete logging of sensitive data reads/updates/deletes and session lifecycle events (creation, renewal, expiry) prevents detection and investigation of misuse or business-logic abuse.
WHY: Without detailed, immutable logs, attackers can exfiltrate, alter, or delete sensitive data and hijack or abuse sessions with little chance of detection or forensic reconstruction.
HOW: For all sensitive resources and authenticated sessions, emit structured logs on read/update/delete and session_created/session_renewed/session_expired, include user ID, object/path, timestamp, and reason; implement “soft delete” (mark as deleted, keep archival copy per legal/privacy rules) and never hard-delete sessions, only expire them.
EXAMPLE: Before: updating or deleting `/users/admin/some/important/path` or expiring a session changes state silently. After: every such action writes an audit record like `sensitive_update:<userid>,<path>` or `session_expired:<userid>,<reason>` to an append-only log that is periodically reviewed and monitored for anomalies.
Security logging for session and system/user events
WHAT: Log security-relevant events, including access with expired sessions, system startup/shutdown/restart/crash, security monitor enable/disable actions, and user account creation/updates, including the acting user and key attributes.
WHY: These logs provide an audit trail to detect session hijacking, unauthorized system control, tampering with security agents, privilege abuse, and to support incident response and forensics.
HOW: Implement structured, timestamped logging for each event type with fields like user ID, event name, target user/monitor, reason (for crashes), and privilege attributes; ensure logs are immutable, centralized, and monitored for suspicious patterns (e.g., repeated expired-session use, unexpected monitor disable).
EXAMPLE: Before: no log on expired session access or user creation. After: on expired session access, write a CRITICAL log entry "session_use_after_expire:[userid]"; on user creation/update, write WARN entries "user_created:[actor,newuser,attributes]" and "user_updated:[actor,target,attributes]" to a central log store.
Secure logging of user account lifecycle events
WHAT: Log user account updates, archiving, and deletions with actor ID, target user ID, and relevant attributes, while excluding private or secret data (passwords, keys, certs, source code, etc.).
WHY: Detailed, non-sensitive logs support auditing, incident response, and detection of malicious use of admin capabilities (e.g., unauthorized account changes or denial of service by mass archiving/deleting users).
HOW: For each user update/archive/delete operation, emit a structured log entry at WARN (or higher) including timestamp, application ID, event type, actor, target, and changed privileges; implement a strict allowlist of safe fields to log and filter out secrets per OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet.
EXAMPLE: Before: logging full user objects or credentials on update/delete; After: logging only metadata such as `"event":"user_deleted:<actor>,<target>"` and `"description":"<actor> deleted <target>"` without any passwords, tokens, keys, or other sensitive fields.
CI/CD pipeline security
WHAT: CI/CD pipelines, build servers, and related components often run with high privileges and can be compromised via weak flow control, IAM, configuration, dependencies, third-party services, or artifact validation.
WHY: A compromised pipeline lets attackers inject or alter code, artifacts, or deployments, leading to large-scale supply-chain breaches and full environment compromise.
HOW: Enforce strict IAM and PBAC for all CI/CD identities, harden and securely configure CI/CD systems, validate artifact integrity, restrict and govern third-party services, manage credentials securely, and enable detailed logging and monitoring across all pipeline stages.
EXAMPLE: In a CI job definition, avoid running all steps as an admin/root service account; instead, assign a dedicated least-privilege CI role per stage (e.g., “build”, “test”, “deploy”) with only the minimal permissions required for that stage.
Secure CI/CD SCM and Pipeline Configuration
WHAT: Misconfigured SCM and CI/CD pipeline environments (e.g., default settings, weak branch protections, unsigned commits, broad permissions, unreviewed merges) can allow untrusted or malicious code to be deployed automatically to production.
WHY: Attackers can inject or modify code, escalate privileges, or exfiltrate data through the build and deployment process, compromising production systems and supply chain integrity.
HOW: Disable auto-merge; require non-bypassable pull-request reviews; enforce protected branches; require signed commits; restrict ephemeral/external contributors and default permissions; enable MFA; restrict forking and visibility changes; harden and patch CI/CD infrastructure following CIS/STIG; manage changes via formal change management and governance; use tools (e.g., SCM misconfiguration scanners) to continuously detect and fix insecure settings.
EXAMPLE (Git): Before: auto-merge enabled, no required reviews, anyone can push to main. After: `main` marked as protected; require ≥1 code review and signed commits; disable auto-merge; restrict push/merge to a limited maintainer group; enforce MFA on all SCM accounts.
Secure Secrets Management in CI/CD Pipelines
WHAT: Secrets (API keys, passwords, credentials) are hardcoded in code/CI configs, embedded in images/binaries, or exposed via logs/console/history, allowing theft in usable form.
WHY: Exposed secrets can let attackers impersonate services, access sensitive systems, and pivot through your environment, leading to data loss or production compromise.
HOW: Never hardcode secrets in repos or CI configs; scan with tools (e.g., git-leaks/git-secrets); remove secrets from images/binaries; store secrets only in encrypted vaults using industry-standard crypto; ensure secrets are never printed, logged, or written to shell history; use temporary/OTP credentials with IP or contextual access restrictions.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): `DB_PASSWORD="SuperSecret123"` in `ci.yml` or Dockerfile, echoed in build logs. After (secure): read `DB_PASSWORD` from a secrets manager at runtime via environment variables or short-lived tokens, with logging configured to redact or omit secret values.
CI/CD Least Privilege, Identity, and Dependency Security
WHAT: Over-privileged CI/CD pipelines, OS accounts, and identities, plus unvalidated third-party dependencies, can allow attackers to access secrets, resources, or execute malicious code via the dependency chain.
WHY: Compromise can lead to unauthorized access to external services, lateral movement across pipelines, privilege escalation on build agents, and execution of attacker-controlled code.
HOW: Enforce least privilege for all pipeline identities and OS users; segregate secrets per pipeline/sensitivity; use a centralized IdP with no shared/local/self-provisioned accounts; maintain an up-to-date inventory of identities and their actual permissions; and integrate automated SCA/dependency-chain protections (e.g., checks against typosquatting, dependency confusion, and compromised maintainers).
EXAMPLE: Before (CI config): pipeline runs as root, uses a shared AWS key with `AdministratorAccess`, and installs dependencies directly from public registries. After: pipeline runs as a non-root service account; uses a pipeline-specific AWS role limited to required actions on specific resources; and installs dependencies only from an approved internal mirror with SCA and dependency-chain validation enabled.
Secure Dependency and CI/CD Extension Management
WHAT: Risk of supply-chain compromise via mutable or unverified dependencies and unvetted CI/CD plug-ins/integrations.
WHY: Attackers can inject malicious packages or abuse over-privileged extensions to execute arbitrary code, exfiltrate secrets, or tamper with builds.
HOW: Pin dependency versions to known-good releases, verify package integrity via hashes/checksums and lock files, use a single private package feed with scoped/ID-prefixed private packages, commit package-manager config files to source control, strictly limit who can install CI/CD plug-ins, and formally vet all extensions before use.
EXAMPLE: Before: package.json with "^1.0.0" dependencies, no lock file, public feeds only, any CI/CD admin can install arbitrary plug-ins. After: exact versions pinned with package-lock.json, hashes verified, single private registry with scoped packages, .npmrc in source control, and a controlled approval process plus least-privilege roles for installing CI/CD extensions.
CI/CD Integrity and Logging Controls
WHAT: Risk of CI/CD compromise via tampered code, dependencies, or pipeline steps, and exposure of sensitive data through improper logging (e.g., logging plaintext passwords or tokens).
WHY: Leads to supply-chain attacks, unauthorized code execution, data breaches, and undetected attacker persistence in the build/release process.
HOW: Enforce signed commits in SCM; verify package integrity with hashes; use code signing (e.g., Sigstore/Signserver) and secure the signing process; integrate frameworks like in-toto; configure CI/CD logging per policy, in parsable formats, with centralized aggregation/SIEM alerts; explicitly exclude secrets (passwords, tokens, API keys) from logs.
EXAMPLE: Before: CI logs every HTTP header and request body, including `Authorization: Bearer <token>` and user passwords. After: Configure logging middleware to redact or drop sensitive fields (e.g., headers `Authorization`, `Cookie`, JSON keys `password`, `api_key`) before writing logs, while still logging authentication event types and outcomes.
Attack Surface Analysis for Applications
WHAT: Failing to identify and manage all entry/exit points, protective controls, and sensitive data in an application leaves unreviewed, high‑risk code paths exposed to external attackers.
WHY: Unmanaged attack surface increases the chance that vulnerabilities in exposed interfaces or data flows will be exploited, leading to data theft, privilege escalation, or system compromise.
HOW: Enumerate all data/command paths into and out of the app; list all sensitive data and secrets; map the code that protects these (authn/z, logging, validation, encoding, encryption, integrity checks); regularly reassess this map whenever features, interfaces, or integrations change, and apply defense‑in‑depth to high‑risk areas.
EXAMPLE: (Conceptual) Maintain an “attack surface register” listing each API endpoint, message queue, file interface, and admin function with its validation, authentication, authorization, and logging status, and require review/update of this register in your change/deployment process.
Attack Surface Identification and Protection
WHAT: Failing to systematically identify and protect all data/command entry and exit points, and all valuable data (including secrets, keys, PII, admin interfaces, and external-facing microservices) leads to unprotected endpoints and data exposure.
WHY: Unmapped or weakly protected attack points allow unauthorized access, data theft, privilege escalation, and compromise of critical business and personal data at scale.
HOW: Enumerate all entry/exit points (UI, APIs, files, DB, messages, runtime args, etc.) and all sensitive data; bucket endpoints by risk (external/internal, role, privilege, purpose, tech); prioritize anonymous and highly privileged paths; ensure each bucket has strong authN/Z, validation/encoding, encryption, logging/auditing, and integrity controls; reassess when endpoint counts or types change (e.g., new microservices exposed via proxies/ingress).
EXAMPLE: Before: Add a new admin API exposed via an ingress controller without updating the attack-surface model or enforcing admin-only authorization and detailed audit logging. After: Classify the new admin API as high-risk external-facing, require strong admin authentication and role checks, validate and encode all inputs/outputs, encrypt data in transit and at rest, and add fine-grained access and activity logs.
Attack surface identification and prioritization
WHAT: Failing to systematically identify and map all external entry points (e.g., login, admin interfaces, web forms, APIs, file inputs, legacy interfaces) and valuable data flows leads to unprotected or weakly protected attack points.
