WHY: Unmapped attack surface areas are more likely to contain exploitable vulnerabilities, especially on remote, internet-facing, anonymous-access interfaces and in security-critical code (crypto, auth, access control, sessions).
HOW: Enumerate all interface types and data flows (by code review, developer/user interviews, and automated scanning tools like ZAP/Arachni/etc.), identify sensitive data and external connections, then prioritize hardening and testing of high-risk, remote, and legacy interfaces; repeat this whenever the attack surface changes.
EXAMPLE: Before: Only login and main UI are reviewed and tested, while legacy file-upload API and admin endpoints remain unassessed. After: All external endpoints, workflows, and data stores are cataloged; high-risk ones (admin, uploads, public APIs, security modules) receive focused validation, access control checks, and security testing.
Attack Surface Management
WHAT: Failing to identify and minimize all entry/exit points, channels, and untrusted data paths (including old versions, unused features, and backups) increases the application’s attack surface and exposes more ways to be compromised.
WHY: A larger, unmanaged attack surface raises the likelihood and impact of successful attacks, including data theft, system compromise, and abuse of legacy or forgotten components.
HOW: Enumerate all externally reachable interfaces, channels, and untrusted data elements; calculate and track an attack surface metric over time; remove or disable unused features, old protocols, legacy endpoints, and backup copies from active environments; and enforce strict source control, change management, and backup protection (access control, encryption, and segregation).
EXAMPLE: Before: Deploy multiple app versions, keep unused debug endpoints and old backups in web-accessible directories. After: Remove legacy endpoints and versions from deployment, disable debug features, move backups to restricted offline storage, and update documentation and configuration so only required interfaces are exposed.
Attack surface and access model risk assessment
WHAT: Failing to reassess security when adding or changing interfaces, roles, or core security mechanisms (auth, session, crypto, validation, architecture) can leave new attack paths and over-privileged access unnoticed.
WHY: Unreviewed changes can expose sensitive data/functions, enable privilege escalation, or bypass existing controls, especially in negative (allow-by-default) access models.
HOW: For each change, classify it (new page vs new API vs file upload, new role, new platform, etc.), check whether existing controls apply, and perform deeper risk assessment for anything outside existing buckets; prefer positive (deny-by-default) access models, reduce unused interfaces/roles/data, and disable or firewall unused features.
EXAMPLE: Before (negative model): `if (!denied[user][action]) allow();` After (positive model): `if (allowed[user].includes(action)) allow(); else deny();`
CSS role-based styling information disclosure
WHAT: Global CSS files with descriptive, role- or feature-specific selectors (e.g., `.addUser`, `.deleteAdmin`, `AdministratorStyling.css`) expose application roles, permissions, and hidden features to unauthenticated users via direct CSS access.
WHY: Attackers can use this metadata for reconnaissance to discover privileged functionality, guess sensitive URLs, and plan targeted attacks against high-privilege roles.
HOW: Split CSS by access-control level and serve each stylesheet only after authorization checks; prevent forced browsing of privileged CSS; avoid descriptive selector names by using generic/obscure selectors or automated class-name obfuscation, and prefer general, reusable styling rules.
EXAMPLE: Before (leaky): `link rel="stylesheet" href="/css/global.css"` with `.addUser { ... } .deleteAdmin { ... }` accessible to all; After (safer): only load `/css/admin.css` after confirming admin role on the server, and use non-descriptive selectors like `#page_u header button:first-of-type { ... }` or obfuscated class names.
Mitigate malicious CSS in user-authored HTML content
WHAT: User-supplied HTML that includes CSS (inline styles, style tags, or linked stylesheets) can be abused to alter layout or overlays, enabling clickjacking or other unintended interactions (e.g., making invisible full-page links).
WHY: Malicious CSS can trick users into clicking hidden or disguised elements, potentially loading attacker-controlled sites, stealing actions, or degrading application integrity and trust.
HOW: Treat all user-authored HTML/CSS as untrusted: sanitize HTML to strip or tightly restrict style attributes and style tags, disallow or validate external stylesheets, and enforce clickjacking defenses (e.g., X-Frame-Options/Content-Security-Policy frame-ancestors) on sensitive pages.
EXAMPLE: Before: accepting and rendering `<div style="position:absolute;top:0;left:0;width:100%;height:100%" onclick="location='https://evil.com'"></div>` from user input; After: sanitizing input to remove style and event attributes, or rendering user content in a sandboxed iframe with strict CSP and no navigation privileges.
Prompt Injection in LLM-Integrated Applications
WHAT: LLM prompts are built by directly concatenating system instructions with user-controlled input, allowing attackers to inject instructions like “IGNORE ALL PREVIOUS INSTRUCTIONS” that override intended behavior.
WHY: This can bypass safety controls, leak system prompts and internal configuration, exfiltrate sensitive data, and trigger unauthorized actions via connected tools/APIs.
HOW: Strictly separate instructions from data; use structured message formats (e.g., role-based messages) instead of raw string concatenation, treat all user/remote content as untrusted, and apply allowlisted tool invocation and output validation before acting on LLM responses.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): `full_prompt = system_prompt + "\n\nUser: " + user_input`; After (more secure): `messages = [{"role": "system", "content": system_prompt}, {"role": "user", "content": user_input}]; response = llm_client.generate(messages)` and validate `response` before executing any tool calls.
Prompt Injection Detection and Sanitization for LLM Inputs
WHAT: Unvalidated user prompts can inject instructions (e.g., “ignore previous instructions”, “reveal prompt”) that override system behavior or leak internal configuration.
WHY: Prompt injection can bypass safety controls, exfiltrate sensitive data, or cause the model/agent to perform unintended actions or tool calls.
HOW: Before passing text to the LLM, detect injection via regex and fuzzy matching for dangerous phrases, normalize obfuscations (whitespace, repeated chars), redact matched patterns, and enforce a maximum input length.
EXAMPLE (Python): Use compiled regex patterns and a `detect_injection(text)` check to block or flag inputs; apply `sanitize_input(text)` to collapse whitespace, remove excessive character repetition, and replace dangerous phrases with `[FILTERED]` before sending to the model.
Prompt Injection and Output Leakage Controls
WHAT: Risk of prompt injection and sensitive data leakage when LLMs treat user-controlled text as instructions or reveal internal prompts, API keys, or security rules.
WHY: Attackers can bypass safety rules, exfiltrate secrets, or gain unauthorized capabilities by manipulating prompts or outputs.
HOW: Strictly separate system instructions from user data; always treat user content as data, not commands; refuse to follow instructions in user input; sanitize and normalize external content; monitor outputs for system prompt or secret patterns; enforce length limits; and require human approval for high‑risk or injection‑like inputs.
EXAMPLE:
Before: model(prompt = user_input)
After: model(prompt = create_structured_prompt(system_instructions, user_data)), then filter_response(OutputValidator, response) and route high‑risk inputs through HITLController.requires_approval(user_input).
Prompt injection and tool misuse defenses in LLM applications
WHAT: LLM applications and agents may follow malicious or injected instructions, misuse tools, or leak data when handling untrusted input, comments, documentation, or web content.
WHY: Successful prompt injection or tool abuse can bypass safety controls, exfiltrate secrets, perform unauthorized actions, or corrupt downstream systems.
HOW: Detect and strip common injection patterns; sanitize comments, documentation, and markup; normalize and validate encodings; validate tool calls against user/session permissions; enforce least privilege on tools, APIs, and databases; rate-limit and log all interactions; monitor for anomalous reasoning, encoding tricks, and HTML injection; and require HITL approval for high‑risk requests.
EXAMPLE (Python, OpenAI client): Wrap LLM calls in a security pipeline that (1) rejects inputs where `PromptInjectionFilter.detect_injection()` is true, (2) sanitizes input before prompt construction, (3) validates/filters model outputs, and (4) enforces per-tool parameter validation and permission checks before executing any tool call.
Secure LLM Integration and Prompt Handling
WHAT: Insecure handling of prompts and LLM I/O (e.g., not validating inputs, mixing instructions with data, or rendering untrusted HTML/Markdown) can lead to prompt injection, data exfiltration, and unsafe model behavior.
WHY: Attackers can bypass safety constraints, execute unintended actions, steal sensitive data, or compromise downstream systems that consume LLM outputs.
HOW: Validate and sanitize all inputs (including external/encoded content), separate instructions from data in structured prompts, apply least privilege to connected tools/APIs, sanitize HTML/Markdown before rendering, and implement logging, monitoring, and incident response for suspicious usage.
EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe): `response = llm(user_input)` and then directly render `response` as HTML. After (safer): `clean_input = validate(user_input); response = llm(system_prompt, clean_input); safe_html = sanitize_html(response); render(safe_html)`
Django REST Framework API Security Guidelines
WHAT: Misconfigured DRF settings (authentication, permissions, throttling, serializers, object checks) can lead to unauthorized access, excessive data exposure, and DoS via unthrottled endpoints.
WHY: Attackers may call non-public APIs without authentication, access or modify objects they do not own, exfiltrate sensitive fields, or overload the service with uncontrolled requests.
HOW: Set secure defaults in REST_FRAMEWORK: define strict DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES and DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES (never leave AllowAny as default for non-public APIs), configure DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES and pagination to limit resource usage, and always call check_object_permissions(request, obj) in overridden get_object methods; avoid overriding authentication_classes and throttle_classes unless you fully understand the impact; when using ModelSerializer, explicitly list allowed fields instead of using exclude.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES = ['rest_framework.permissions.AllowAny']; class MyView(RetrieveAPIView): def get_object(self): return get_object_or_404(MyModel, pk=self.kwargs["pk"]). After (more secure): DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES = ['rest_framework.permissions.IsAuthenticated']; class MyView(RetrieveAPIView): def get_object(self): obj = get_object_or_404(self.get_queryset(), pk=self.kwargs["pk"]); self.check_object_permissions(self.request, obj); return obj.
Lack of resources, rate limiting, authorization, and configuration hardening for APIs
WHAT: APIs are exposed to resource exhaustion, broken function-level authorization, mass assignment, misconfiguration, injection, poor asset management, and insufficient logging/monitoring when defaults are left insecure or dangerous methods are used with user input.
WHY: These issues can lead to denial of service, privilege escalation, data exfiltration or corruption, remote code execution, unauthorized access to environments, and inability to detect or investigate attacks.
HOW: Enable and centrally configure rate limiting (e.g., DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES or WAF) and avoid per-view overrides unless fully understood; set strict DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES and only use AllowAny on explicitly public endpoints; in ModelForms use Meta.fields allowlists and never "__all__" or Meta.exclude; harden configuration with non-default passwords, random SECRET_KEY, DEBUG flags off, restricted HTTP verbs, and automated configuration assessment; validate/filter/sanitize all external data; use parameterized queries and never concatenate user input into raw(), extra(), or cursor.execute(); use safe loaders (e.g., yaml.SafeLoader), never eval/exec/execfile or untrusted pickle/read_pickle on user input; maintain an inventory of all API hosts, versions, environments, access scopes, and document authentication, errors, redirects, rate limiting, CORS, and endpoints; implement structured logging of auth failures, access denials, and validation errors without sensitive data, protect log integrity, and feed logs into SIEM with alerts and dashboards.
EXAMPLE: Before (Django/DRF): DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES = ['rest_framework.permissions.AllowAny']; class MyForm(ModelForm): class Meta: model = User; fields = "__all__"; cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + user_input + "'"). After: DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES = ['rest_framework.permissions.IsAuthenticated']; class MyForm(ModelForm): class Meta: model = User; fields = ['first_name', 'last_name']; cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = %s", [user_input]).
Secure Logging, Secrets, and Dependency Management
WHAT: Insecure logging (overly generic or logging sensitive data), hardcoded secrets, unreviewed business logic, and outdated or insecure dependencies can expose sensitive information, enable undetected attacks, and introduce known vulnerabilities.
WHY: These issues can lead to data breaches (e.g., leaked passwords/API tokens/PII), undetected abuse of business workflows, and exploitation via known library flaws.
HOW: Log detailed but non-sensitive error context (stack trace, error message, non-sensitive user identifier) while strictly excluding passwords, API tokens, and PII; never hardcode secrets—store them in a dedicated secret manager; use threat modeling, design reviews, code reviews, pairing, and unit tests to validate business logic; establish a recurring process to audit and update dependencies (monthly/quarterly, weekly for security advisories, and emergency updates for critical issues), preferring libraries with good “security health.”
EXAMPLE: Before (bad logging & secrets): `Log.Error("Error was thrown"); const API_TOKEN = "hardcoded-token";` After (better): `Log.Error(ex, "Order creation failed for user {UserId}", userId);` and load `API_TOKEN` from a secret manager or environment configuration instead of source code.
Strong cryptography and transport security for user data
WHAT: Failure to use strong, modern cryptography (for data in transit, at rest, and for credentials) and to enforce HTTPS-only transport (e.g., missing TLS best practices, HSTS, or certificate pinning) exposes user identities, private data, and communications.
WHY: Attackers can eavesdrop, modify traffic, or steal credentials (e.g., via MITM, CA compromise, or weak hashes), breaking confidentiality, integrity, and user privacy.
HOW: Use TLS with verified certificates, strong ciphers, and sufficient key lengths; enable HSTS where possible; encrypt sensitive data at rest with strong keys and strict access controls; hash passwords with a strong, collision-resistant, work-factor-based algorithm (e.g., bcrypt, Argon2); and implement certificate/public-key pinning in clients that control the user agent.
EXAMPLE (web, high level): Configure server to redirect HTTP→HTTPS and send `Strict-Transport-Security` header; store user passwords using a slow password-hashing function with per-user salts; in mobile apps, embed expected certificate/public-key hashes and reject connections that do not match.
Panic mode account protection
WHAT: Implement “panic modes” that let users under coercion log into decoy accounts or views that hide or delete real sensitive data, while still appearing like a normal account.
WHY: Coerced disclosure of credentials can expose real accounts, contacts, and data to adversaries, leading to physical harm, surveillance, or data compromise.
HOW: Provide secondary “distress” credentials that open a decoy environment; ensure panic mode is hard to detect (normal operations work, no obvious flags), cannot reveal or enumerate real accounts/panic modes, and is created/managed via secure out-of-band flows when possible.
EXAMPLE: (Conceptual) If user enters normal password → load full mailbox and contacts; if user enters distress password → load limited “innocent” mailbox and contacts, with all sensitive items hidden or wiped, and no UI or API that reveals the existence of the real mailbox or additional panic modes.
Prevent IP Address Leakage
WHAT: User IP addresses can leak when the application automatically loads third-party external content (e.g., images, avatars, signatures, attachments) embedded in user-generated content or HTML emails.
WHY: Adversaries can host external resources and monitor incoming HTTP requests to de-anonymize users, track them, or correlate their activity across services.
HOW: When rendering user-generated content, block or disable automatic loading of external third-party resources by default; provide a user-facing option to selectively enable external content; for HTML emails, follow the same pattern and ensure third-party images are not fetched automatically.
EXAMPLE: In a web app, strip or proxy external image URLs in user posts and only load them after explicit user consent (e.g., “Load external images” button).
HTML5 Cross-Origin Communication and CORS Hardening
WHAT: Insecure use of postMessage, CORS, and related APIs (e.g., using "*" origins, not validating origin/data, evaluating received data as code, or blindly allowing cross-domain URLs) can allow unauthorized message receipt, data exfiltration, code injection, and DOM-based XSS.
WHY: Attackers can impersonate trusted origins, inject arbitrary scripts, steal sensitive data, or abuse cross-origin channels (including CORS and WebSockets) to bypass same-origin protections and escalate to full account or application compromise.
HOW: Always specify an exact expected origin in postMessage; on receive, strictly compare event.origin to an allowlist of full origins and validate event.data; treat messages as data only (no eval, no innerHTML—use textContent or equivalent); validate and constrain URLs used in XMLHttpRequest/fetch; configure Access-Control-Allow-Origin only for specific trusted domains/paths with no sensitive content; enforce CSRF protections and reject mixed-content (HTTPS origin over HTTP) requests; never echo arbitrary Origin or use "*" for sensitive endpoints.
EXAMPLE: // Insecure
window.postMessage(data, "*");
window.addEventListener("message", e => { someElem.innerHTML = e.data; });
xhr.open("GET", userSuppliedUrl);
// Secure
const allowedOrigin = "https://app.example.com";
window.postMessage(data, allowedOrigin);
window.addEventListener("message", e => {
if (e.origin !== allowedOrigin) return;
if (!isValidMessage(e.data)) return;
someElem.textContent = e.data;
});
if (!isAllowedUrl(userSuppliedUrl)) throw new Error("Blocked URL");
xhr.open("GET", sanitizedUrl);
WebSockets and Storage API Security
WHAT: Insecure use of WebSockets, Server-Sent Events, and Web Storage can expose sensitive data, enable XSS-driven hijacking, allow MITM attacks, or bypass authentication (e.g., using outdated WebSocket versions, ws://, eval on JSON, or storing secrets in localStorage).
WHY: Attackers can steal or modify data, tunnel internal services via the browser, spoof clients, hijack sessions, or break same-origin isolation assumptions, leading to data breaches and account compromise.
HOW: Use only RFC 6455+ WebSockets over wss://; implement app-level authz/authn; validate all WebSocket/SSE input and origins; treat messages strictly as data (no DOM injection or eval, use JSON.parse); validate EventSource URLs; never store sensitive data or session IDs in localStorage, prefer sessionStorage for non-persistent, non-sensitive data, and separate apps by subdomain.
EXAMPLE (JavaScript – WebSocket JSON handling):
Before: `ws.onmessage = e => { const obj = eval(e.data); document.body.innerHTML = e.data; };`
After: `ws.onmessage = e => { const obj = JSON.parse(e.data); handleData(obj); };`
Client-side storage and related web APIs security
WHAT: Storing sensitive data in client-side storage (Web SQL, IndexedDB, Local Storage, WebDatabase) or trusting its contents can lead to authentication bypass, SQL injection, and XSS-driven data poisoning; misuse of Geolocation, Web Workers, and window.open can cause privacy leaks, DoS, CORS abuse, and tabnabbing.
WHY: Attackers or local users can read/modify client-side data, inject SQL, execute DOM-based XSS, track users’ locations without clear consent, abuse CPU/network via workers, or hijack parent tabs to phishing pages and steal referrer data.
HOW: Do not store secrets or authentication tokens in client-side storage; treat all client-side stored data as untrusted and validate/parameterize all queries; require explicit user interaction before calling geolocation APIs; never create or load Web Worker scripts from user input and validate all worker messages without using eval; configure CORS safely; break opener links by using rel="noopener noreferrer" on links, 'noopener,noreferrer' in window.open, setting newWindow.opener = null, and sending Referrer-Policy: no-referrer.
EXAMPLE: For tabnabbing mitigation in HTML: <a href="https://example.com" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">Link</a>; in JS: function openPopup(url, name, windowFeatures){ var w = window.open(url, name, 'noopener,noreferrer,' + windowFeatures); if (w) w.opener = null; }
Browser security and privacy controls for web applications
WHAT: Missing or misused browser controls (window.opener, referrer policy, iframe sandboxing, autocomplete on PII, insecure offline caching, weak WebSocket controls) can lead to data leakage, clickjacking, session/account compromise, and injection via untrusted content.
WHY: Attackers can hijack navigation via window.opener, steal or infer sensitive data via referrers, frame your site for clickjacking, recover credentials from browser caches, poison offline caches on insecure networks, or abuse WebSockets without proper origin, auth, and validation checks.
HOW: Use `noopener,noreferrer` when opening new windows and set `newWindow.opener = null`; send `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer` and `X-Frame-Options: deny` or `sameorigin`; sandbox all iframes with untrusted content and only relax needed capabilities; disable autocomplete and related features on credential/PII fields; require explicit user action before serving offline manifests and advise users to clear caches after insecure-network use; for WebSockets, strictly check `Origin`, validate all input/output, enforce authentication/authorization, and explicitly invalidate access tokens, using TLS to protect confidentiality and integrity.
EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe): `window.open(url, name, windowFeatures);`
After (safer): `var w = window.open(url, name, 'noopener,noreferrer,' + windowFeatures); if (w) w.opener = null;`
WebSocket origin allowlist filtering
WHAT: During WebSocket handshake, failing to validate the Origin HTTP header against an allowlist can allow unauthorized sites to establish WebSocket connections (Cross-Site WebSocket Hijacking).
WHY: An attacker’s site can hijack authenticated WebSocket sessions from a victim’s browser, leading to data theft, unauthorized actions, or account compromise.
HOW: On every WebSocket handshake, read the Origin header and compare it against a strict, externally configurable allowlist of trusted origins; reject the handshake if the origin is not in the allowlist, and log both accepted and rejected attempts.
EXAMPLE (Java): Override `ServerEndpointConfig.Configurator.checkOrigin(String origin)` to return `EXPECTED_ORIGINS.contains(origin)` where `EXPECTED_ORIGINS` is loaded from a secure configuration source.
WebSocket authentication and message validation
WHAT: Failing to authenticate WebSocket clients explicitly and to validate message content (input and output) can allow unauthorized access and processing of malformed or malicious data.
WHY: Attackers can hijack sessions, impersonate users, bypass browser protections, or perform DoS and data tampering if tokens are auto-sent by the browser or messages are not strictly validated.
HOW: Use an explicit authentication mechanism (e.g., HMAC-based tokens or JWTs) that are not automatically sent by the browser and must be provided by client code on each exchange; enforce token integrity, validity timeframe, and claims checks on every message; and validate all JSON payloads against a strict JSON Schema for both incoming and outgoing messages.
EXAMPLE: Before: WebSocket relies only on origin or cookies automatically sent by the browser, and accepts arbitrary JSON without checks. After: Client sends a JWT in each message payload; server verifies signature, expiry, and claims, then validates the message body against a predefined JSON Schema before processing or responding.
Authentication response handling in WebSocket message handlers
WHAT: Ensure WebSocket authentication handlers always send a well-formed, non-null response object to the client, even when exceptions occur during authentication or response creation.
WHY: Null or malformed responses can cause unhandled exceptions, denial of service, or inconsistent client state, potentially exposing error details or breaking authentication flows.
HOW: Wrap authentication and response-building logic in try/catch/finally, initialize a safe default failure response, and guarantee that the object passed to sendObject(...) is non-null and validated before sending.
EXAMPLE: Before: `AuthenticationResponse response = null; ... clientConnection.sendObject(response);` After: `AuthenticationResponse response = new AuthenticationResponse(false, "", "Authentication failed"); ... if (response != null) clientConnection.sendObject(response);`
JWT token handling and secret management
WHAT: JWT tokens are issued and validated using a shared HMAC secret loaded from a file; insecure handling (weak/guessable secret, predictable path, missing hardening) can let attackers forge or reuse tokens.
WHY: Compromised or predictable JWT secrets allow privilege escalation, impersonation, and unauthorized access to protected WebSocket endpoints.
HOW: Use a strong, randomly generated secret stored outside source/control (e.g., environment/secret manager), restrict file permissions, rotate secrets, enforce short expirations, validate issuer/audience/claims, and follow a JWT hardening cheat sheet (e.g., disable `none` alg, pin expected algorithm).
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): `Algorithm algorithm = Algorithm.HMAC256("mysecret");` After (hardened): `Algorithm algorithm = Algorithm.HMAC256(loadSecretFromEnvOrSecretManager());`
Secure handling and validation of JSON authentication messages
WHAT: Authentication JSON messages must be strictly validated against a JSON Schema before deserialization; any message that fails schema validation must be rejected and must not be deserialized.
WHY: Prevents injection, malformed data processing, and unexpected object states that could lead to authentication bypass, crashes, or other security issues.
HOW: Load a trusted JSON Schema at startup, validate each incoming JSON string with full reporting, check `validationReport.isSuccess()`, and throw an error or reject the request on any validation failure before calling the JSON deserializer.
EXAMPLE: Before: `AuthenticationRequest req = new Gson().fromJson(s, AuthenticationRequest.class);` After: `if (!schema.validate(JsonLoader.fromString(s), true).isSuccess()) throw new DecodeException(...); AuthenticationRequest req = new Gson().fromJson(s, AuthenticationRequest.class);`
JSON schema validation for WebSocket messages
WHAT: WebSocket encoder/decoder accepts JSON and converts it to domain objects; if JSON structure is not validated, malformed or unexpected data may be processed.
WHY: Unvalidated or malformed JSON can lead to logic flaws, denial of service, or injection-style issues when downstream code assumes a trusted structure.
HOW: Before decoding or sending JSON over WebSockets, validate the JSON structure against a strict JSON Schema and reject messages whose validation report is not successful; do not ignore parsing/validation exceptions.
EXAMPLE: Before decoding, load a JSON Schema once per endpoint/session and call `validationSchema.validate(JsonLoader.fromString(json), true)`; if `!report.isSuccess()` or an exception is thrown, close/reject the WebSocket message instead of using the decoded object.
JWT access-token denylist and explicit invalidation
WHAT: Implement explicit invalidation for long-lived JWT access tokens by maintaining a denylist of token hashes and rejecting any request whose token hash is present in the denylist.
WHY: Without explicit invalidation, stolen or reused tokens remain valid until expiry, enabling session hijacking and unauthorized access even after a user intends to log out or revoke access.
HOW: On user logout or explicit revoke request, hash the token (e.g., SHA-256) and store the hash in a time-limited cache; on each request, validate authorization first and then compute the token hash and check it against the denylist, rejecting requests with denylisted tokens.
EXAMPLE: Before: accept any JWT that passes signature/expiry checks. After: `if (isBlocklisted(token)) { denyRequest(); } else { proceedIfAuthorized(); }`
Authorization validation for message handling
WHAT: Authorization is based solely on a token’s `access_level` claim without verifying that the claim value is valid, expected, and mapped to the correct permissions for the requested action.
WHY: Attackers can forge or manipulate tokens to escalate privileges (e.g., set `access_level=ADMIN`) and gain unauthorized access to other users’ messages.
HOW: Treat tokens as untrusted input: validate signature and issuer/audience, enforce token expiration, strictly allowlist acceptable `access_level` values, and map them to explicit permissions for each operation before processing any user message.
EXAMPLE: Before processing a message, check `validateToken(token)` for signature/expiry/issuer, then ensure `access_level` is in `{USER, ADMIN}` and that the requested operation (e.g., viewing all messages) is only allowed when `access_level == ADMIN`.
Secure WebSocket Channel Usage
WHAT: WebSocket endpoints that accept connections over insecure ws:// expose all transmitted data (e.g., credentials) to eavesdropping and on-the-fly modification.
WHY: Attackers on the network can read or tamper with unencrypted WebSocket traffic, compromising confidentiality (password leakage) and integrity (message alteration).
HOW: Expose WebSocket endpoints only over wss:// (SSL/TLS); at endpoint level, check session.isSecure(), attach message handlers only if true, and explicitly close insecure sessions with an appropriate close reason.
EXAMPLE (Java):
Before: `@OnOpen public void start(Session session) { session.addMessageHandler(new AuthenticationMessageHandler(session.getBasicRemote())); }`
After: `@OnOpen public void start(Session session) { if (session.isSecure()) { session.addMessageHandler(new AuthenticationMessageHandler(session.getBasicRemote())); } else { session.close(new CloseReason(CloseReason.CloseCodes.CANNOT_ACCEPT, "Insecure channel used!")); } }`
Cloud Architecture Risk and Threat Assessment
WHAT: Failing to perform systematic risk assessments, threat modeling, and attack surface analysis leads to unrecognized threats and insecure architectural decisions.
WHY: Undiscovered threats and exposed attack surfaces can result in data loss, service disruption, and higher impact from successful attacks.
HOW: For each application and cloud component, regularly perform risk assessments, structured threat modeling, and attack surface reviews; document threats, likelihood, affected interfaces, and business impact, and use these results to prioritize and implement security controls.
EXAMPLE: N/A
Secure use of object storage access methods
WHAT: Risk of exposing sensitive data or control-plane access by using broad IAM policies, hardcoded credentials, long-lived or overly permissive signed URLs, or public object storage for non-public data.
WHY: These failures can allow anonymous or unauthorized users to read/modify objects, perform privileged API actions, or gain reconnaissance on your environment.
HOW: Use least-privilege IAM policies; never hardcode credentials (use managed identities/secret stores); generate signed URLs with minimal scope and short expirations using vetted libraries; restrict signed-URL issuance to authenticated/authorized users; and use public object storage only for explicitly non-sensitive, generic assets.
EXAMPLE: Before (bad): hardcode access keys and use a wildcard IAM policy that allows `s3:*` on `*`, or generate never-expiring signed URLs for all user files. After (good): use a role-based identity from the runtime environment, restrict IAM to specific buckets and actions, and issue short-lived signed URLs only for the requesting user’s objects.
Network Segmentation for Application Components
WHAT: Failing to separate public-facing components from sensitive backend services in distinct VPCs/subnets allows direct or lateral access to databases and internal systems from the internet or compromised hosts.
WHY: Inadequate network isolation can lead to data exfiltration, unauthorized access to “soft” backend systems, and full environment compromise if a public component is breached.
HOW: Place internet-facing components (gateways, load balancers, web frontends, bastions) only in public subnets; place databases, data stores, and backend servers only in private subnets with no direct internet route; restrict traffic so private subnets only accept connections from specific public-tier components and separate applications/customers into distinct VPCs or accounts.
EXAMPLE: Before: Database and web server share a public subnet with a route to an internet gateway, allowing direct internet access to the DB. After: Web server and load balancer in a public subnet; database in a private subnet with a security group that only allows connections from the web server’s security group and no route to the internet gateway.
Trust boundary validation between components
WHAT: Failing to validate and authenticate data, identities, and permissions at each trust boundary between components (e.g., API gateway, compute, storage, auth/IAM servers) can allow untrusted inputs or identities to be treated as trusted.
WHY: This can lead to unauthorized access, data exposure, privilege escalation, and integrity loss, especially in high‑risk or sensitive systems.
HOW: Treat every cross-component call as untrusted: enforce strong authentication and authorization per request, use ephemeral identities/credentials for compute to access storage, and apply rigorous validation and cryptographic protection on all data crossing boundaries.
EXAMPLE: Before: `storage.write(request.userId, request.body)` directly from compute. After: `token = iam.getEphemeralToken(request.authContext); iam.verify(token); storage.write(authorizedUserId(token), validatePayload(request.body));`
Trust Boundaries and Input Validation
WHAT: Failing to validate and constrain “dangerous” or user-controlled input before it crosses trust boundaries into high‑criticality components, or bypassing auth/identity checks, leads to direct use of untrusted data in sensitive operations.
WHY: This significantly increases the likelihood of successful attacks (e.g., injection, data corruption, unauthorized access) and wastes existing security infrastructure that is not being used as intended.
HOW: Treat all external input as untrusted; enforce authentication and authorization at entry points (e.g., API gateways), validate and sanitize user input based on strict allowlists, and ensure downstream components assume least-privilege identities when accessing storage or other sensitive resources.
EXAMPLE: Before: API directly forwards user JSON body to a high‑criticality service without auth or validation. After: API gateway enforces auth/identity, validates request schema and fields against an allowlist, then passes only validated, normalized data to the backend, which uses a constrained service identity for data access.
Web application logging, monitoring, and WAF hardening
WHAT: Failure to configure application-specific WAF rules and comprehensive logging/monitoring can leave critical endpoints unprotected, make attacks (e.g., scraping, abuse of sensitive APIs, DDoS) hard to detect, and hinder incident response.
WHY: Missing or weak controls can lead to data exposure, service disruption, undetected intrusion, and inability to reconstruct attacker actions for forensics or compliance.
HOW: Add custom WAF rules to filter routes to allowed endpoints, protect key technologies/endpoints, and rate-limit sensitive APIs; log all HTTP layer-7 calls with headers/metadata, internal actions with actor/permissions, trace IDs, and masked sensitive data; configure alerts for abnormal error rates, resource usage, DB access, health-check failures, deployment/container issues, and cost anomalies, tuned to a baseline and risk.
EXAMPLE: Configure WAF to allow only `/api/v1/public/*` and `/api/v1/auth/*` for anonymous users and apply strict rate limits to `/api/v1/payments/*`; log each request with `request_id`, `user_id`, `roles`, `path`, `status`, and omit or mask fields like `ssn` and `health_info` before writing to logs.
Cloud Service Model Security Responsibilities
WHAT: Misconfiguring security responsibilities when using IaaS, PaaS, or SaaS can leave authentication, authorization, data access, and networking controls unprotected where the CSP does not cover them.
WHY: Incorrect assumptions about what the cloud provider secures can lead to exposed services, data breaches, privilege escalation, and unpatched vulnerabilities in your application stack.
HOW: For each service (IaaS/PaaS/SaaS), explicitly document which layers you own (authN/Z, data stores, app code, network rules, OS/containers) and implement: strong authN/Z, least-privilege access, secure network configurations, and timely patching for all components under your control.
EXAMPLE: For an IaaS-hosted app, you must configure security groups/NACLs, patch the OS, secure the database, and implement application-level auth; for a PaaS app, you still implement application auth and secure external data stores, but rely on the provider for OS/container patching and internal network isolation.
Cloud shared-responsibility security
WHAT: Failing to understand and implement your share of security responsibilities (e.g., authz/authn, logging, code security, dependency patching) when using SaaS/managed/self-managed cloud services can leave critical gaps (unlogged access, unpatched libraries, weak access control).
WHY: Misaligned assumptions with the provider can result in data breaches, unauthorized access, or integrity loss because neither party fully secures some layers.
HOW: For each cloud tool/service, read the provider’s shared-responsibility and security docs; explicitly list which team owns: authentication/authorization, logging/monitoring, code security (e.g., OWASP Top 10 issues), and third‑party library patching; implement automation for updates/patching and review this mapping whenever services or configurations change.
Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) Input Validation and Allowlisting
WHAT: User-controlled URLs, IPs, or domains are passed directly to server-side request APIs, allowing attackers to make the application send arbitrary internal/external network requests (SSRF).
WHY: This can expose internal services, bypass network controls, and enable data exfiltration or further injection attacks.
HOW: Treat all user-supplied endpoints as untrusted; parse and validate them with robust libraries, then enforce an allowlist of known-good hosts/URLs or service identifiers before issuing any outbound request.
EXAMPLE: Before: `requests.get(user_input_url)`; After: `if user_input_url in ALLOWED_ENDPOINTS: requests.get(user_input_url)`
SSRF input validation and allowlisting for IPs and domains
WHAT: User-controlled network targets (IP, domain, URL) may be validated incorrectly, allowing SSRF via malformed encodings, unsafe redirects, or DNS-based tricks.
WHY: Attackers can reach internal services, exfiltrate data, or exploit internal DNS/resolver/APIs by bypassing naive format checks or DNS resolution logic.
HOW: For SSRF sinks, disable client-side redirect following; validate simple strings with strict regex; for IPs/domains, use vetted libraries for format/encoding validation, then compare the normalized result against a strict allowlist (both IPv4/IPv6 or trusted domains) using exact string comparison; avoid relying on DNS resolution alone for validation.
EXAMPLE: Before (Java): `URL url = new URL(userUrl); HttpURLConnection c = (HttpURLConnection) url.openConnection(); c.setInstanceFollowRedirects(true);`
After: `URL url = new URL(userUrl); HttpURLConnection c = (HttpURLConnection) url.openConnection(); c.setInstanceFollowRedirects(false); InetAddress ip = InetAddress.getByName(url.getHost()); if (!allowedIps.contains(ip.getHostAddress())) reject();`
SSRF domain validation and allowlisting
WHAT: User-controlled domain names used in outbound requests can be malformed or point to untrusted or internal targets, leading to SSRF even when basic validation is present.
WHY: Attackers can access internal services, local IPs, or sensitive infrastructure by abusing DNS resolution, DNS pinning, and insufficient domain/allowlist checks.
HOW: Validate domain syntax using a battle-tested library that does not perform DNS resolution; then strictly compare the normalized domain against a maintained allowlist of trusted application domains; ensure your organization’s domains resolve via internal DNS first; continuously monitor allowlisted domains to detect resolution to local or internal IPs that should not be reachable.
EXAMPLE: Before (Java): `URL url = new URL(userInput); httpClient.get(url);` After: `if (DomainValidator.isValid(host) && allowedDomains.contains(host)) { httpClient.get(new URL("https://" + host)); } else { reject(); }`
Network URL and IP handling for outbound requests
WHAT: Accepting and using arbitrary user-supplied URLs for outbound requests (e.g., webhooks) can let attackers trigger SSRF and reach internal or unintended services.
WHY: An attacker can pivot through the application to scan internal networks, access internal-only services, or exfiltrate data via the server’s network privileges.
HOW: Do not accept full URLs from users; instead, accept only validated IP addresses or domain names, and enforce network-layer controls (firewall/segregation) so the application can only reach explicitly allowed destinations or external ranges as per policy.
EXAMPLE: Before: `requests.get(user_input_url)`. After: accept `user_domain`, validate it as a domain/IP, resolve it, verify it is not internal or in a forbidden range, then perform `requests.get("https://" + validated_domain)` only if it passes all checks and firewall rules.
Server-side request validation for external targets
WHAT: Failure to properly validate user-supplied target IPs/domains and request parameters can allow SSRF or calls to internal networks, including via DNS pinning and redirects.
WHY: Attackers can reach internal services, exfiltrate data, or pivot inside the network by abusing application-layer URL handling.
HOW: Treat target IP/domain/protocol/parameters as untrusted; validate IPs as public (not private/localhost/link-local), verify domains as external via an internal-only DNS resolver, resolve all A/AAAA records and re-check IPs, enforce an allowlist of protocols (HTTP/HTTPS), strictly constrain token name/value character sets and lengths, require POST only, and disable HTTP redirects.
EXAMPLE (Python): `ip = ipaddress.ip_address(user_ip); assert ip.is_global` to reject private/loopback/link-local before building and sending the POST request.
Protecting cloud metadata services from SSRF
WHAT: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) can be used to access cloud instance metadata services (e.g., AWS IMDS, Azure, GCP) and steal credentials or access tokens.
WHY: Successful SSRF against metadata services can lead to credential theft, privilege escalation, and full compromise of cloud resources.
HOW: In AWS, migrate instances to IMDSv2 and disable IMDSv1; in all clouds, restrict network access to metadata endpoints and use static analysis (e.g., Semgrep SSRF rules) to detect unsafe outbound requests.
EXAMPLE: Before (AWS): EC2 instance with IMDSv1 enabled by default. After: Configure instance metadata options with `HttpTokens=required`, `HttpEndpoint=enabled`, and ensure application code cannot make arbitrary HTTP calls to `169.254.169.254`.
JWT algorithm validation for Java
WHAT: Tokens must never be accepted with the "none" algorithm or with any algorithm other than the one explicitly expected; otherwise altered tokens may be treated as valid and their claims trusted.
WHY: Accepting tokens without a valid signature lets attackers modify claims (e.g., roles, user IDs) and gain unauthorized access or escalate privileges.
HOW: Use a JWT library that does not support or accept "none" as a valid algorithm; during verification, always configure the verifier with a specific algorithm and key instead of accepting the algorithm from the token header.
EXAMPLE:
Before (unsafe): `JWTVerifier verifier = JWT.require(Algorithm.NONE).build();`
After (safe): `JWTVerifier verifier = JWT.require(Algorithm.HMAC256(keyHMAC)).build(); DecodedJWT jwt = verifier.verify(token);`
Session cookie security for authentication
WHAT: Use a random string as an auth cookie value and never store or expose the raw value in client-accessible contexts.
WHY: Exposing the raw token (e.g., via XSS) lets attackers set valid cookies and hijack sessions.
HOW: Send the random string as a hardened cookie (HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite, Max-Age, appropriate prefixes), avoid the Expires attribute so it’s cleared on browser close, ensure Max-Age ≤ JWT expiry, and store only a SHA256 hash of the random string server-side or in tokens.
EXAMPLE: Before: `cookie.value = randomString; token.session = randomString;` After: `cookie.value = randomString; token.sessionHash = SHA256(randomString);`
JWT token context binding and revocation
WHAT: Tokens that are not bound to a stable, non-IP client context (e.g., a random fingerprint stored in a secure cookie and hashed in the token) can be replayed by attackers if stolen, and JWTs also lack built-in user-driven revocation.
WHY: An attacker who obtains a valid unbound or non-revocable token can impersonate the user until token expiry, bypassing authentication and session controls.
HOW: Bind tokens to a random, per-user fingerprint stored in a hardened cookie (Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite) and store only its cryptographic hash in the token; on validation, recompute and verify the hash and reject tokens with mismatched or missing context. Avoid using IP addresses as context, and implement a server-side revocation mechanism (e.g., a blacklist or token versioning) to invalidate tokens before expiry when needed.
EXAMPLE: Before: issue JWTs with only subject and expiry, validate only signature and expiry. After: issue JWTs with a hashed fingerprint claim derived from a secure cookie, validate signature, expiry, issuer, and that the recomputed fingerprint hash from the cookie matches the claim; additionally, check token ID/version against a revocation list or user session store.
JWT token revocation and logout handling
WHAT: JWTs are stateless and cannot be explicitly revoked by users; stolen tokens remain valid until expiration unless you implement server-side revocation (denylist) or a secure sidejacking-resistant pattern.
WHY: Without revocation, an attacker who steals a valid JWT can continue to access protected resources until the token expires, enabling prolonged account compromise.
HOW: Implement a server-side denylist storing a digest (e.g., SHA-256 HEX) of revoked tokens checked on every request, and/or use hardened cookies plus short-lived JWTs and clear JWTs on logout/close; ensure the denylist entry lives at least until token expiry and is shared across all service instances.
EXAMPLE: Before: accept any structurally valid, unexpired JWT. After: on each request, compute SHA-256 digest of the presented token, look it up in a centralized `revoked_token` table (`jwt_token_digest` + `revocation_date`); if present, reject the request as logged-out/invalid.
Token Information Disclosure in JWTs
WHAT: Tokens (e.g., JWTs) that are only base64-encoded and not encrypted can expose internal information (roles, identifiers, formats) when an attacker gains access to them.
WHY: Exposed token contents can aid reconnaissance, privilege escalation, or targeted attacks by revealing system internals and security-related data.
HOW: Encrypt tokens using a strong symmetric AEAD algorithm (e.g., AES-GCM via a vetted library like Google Tink), ensure protection against padding-oracle and similar cryptanalytic attacks, and always keep token signatures and verification in place for integrity.
EXAMPLE: Before: issue plain signed JWTs and send them directly to clients; After: sign the JWT as usual, then encrypt the entire token with AES-GCM (via Tink AEAD) before transport, and decrypt + verify signature on receipt.
Secure storage of JWT tokens in the browser
WHAT: Storing JWT tokens in cookies or browser storage (localStorage/sessionStorage) without controls can expose them to theft via automatic browser sending, persistence across restarts, or XSS access.
WHY: A stolen token allows attackers to impersonate users, maintain unauthorized sessions, and bypass authentication until the token expires.
HOW: Prefer sessionStorage or short-lived tokens in localStorage; never store tokens in cookies accessible to JavaScript; add device/browser fingerprint data to tokens; implement short expirations, idle/absolute timeouts, token rotation, refresh tokens, and a strict Content Security Policy to reduce XSS risk.
EXAMPLE: When calling APIs, read the token from sessionStorage/localStorage in JavaScript and send it explicitly in the `Authorization: Bearer <token>` header instead of relying on cookies that are automatically attached to every request.
Secure handling of browser-stored authentication tokens
WHAT: Storing long-lived authentication tokens in localStorage/sessionStorage without rotation, origin checks, or encapsulation exposes them to theft and abuse (e.g., via XSS or cross-origin requests), and using cookies for tokens without CSRF protection enables unauthorized requests.
WHY: Compromised tokens or CSRF can let attackers act as legitimate users, persist access across sessions, and exfiltrate data or perform sensitive operations.
HOW: Use short token lifetimes (e.g., 15–30 min idle, 8-hour absolute), implement token rotation and refresh tokens, restrict token use to an allowlist of origins, encapsulate tokens in JavaScript modules/closures instead of direct storage when possible, use CSP to block unexpected domains, and if tokens are in cookies, mark them as secure/HttpOnly and add robust CSRF protections (e.g., same-site cookies plus anti-CSRF tokens).
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): `localStorage.setItem("token", data.token);` and sending it to any URL. After (safer): encapsulate token in a module with an origin allowlist and short-lived/rotated tokens: `myFetchModule.setToken(data.token); myFetchModule.fetch("/services/validate", { method: "POST" });` with the module only attaching `Authorization` when `new URL(req.url).origin` is in a predefined allowlist.
Weak JWT HMAC Secret
WHAT: Using JWTs signed with an HMAC algorithm and a weak, guessable, or reused secret allows attackers who obtain a token to perform offline cracking and forge valid tokens.
WHY: If the HMAC secret is cracked, attackers can modify and re-sign tokens to escalate privileges, hijack accounts, or impersonate other users.
HOW: Use a strong, unique HMAC secret of at least 64 random characters generated from a cryptographically secure random source, store it securely, and consider using asymmetric signing (e.g., RSA) instead of HMAC where appropriate.
EXAMPLE: Before: `JWT_SECRET="mysecret"`; After: `JWT_SECRET` set to a 64+ character cryptographically random value (e.g., from a secure key management system or OS CSPRNG).
Certificate/Public Key Pinning in Client Applications
WHAT: Risk of Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) attacks when relying solely on generic CA-based TLS validation, especially if a rogue certificate is issued or a malicious CA is injected into the client trust store; failure mode is accepting a certificate that is valid per CA chain but not the expected one for the host.
WHY: An attacker who can obtain or install such a certificate/CA can transparently intercept, read, or modify supposedly secure traffic, and in some environments can also change how the mobile or client application behaves.
HOW: Only consider pinning if you fully control both client and server and can securely and non-disruptively update pins; preload expected certificates or public keys at development time where possible; on each connection, use the platform’s TLS callback (e.g., OnConnect) to validate that the server’s leaf or intermediate certificate/public key matches one of a maintained pinset, and fail closed if it does not; do not pin when you cannot predict keys in advance, cannot update pins securely, or do not control both ends.
EXAMPLE: In a mobile app using a TLS library with an OnConnect callback, after normal TLS verification succeeds, retrieve the server certificate’s public key, compute its hash, and compare it against a hard-coded allowlist of expected hashes; if no match is found, abort the connection and surface a hard failure.
Certificate and Public Key Pinning Strategy
WHAT: Improper or overly broad certificate/public key pinning (e.g., pinning a root CA or a wide intermediate CA, or allowing users to bypass pin failures) can cause excessive trust in unintended certificates or complete loss of connectivity when certificates rotate.
WHY: Over-trusting CAs increases exposure to misissued or compromised certificates; brittle pinning without backups or strict failure handling can brick the application or allow man-in-the-middle attacks if users can click through warnings.
HOW: Prefer pinning the leaf certificate or its subjectPublicKeyInfo, and maintain a small pinset with backup pins (e.g., an alternate leaf or intermediate) to handle rotation; compare the runtime certificate/key (or its hash) to embedded pins and, on mismatch, hard-fail the connection, log locally, and do not offer a user override.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): trust any certificate chaining to a pinned root CA and allow users to “accept anyway” on pin mismatch. After (more secure): embed hashes of the expected leaf certificate’s subjectPublicKeyInfo plus one backup pin; on TLS handshake, extract the peer’s SPKI, hash it, verify it matches one of the pins, and abort the connection with no bypass if it does not.
Certificate and Public Key Pinning Validation
WHAT: Incorrect or incomplete implementation of certificate/public key pinning and TLS verification (e.g., not checking SSL_get_verify_result, not verifying peer certificate is non-NULL, or writing custom pinning logic from scratch) can disable effective TLS security.
WHY: Flawed pinning or certificate validation can allow man-in-the-middle attacks, letting attackers intercept, modify, or impersonate secure connections.
HOW: Use platform-provided or well-reviewed libraries and declarative configs for pinning (Android Network Security Configuration, iOS ATS/TrustKit, OkHTTP pinning, .NET ServicePointManager, electron-ssl-pinning). In OpenSSL, always call SSL_get_verify_result and require X509_V_OK, then call SSL_get_peer_certificate and fail/close the connection if the certificate is NULL or does not match the expected pins.
EXAMPLE: In OpenSSL, after SSL_connect: `if (SSL_get_verify_result(ssl) != X509_V_OK) { /* log & close */ } X509 *cert = SSL_get_peer_certificate(ssl); if (!cert) { /* log & close */ } /* verify pin against cert */`
TLS certificate verification in OpenSSL/Electron
WHAT: Failing to verify the TLS peer certificate (e.g., not checking SSL_get_verify_result == X509_V_OK or accepting a NULL certificate from SSL_get_peer_certificate / ses.setCertificateVerifyProc) causes insecure connections that can be silently intercepted.
WHY: Attackers can perform man-in-the-middle attacks, decrypt or modify traffic, and impersonate trusted services if certificate validation is skipped or incorrectly implemented.
HOW: Always call SSL_get_verify_result and require X509_V_OK; call SSL_get_peer_certificate and reject connections when it returns NULL; in Electron, use electron-ssl-pinning or implement strict checks in ses.setCertificateVerifyProc that only accept valid, expected certificates or pins.
EXAMPLE (C/OpenSSL): Before: `SSL_connect(ssl); /* no verification */` After: `SSL_connect(ssl); X509 *cert = SSL_get_peer_certificate(ssl); if (!cert) fail(); long r = SSL_get_verify_result(ssl); if (r != X509_V_OK) fail();`
Browser Extension Security Guidelines
WHAT: Extensions may over-request permissions, leak or inject data, use insecure communication, load untrusted code/updates, or rely on vulnerable dependencies, leading to privacy and integrity failures.
WHY: These flaws can expose browsing history and personal data, enable XSS/code execution, allow man‑in‑the‑middle attacks, and propagate malicious updates to all users.
HOW: Request only minimal permissions (use optional permissions, audit and remove unused ones); sanitize and safely render user input (avoid innerHTML, prefer textContent, use CSP and libraries like DOMPurify); always use HTTPS and validate responses; never load or eval remote scripts, restrict sources via CSP and use extension messaging; sign and distribute updates only via trusted marketplaces with integrity checks; keep third‑party libraries updated and remove vulnerable ones.
EXAMPLE: Before (over‑privileged manifest): "permissions": ["tabs","http://*/*","https://*/*","storage"]; After (least privilege): "permissions": ["storage"], "optional_permissions": ["tabs","https://example.com/*"].
Third-Party Dependencies in Browser Extensions
WHAT: Using outdated or vulnerable third-party libraries (e.g., fixed versions with known CVEs) in an extension can introduce exploitable code paths into your application.
WHY: Attackers can leverage known vulnerabilities in these libraries to execute arbitrary code, escalate privileges, or exfiltrate data through your extension.
HOW: Regularly audit dependencies with tools like `npm audit` or OWASP Dependency-Check, avoid unmaintained libraries, pin to secure versions, and update promptly when security patches are released.
EXAMPLE: Before: `"vulnerable-lib": "1.0.0"` with known issues; After: run audits, remove or upgrade to `"vulnerable-lib": "1.2.3"` or replace with a maintained alternative.
Prototype-based Data Skimming in Extension-Injected Page Scripts
WHAT: Executing extension logic that handles sensitive data (e.g., tokens, API keys, user data) in the web page’s main-world context allows page scripts to intercept it via polluted/overwritten prototypes or APIs (e.g., Object.prototype, window.postMessage).
WHY: A malicious or compromised page can exfiltrate sensitive data by redefining global objects, accessors, or event handlers used by the injected script, leading to credential theft and privacy breaches.
HOW: Never process or store sensitive data in scripts running in the page’s main-world context; keep all sensitive handling in the extension’s isolated world or dedicated extension-controlled UIs (popup, options page, side panel). When communication with page scripts is unavoidable, send only non-sensitive, minimal results (e.g., boolean validation outcome) instead of raw secrets, and do not rely on “native” prototypes or early execution timing for safety.
EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe): Inject a <script> into the page that reads a secret from the extension and assigns it to window.apiController.apiKey or posts it via window.postMessage. After (safer): Keep the secret entirely in the extension context; only send a non-sensitive flag (e.g., isValid: true/false) to the page, and perform all secret-dependent logic inside the extension.
HTTP Security Response Headers
WHAT: Missing or misconfigured HTTP security response headers (X-Frame-Options/CSP frame-ancestors, X-Content-Type-Options, Referrer-Policy, Content-Type, HSTS, and secure Set-Cookie attributes) allow clickjacking, XSS, information disclosure, and insecure transport.
WHY: Attackers can frame your pages for clickjacking, execute scripts via MIME confusion or charset tricks, leak sensitive URLs via referrers, or downgrade users to HTTP and steal or tamper with cookies.
HOW: For all HTML/interactive responses, send: `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none'` (or `X-Frame-Options: DENY`), `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, a strict `Referrer-Policy` (e.g., `strict-origin-when-cross-origin`), correct `Content-Type` with charset, `Strict-Transport-Security` for HTTPS-only, and secure cookie flags (Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite).
EXAMPLE: Before: response has no security headers. After (HTTP): add `Content-Type: text/html; charset=UTF-8`, `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin`, `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none'`; when serving over HTTPS, also add `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains`.
HTTP Security Headers Configuration
WHAT: Misconfigured or missing HTTP security headers (HSTS, CSP, CORS, COOP, COEP) can lead to insecure transport, XSS/data injection, over-broad cross-origin access, or side-channel attacks.
WHY: Incorrect settings may expose users to man-in-the-middle, data theft, script injection, or Spectre-like attacks, or lock out legitimate users if HSTS is misconfigured.
HOW:
- Set HSTS with a reasonable max-age, includeSubDomains, and preload only after validating certificate management and renewal processes.
- Configure CSP explicitly for pages that execute scripts, defining strict allowed sources; avoid applying CSP blindly to non-rendered REST API responses.
- For Access-Control-Allow-Origin, prefer explicit trusted origins over "*", except for intentionally public APIs.
- Use COOP and COEP to isolate browsing contexts and restrict cross-origin resource loading to same-origin or explicitly permitted resources.
EXAMPLE:
Before: Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *
After:  Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://yoursite.com
Cross-origin security and information-leakage hardening headers
WHAT: Missing or misconfigured security-related HTTP response headers (COEP, CORP, Permissions-Policy, Server, X-Powered-By, X-AspNet-Version, X-AspNetMvc-Version, X-DNS-Prefetch-Control) can allow cross-origin data leaks, feature abuse, or unnecessary server fingerprinting.
WHY: Attackers can exploit cross-origin resource inclusion (e.g., Spectre-style leaks, data exfiltration) or use detailed server/stack metadata to more easily target known vulnerabilities and track users.
HOW: Set strict defaults: `Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp`, `Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy: same-site`, and a minimal `Permissions-Policy` that disables unneeded features or limits them to trusted origins; remove or obfuscate `Server`, `X-Powered-By`, `X-AspNet-Version`, and `X-AspNetMvc-Version`; and set `X-DNS-Prefetch-Control: off` when you do not control outbound links to avoid DNS-leakage.
EXAMPLE:
Before (leaky):
Server: Apache/2.4.54 (Ubuntu)
X-Powered-By: PHP/8.1
[no COEP/CORP/Permissions-Policy headers]
After (hardened):
Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp
Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy: same-site
Permissions-Policy: geolocation=(), camera=(), microphone=(), interest-cohort=()
Server: webserver
X-Powered-By:
X-AspNet-Version:
X-AspNetMvc-Version:
X-DNS-Prefetch-Control: off
Use X-Frame-Options to prevent clickjacking
WHAT: Missing or inconsistently set X-Frame-Options headers allow your pages to be embedded in iframes on other sites, enabling clickjacking attacks.
WHY: Attackers can trick users into clicking hidden UI elements (e.g., “Transfer money”, “Delete account”) framed over benign content, causing unauthorized actions.
HOW: Configure your web server or application framework to always send X-Frame-Options with a safe value (DENY or SAMEORIGIN) on all sensitive responses, and ensure it applies to all status codes (e.g., use “always” flags where supported).
EXAMPLE: Before (PHP): // no header set
After (PHP): header("X-Frame-Options: DENY");
SQL Injection Prevention
WHAT: Dynamic SQL queries built via string concatenation with user-supplied input (e.g., request parameters) allow attackers to inject and execute arbitrary SQL commands.
WHY: Successful SQL injection can expose or modify sensitive data, bypass authentication/authorization, and compromise the entire database or underlying system.
HOW: Avoid building SQL with string concatenation; instead use prepared/parameterized queries or safely constructed stored procedures, and apply allow-list input validation to user-controlled fields; do not rely solely on escaping user input.
EXAMPLE (Java – before): `String q = "SELECT balance FROM users WHERE name = " + request.getParameter("name");`
EXAMPLE (Java – after): `PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement("SELECT balance FROM users WHERE name = ?"); ps.setString(1, request.getParameter("name"));`
Use parameterized queries and safe stored procedures to prevent SQL injection
WHAT: Building SQL queries by concatenating or interpolating user-controlled input into query strings allows attackers to inject and execute arbitrary SQL.
WHY: SQL injection can lead to data theft, data corruption, authentication bypass, or full compromise of the database server.
HOW: Always use prepared/parameterized queries or safely implemented stored procedures; bind user input as parameters (never into the SQL text), and perform input validation where appropriate.
EXAMPLE: Before (Java, unsafe): `Query q = session.createQuery("from Inventory where productID='" + userSupplied + "'");`
EXAMPLE: After (Java, safe): `Query q = session.createQuery("from Inventory where productID=:productid"); q.setParameter("productid", userSupplied);`
Stored procedures and dynamic SQL security
WHAT: Granting overly privileged database roles (e.g., db_owner) to execute stored procedures, or building dynamic SQL inside stored procedures with unvalidated user input, allows attackers to run arbitrary SQL or gain full database control if the app is compromised.
WHY: Excessive DB privileges and injectable dynamic SQL can lead to data disclosure, data tampering, or full database takeover.
HOW: Assign the minimum DB role needed (create explicit EXECUTE-only roles instead of db_owner), avoid dynamic SQL in stored procedures, and where dynamic SQL is unavoidable, strictly validate or map user-controlled values via allowlists before use; never concatenate raw user input into SQL.
EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe dynamic SQL in stored procedure): `SET @sql = 'SELECT * FROM ' + @tableName; EXEC(@sql);` After (safer): map `@param` via a CASE/lookup to a fixed set of table names and use that mapped value in the query; reject any unexpected value.
Safe Dynamic SQL Query Construction
WHAT: Risk of SQL injection when user input is concatenated directly into SQL queries, including for sort order or other dynamic clauses.
WHY: Unsanitized or improperly handled input can alter the intended query, leading to data exposure, modification, or full database compromise.
HOW: Never concatenate raw user input into SQL; convert user-controlled values to non-String types (boolean, numeric, date, enums) and/or use them only to select from fixed, hard-coded options; always use parameterized queries, stored procedures, or an ORM, and apply strict input validation as a secondary defense; avoid relying solely on escaping user input.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): `String q = "SELECT * FROM emp ORDER BY Salary " + userSort;` After (safer): `String q = "SELECT * FROM emp ORDER BY Salary " + (sortAsc ? "ASC" : "DESC");` where `sortAsc` is a validated boolean and other user inputs are bound via prepared statement parameters.
Least privilege for database and OS accounts
WHAT: Over-privileged database and OS accounts (e.g., app using DBA/root, shared admin DB users, direct table access) allow attackers to read/modify/delete data or the OS even via minor bugs or SQL injection.
WHY: Excessive privileges turn small injection or logic flaws into full database/host compromise, unauthorized data access, and irreversible data tampering.
HOW: Create separate DB users per application and per function (read vs write); grant only required SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE rights on specific tables/views; avoid CREATE/DROP/DELETE for app accounts; restrict app accounts to needed stored procedures; never run the DBMS as root/system—use a dedicated, minimally privileged OS account.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): `app_user` is DBA and DBMS runs as `root`; app executes `SELECT * FROM users`. After (safer): `login_app_user` has only `SELECT username, password_hash FROM v_users_login` on a view; `signup_app_user` has only `INSERT` on `users`; DBMS runs as `dbsvc` with no admin OS rights.
Allow-list input validation for SQL
WHAT: Relying solely on input validation and then inserting validated data into SQL queries via string concatenation can still lead to SQL injection vulnerabilities.
WHY: Attackers may craft inputs that pass validation but alter the SQL query, leading to data theft, corruption, or unauthorized access.
HOW: Use parameterized queries/bind variables for all dynamic values; use allow-list validation only as a secondary defense, and never build SQL statements by concatenating user-controlled strings.
EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe): `query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = " + userInput;` → After (safe): `query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?"; stmt.setInt(1, userInputInt);`
SQL injection prevention
WHAT: Risk of SQL injection when SQL queries are built by concatenating or interpolating user-controlled input into query strings.
WHY: Attackers can modify queries to read, alter, or delete data, or execute administrative operations on the database.
HOW: Always use parameterized queries with prepared statements or safe stored procedures; never concatenate raw user input into SQL; validate and constrain input to expected formats and types.
EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe): `query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = " + userInput;` After (safe): `query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?"; stmt = conn.prepareStatement(query); stmt.setInt(1, userId);`
HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) configuration
WHAT: Failing to configure HSTS (or misconfiguring max-age/includeSubDomains/preload) allows browsers to use HTTP or accept invalid certificates, enabling man-in-the-middle attacks and some cookie-related attacks.
WHY: Attackers can intercept or modify traffic, downgrade HTTPS to HTTP, or abuse subdomains to manipulate cookies and track users.
HOW: Always serve your site over HTTPS with a valid certificate, then send a Strict-Transport-Security header with a sufficiently long max-age and includeSubDomains; use preload only after confirming all present and future subdomains will support HTTPS, and set the secure flag on all cookies.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000`
After (more secure): `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains; preload`
Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) prevention
WHAT: Missing per-object access control allows users to access or modify other users’ objects by tampering with identifiers in URLs, POST bodies, or hidden fields (e.g., changing /users/123 to /users/124).
WHY: Attackers can read or modify data belonging to other users, leading to data breaches, account takeover, or unauthorized actions.
HOW: Always derive the acting user from authenticated session data; on every object access/update, query only within objects owned/allowed for that user and enforce permission checks; store step-flow identifiers in server-side session; use non-enumerable random/UUID identifiers as defense-in-depth, but never as a replacement for access control.
EXAMPLE: Vulnerable (Rails): `@project = Project.find(params[:id])`
EXAMPLE: Secure (Rails): `@project = @current_user.projects.find(params[:id])`
Credential stuffing and password spraying protection via adaptive MFA
WHAT: Failure to enforce multi-factor authentication (MFA), especially under suspicious login conditions, allows attackers to compromise accounts using credential stuffing, password spraying, or brute-force attacks.
WHY: Successful account takeover can lead to data theft, financial fraud, and unauthorized privileged or administrative actions.
HOW: Implement MFA for all accounts where possible, and enforce adaptive/step-up MFA when risk signals are present (new device/IP, unusual or untrusted country, IP on denylist or anonymization service, IP trying many accounts, high login volume, or before high-risk actions like large transactions or admin changes).
EXAMPLE: On login, evaluate risk signals (IP reputation, geo-location, device fingerprint, login volume); if any are triggered or a high-risk action is requested, require a second factor (e.g., FIDO2 passkey, OTP) before granting or continuing the session.
Multi-factor and Layered Authentication for High-Risk Actions
WHAT: Missing or inconsistent strong authentication for high-risk actions (e.g., large financial transactions, admin configuration changes) and privileged roles, leaving accounts protected only by passwords.
WHY: Increases exposure to credential stuffing, password spraying, and brute-force attacks, potentially leading to account takeover and unauthorized high-impact operations.
HOW: Require MFA “step-up” authentication for high-risk actions and all administrator accounts; optionally allowlist only well-validated enterprise IP ranges for reduced prompts; where MFA is not possible, implement layered defenses (rate limiting, anomaly detection, IP reputation, device fingerprinting) and ensure defenses are monitored with metrics and coordinated across teams.
EXAMPLE: Before: Directly execute admin configuration changes after a single password login. After: On any admin action or large transaction, trigger an MFA challenge (e.g., TOTP or WebAuthn) and log the attempt with IP and user role for monitoring.
Credential stuffing and automated login mitigation
WHAT: Failure to detect and mitigate credential stuffing and automated login attempts (e.g., bots rotating IPs, bypassing simple rate limits) allows large-scale unauthorized access attempts against user accounts.
WHY: Successful automated attacks can lead to account takeover, data theft, and service abuse, even when passwords are not directly leaked from your system.
HOW: Implement layered defenses: conditional CAPTCHA on suspicious/high‑risk logins; IP-based mitigation with graduated, temporary blocking using both short/long time windows, volume patterns, IP classification, and geolocation; correlate traffic with proxy/hosting IP intelligence; store and analyze per‑account IP and device fingerprints to trigger locks/alerts on anomalous activity.
EXAMPLE: Before: Only per‑IP rate limiting on /login. After: Add risk engine that, on high‑risk signals (hosting IP + unusual geolocation + new device), forces CAPTCHA, tightens rate limits, and temporarily blocks or challenges further attempts while logging and alerting on abnormal patterns.
Require unpredictable, non-enumerable usernames
WHAT: Credential stuffing and password spraying become easier when usernames are predictable (e.g., email addresses, full names, or sequential IDs).
WHY: Predictable usernames allow attackers to reuse credential dumps and to enumerate valid accounts with low-volume requests.
HOW: Do not use email as the login identifier; generate or require unique usernames that are not derived from personal data or simple sequences, and enforce server-side checks to reject predictable patterns.
EXAMPLE: Before: username = user.email; After: username = randomSlug(10) stored and shown to user, with validation rejecting usernames matching /^john\.doe\d+@example\.com$/ or incremental IDs.
Credential stuffing defenses, leaked-password checks, and security notifications
WHAT: Risk of ineffective or harmful defenses against credential stuffing, failure to check new passwords against known-breached datasets, and missing or noisy notifications about suspicious account activity (e.g., logins failing MFA, unusual password resets, concurrent sessions).
WHY: Poor controls can allow automated account takeover, reuse of compromised passwords, and undetected hijacking of user accounts, or can degrade availability and usability for legitimate users.
HOW: Implement rate-limiting and friction that slow automated attacks without blocking JavaScript or excessively delaying all users; verify new passwords against breached-password datasets (e.g., ASVS 2.1.7, Pwned Passwords or self-hosted equivalent); generate user notifications only for high‑risk events (successful login failing MFA, unusual password reset patterns, suspicious concurrent sessions), and provide UI to review recent logins and terminate active sessions.
EXAMPLE: When creating/updating a password, call a breached-password lookup service and reject matches; on successful password login followed by MFA failure, send an out‑of‑band alert and flag the account for additional verification before honoring multiple reset requests from new devices/IPs.
Secure automotive software and communication design
WHAT: Automotive software and communication protocols (e.g., CAN, OTA, telematics, integrated systems) may lack authentication, encryption, access control, and patching, allowing message injection, malicious firmware, remote control, or data exfiltration.
WHY: Exploitation can lead to arbitrary code execution, unauthorized control of safety‑critical functions (brakes, steering), privacy violations, and persistent compromise via unpatched or legacy components.
HOW: Require mutual authentication and encryption on all in-vehicle and external channels; enforce strict role-based access control and least privilege for apps, APIs, and diagnostic interfaces; validate and sign all firmware/software (including third-party components) and verify signatures before install; segregate safety‑critical networks from infotainment/telematics; regularly patch known vulnerabilities and deprecate insecure legacy protocols.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure OTA): device downloads firmware from any reachable URL and flashes it without checks. After (secure OTA): device connects only to pinned update servers over TLS, validates server certificate, verifies firmware signature against an embedded public key, and aborts update if any check fails.
Secure Password Storage with Modern Hashing
