WHAT: Storing passwords with weak, fast, or reversible mechanisms (e.g., encryption or unsalted/low-cost hashes) allows attackers who obtain the password store to crack passwords offline via brute force or dictionary attacks.
WHY: Compromised password hashes can be efficiently brute forced, leading to account takeover, credential stuffing on other sites, and large-scale user compromise.
HOW: Always hash passwords (do not encrypt) using a modern, slow, memory-hard password hashing function with strong parameters: prefer Argon2id (≥19 MiB memory, iterations ≥2, parallelism =1); if unavailable use scrypt (CPU/memory cost ≥2^17, block size ≥8, parallelization =1); for legacy bcrypt use work factor ≥10 and enforce max password length ≤72 bytes; for FIPS-140 use PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA-256 with iterations ≥600,000; optionally add a server-side pepper in addition to per-password salts.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure, pseudocode): `stored = SHA256(user_password)` or `stored = encrypt(user_password, key)`; After (more secure): `stored = Argon2id.hash(user_password, memory=19*1024*1024, iterations=2, parallelism=1)`.
Secure password storage with salting and peppering
WHAT: Passwords stored with unsalted or weak hashes are vulnerable to offline cracking using wordlists, brute force, and rainbow tables once an attacker obtains the hash database.
WHY: Compromised password hashes can be efficiently cracked with modern hardware, leading to account takeover and reuse attacks across other sites.
HOW: Use modern password hashing algorithms (e.g., Argon2id, bcrypt, PBKDF2) that include per-user random salts; additionally, use a secret pepper stored separately in a secrets vault or HSM, never in the password database, and plan for pepper rotation via forced password resets if the pepper is compromised.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): `stored_hash = SHA256(password)`; After (more secure): `stored_hash = Argon2id(hash(password + per_user_salt + secret_pepper))` with `per_user_salt` in DB and `secret_pepper` in a secure vault.
Password Hashing with Peppers and Work Factors
WHAT: Improper password hashing (e.g., using fast hashes, weak/random-less peppers, or misconfigured work factors) can lead to easily crackable password databases and potential DoS via excessive CPU usage on login.
WHY: Weak or misconfigured password hashing allows attackers who obtain the hash database to recover passwords more easily, and overly expensive verification can be abused to exhaust server resources.
HOW: Use a modern password hashing algorithm (e.g., Argon2id, scrypt) with recommended parameters; add a securely generated random pepper either before hashing or as an HMAC key after hashing; tune work factors/parameters so verification takes <1s on production hardware and periodically increase them as hardware improves.
EXAMPLE (pseudocode, pre-hash pepper): `stored_hash = Hash( password || server_pepper )` with `server_pepper` generated via a CSPRNG and stored separately from the DB; on login, recompute with the same algorithm and parameters and compare in constant time.
Password hashing configuration and pre-hashing with bcrypt
WHAT: Misconfiguring password hashing (weak cost/parameters, exceeding bcrypt input limits, or unsafe pre-hashing) can lead to easily crackable password hashes or collisions when combining bcrypt with other hash functions.
WHY: Attackers who obtain password hashes (e.g., via breach) can crack weakly hashed passwords much faster, reuse them elsewhere, or exploit collisions/password shucking to reduce cracking to breaking a fast hash.
HOW: Use Argon2id when available; otherwise use scrypt with recommended (N,r,p) sets, or bcrypt only for legacy with cost ≥ 10 and enforce max password length ≤ bcrypt’s limit (typically 72 bytes). If pre-hashing for bcrypt is unavoidable, encode the hash (e.g., base64) and use a keyed HMAC with a secret pepper stored outside the database to prevent null-byte issues and password shucking.
EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe): bcrypt(sha512(password), salt, cost); After (safer): bcrypt(base64(hmac_sha384(password, pepper)), salt, cost) with pepper stored separately from the database and password length checked ≤ 72 bytes before bcrypt.
Password hashing configuration and migration
WHAT: Using weak, inconsistent, or inefficient password hashing (e.g., legacy MD5/SHA-1, PBKDF2 implementations that pre-hash on every iteration, or hashes that cannot handle full Unicode/NULL bytes) can lead to easier password cracking or denial of service when users choose long passwords.
WHY: Attackers can crack weak or layered legacy hashes more easily, exploit expensive hashing of long passwords for DoS, or prevent some users from using strong, high-entropy passwords, increasing account-compromise risk.
HOW: Use a modern password hashing algorithm (e.g., PBKDF2-HMAC with appropriate iteration counts or parallel variants) that pre-hashes long passwords once with a salt before iteration, supports all Unicode codepoints and NULL bytes, and stores algorithm + work factor alongside the hash to allow seamless upgrades; on login, transparently re-hash legacy hashes with the new scheme and replace them, optionally expiring or deleting hashes for long-inactive users.
EXAMPLE: Before (legacy): `stored_hash = md5(password)`; on login, compare `md5(input) == stored_hash`. After (transition): on login, if `stored_hash` is MD5, verify `md5(input) == stored_hash`, then set `stored_hash = PBKDF2_HMAC_SHA256(input, salt, iterations)` and mark the account as upgraded.
Unvalidated Redirects and Forwards
WHAT: The application performs redirects or forwards to URLs taken directly from untrusted input, allowing attackers to control the destination.
WHY: Attackers can use this to conduct phishing (stealing credentials) or bypass access control by forwarding to privileged functions.
HOW: Do not redirect/forward to arbitrary user-supplied URLs; use a server-side allowlist of permitted targets, map user input to internal identifiers, and validate/normalize URLs before use.
EXAMPLE: Before (Java): `response.sendRedirect(request.getParameter("url"));` After: `String target = mapIdToUrl(request.getParameter("pageId")); if (isAllowed(target)) response.sendRedirect(target);`
Open Redirects and Unsafe Forwards
WHAT: Unvalidated user-controlled URLs (e.g., query parameters like `url`, `returnUrl`, `fwd`) used directly in redirects or forwards cause open redirection or unauthorized forwarding to attacker-chosen locations or functions.
WHY: Attackers can use trusted-site links to redirect victims to phishing/malicious sites or bypass access control by forwarding into admin or restricted pages.
HOW: Never redirect/forward to raw user input; instead use server-side allowlists of relative paths or route names, normalize and verify targets stay within your domain/context, and for frameworks with known issues, upgrade to fixed versions and use built-in safe redirect helpers.
EXAMPLE: Before (Java): `response.sendRedirect(request.getParameter("url"));` After: `String target = request.getParameter("url"); if (!ALLOWED_PATHS.contains(target)) { target = "/home"; } response.sendRedirect(request.getContextPath() + target);`
Unvalidated redirects and forwards in Java servlets
WHAT: Application forwards requests to a path taken directly from a user-controlled parameter (e.g., `fwd`) without validation, enabling unvalidated redirects/forwards.
WHY: Attackers can redirect users to malicious pages, bypass access controls, or access unintended internal resources, leading to phishing or authorization bypass.
HOW: Do not forward to arbitrary user input; instead, map user-supplied tokens to a server-side allowlist of valid targets, or construct forward targets from constants only. Reject or log any value not in the allowlist.
EXAMPLE:
Before: `String fwd = request.getParameter("fwd"); request.getRequestDispatcher(fwd).forward(request, response);`
After: `Map<String,String> allowed = Map.of("home","/home.jsp"); String key = request.getParameter("fwd"); if (allowed.containsKey(key)) request.getRequestDispatcher(allowed.get(key)).forward(request, response); else response.sendError(400);`
CWE-601: URL Redirection to Untrusted Site
WHAT: Application performs redirects/forwards to a URL that is directly or indirectly controlled by user input, allowing open redirect attacks.
WHY: Attackers can use open redirects for phishing, credential theft, or to chain into other vulnerabilities (e.g., token theft, SSRF).
HOW: Avoid redirects/forwards where possible; otherwise never use raw user-supplied URLs as destinations. Map user-provided short names/IDs/tokens to server-side URL allowlists (hosts or strict regex). Validate and authorize any unavoidable user input, and ensure IDs are not easily enumerable. Optionally interpose a warning/confirmation page before leaving your site.
EXAMPLE (C#): // Insecure: Response.Redirect(Request.QueryString["url"]);
// Secure: var target = GetRedirectUrlById(Request.QueryString["id"]); if (IsAllowedHost(target)) Response.Redirect(target);
Secure transaction authorization visibility
WHAT: Failing to show users the significant transaction data (e.g., target account, amount) during authorization can let attackers trick them into approving altered or fraudulent transactions.
WHY: If users cannot verify what they are authorizing, malware or compromised clients can silently change transaction details, leading to unauthorized transfers or account changes.
HOW: Implement “What You See Is What You Sign” (WYSIWYS): use an external or trusted authorization component that displays all critical transaction fields and requires explicit user confirmation of those exact values before approval.
EXAMPLE: Before: User approves a generic “Confirm transfer?” prompt with no details. After: Authorization device/app shows “Transfer 500.00 USD to IBAN DE89 3704 0044 0532 0130 00 – Confirm? [Yes/No]”.
Secure transaction authorization and authentication design
WHAT: Failing to clearly separate authentication from transaction authorization, or to confirm changes to authorization tokens/methods using existing credentials, allows malware or social engineering to authorize fraudulent operations.
WHY: Attackers can change authorization tokens/methods to weaker ones or reuse authentication steps (e.g., repeated OTP entry) to silently authorize unauthorized transactions, leading to account takeover and financial loss.
HOW: Require all significant transaction data to be explicitly confirmed by the user; authorize any change of authorization token using the current token; authorize any change of authorization method using the current method and warn about its risks; and ensure authentication steps are clearly distinct (in method and UI) from transaction authorization steps, including clear “what you are signing” messages.
EXAMPLE: Before: Using the same SMS OTP flow and UI text for login and for approving transfers, and allowing phone-number changes without confirming via the old number. After: Use password+OTP for login, a separate device or mode for transaction signing that displays/asks to confirm target account and amount, and require an OTP sent to the existing phone to confirm any phone-number or authorization-method change.
Transaction authorization security
WHAT: Weak or client-controlled transaction authorization allows attackers to reuse credentials, tamper with parameters, downgrade methods, or brute-force authorization to approve unintended transactions.
WHY: Leads to unauthorized transactions, credential theft abuse, and bypass of stronger authorization methods, enabling fraud and account compromise.
HOW: Use distinct mechanisms for authentication vs. authorization; require unique per-transaction authorization credentials; enforce all authorization logic, method selection, and transaction state transitions on the server; apply default-deny, remove debug features in production, and protect transaction/verification data with server-side generation, storage, and integrity checks; rate-limit and lock or restart flows after repeated failures.
EXAMPLE (server-side enforcement pattern): On the server, load the transaction by ID from the database, verify it belongs to the authenticated user, confirm its current state allows the requested transition, verify the chosen authorization method and its one-time credential, and reject or restart the flow on any mismatch or excessive failures.
Secure Transaction Authorization Flow and Data Protection
WHAT: Transaction authorization flows can be abused if steps are performed out of order, skipped, or if transaction data is modified or replayed between entry, authorization, and execution.
WHY: Attackers can overwrite transaction details, inject new parameters, replay or reuse authorization credentials, or execute unauthorized transactions (including TOCTOU-style attacks), leading to fraud and data compromise.
HOW: Enforce a strict, server-side–validated sequence of authorization steps; bind transaction data to the authorization challenge; invalidate and restart authorization on any data change; ensure all client–server communication is protected; verify at execution time that the transaction matches what was authorized; and use short-lived, per-operation, unique authorization credentials.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): server accepts an OTP and executes whatever transaction data is in the request, even if changed after OTP generation, and reuses the same OTP for multiple operations. After (secure): server generates a unique, short-lived OTP bound to a specific transaction snapshot; if any transaction field changes, the OTP and challenge are invalidated and a new flow is required; before execution, the server checks that the OTP is valid, unexpired, unused, and tied exactly to the stored transaction data.
Transaction authorization and signing-key protection
WHAT: Inadequate authorization of sensitive transactions and improper protection of device signing keys (e.g., keys injected/replaced/stolen during pairing or use) can allow unauthorized or modified transactions to be accepted.
WHY: Attackers or malware can perform fraudulent transactions, tamper with transaction data, or impersonate users, breaking integrity, confidentiality, and non-repudiation.
HOW: Perform a risk analysis to decide which transactions require explicit authorization; use strong cryptography (signing and encryption) for all high-risk transactions; securely provision signing keys during device pairing; store keys in secure elements (TEE, TPM, smart card) and protect their use with a second factor (password, biometrics); never allow keys to be exportable or modifiable by untrusted code.
EXAMPLE: Before: Application sends transaction details over the network and marks them “approved” client-side without cryptographic signing or secure key storage. After: Application requires explicit user authorization for high-risk transactions, signs transaction data with a key stored in a TPM-backed keystore, and verifies the signature server-side before processing.
Managing secrets in Infrastructure as Code
WHAT: Storing secrets (tokens, passwords, SSH keys) directly in IaC files, plain text, or source control (e.g., Git) exposes them to unauthorized access and leakage.
WHY: Exposed secrets can let attackers authenticate as your services, move laterally, exfiltrate data, or modify infrastructure.
HOW: Never hard-code secrets in IaC; store them in a dedicated secrets manager or secure vault, reference them via environment-specific bindings, and use automated scanners (e.g., truffleHog, git-secrets, GitGuardian) in CI/CD to detect and block committed secrets.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): `db_password = "SuperSecret123"` in Terraform; After (secure): `db_password = data.vault_generic_secret.db.data["password"]` with the actual password stored and access-controlled in a secrets management system.
Secure deployment and runtime management of infrastructure resources
WHAT: Failure to properly tag, track, log, and fully decommission deployed resources can create ghost/abandoned assets and unmonitored services, leading to configuration drift and unobserved runtime behavior.
WHY: Ghost or unlogged resources hinder detection and response, increase attack surface and costs, and make it difficult to analyze incidents or enforce security/compliance controls.
HOW: On every deploy, programmatically enforce tagging, inventory registration, and enabling of security/audit logging; on decommission, ensure code erases configurations, securely deletes data, and removes resources from runtime and inventory; integrate automated dynamic analysis, monitoring, and runtime threat detection into deployment pipelines and runtime environments.
EXAMPLE: (Pseudocode) Before: createResource(cfg); // no tags, no logging, no inventory update. After: tags = requiredTags(app, env, owner); res = createResource(cfg.withTags(tags)); enableSecurityAndAuditLogs(res); inventory.register(res.id, tags); onDelete(res.id): securelyDeleteData(res); destroyResource(res); inventory.remove(res.id);
Kubernetes cluster hardening guideline
WHAT: Insecure configuration of Kubernetes hosts, components, dashboard, and workloads across build, deploy, and runtime phases can expose the cluster to compromise.
WHY: Misconfigurations can lead to unauthorized access, privilege escalation, data exfiltration, and disruption of services.
HOW: Regularly apply Kubernetes security updates, harden and patch hosts, securely configure core components and the dashboard, and enforce security controls and monitoring during build, deploy, and runtime phases.
EXAMPLE: N/A
Kubernetes Host and Container Patch Management
WHAT: Failing to keep Kubernetes hosts, OS, and container images updated and patched leads to running known-vulnerable software in the cluster.
WHY: Attackers can exploit known vulnerabilities in outdated OS packages, Kubernetes versions, or container images to gain unauthorized access, escalate privileges, or disrupt workloads.
HOW: Always run the latest stable Kubernetes version; regularly patch and harden host operating systems; use configuration/patch management tools; update base container images when vulnerabilities are found and redeploy containers instead of patching them in-place.
EXAMPLE: Before (bad): Manually running `apt-get update` and `apt-get install` inside a running container. After (good): Update the Dockerfile/base image, rebuild the image with patched packages, push it to the registry, and roll out the new image via Kubernetes rolling updates.
Securing Kubernetes Dashboard Access
WHAT: Misconfigured Kubernetes Dashboards often run with overly-privileged service accounts and are exposed without strong authentication, allowing attackers to gain cluster-admin–level access via the web UI.
WHY: An attacker who reaches a privileged or unauthenticated dashboard can take over the cluster, exfiltrate data, or run arbitrary workloads (e.g., cryptomining).
HOW: Do not expose the dashboard publicly; require strong authentication (e.g., MFA via an authenticating reverse proxy with OIDC or impersonation); enable RBAC; use a minimally-privileged service account for the dashboard; grant permissions per user; remove any legacy cluster-admin bindings; and, if using network policies, restrict pod access to the dashboard.
EXAMPLE: Before: Dashboard ServiceAccount bound to `cluster-admin` and exposed via public LoadBalancer without auth. After: Dashboard behind an auth proxy with MFA, ServiceAccount bound only to needed Roles, per-user RBAC, and NetworkPolicy allowing access only from admin IPs or namespaces.
Secure Kubernetes Control Plane and etcd Access
WHAT: Unrestricted or weakly protected access to etcd, Kubernetes API, and control-plane ports allows attackers to bypass API validation, read/write secrets, and gain cluster-admin–equivalent control.
WHY: Attackers with read/write etcd or API access can schedule arbitrary pods, bypass PodSecurityPolicies, escalate privileges, exfiltrate secrets, and fully compromise the cluster.
HOW: Use strong mutual TLS between API servers and etcd; isolate etcd behind firewalls so only API servers can reach it; use separate etcd instances or ACLs to restrict keyspace access; enable robust authentication/authorization (prefer external auth) on the API; deny-by-default RBAC; and restrict network access to Kubernetes control-plane and kubelet ports to trusted networks.
EXAMPLE: Before: etcd and API server bound to 0.0.0.0 with no client cert auth and open firewall rules to 2379–2380 and 6443 from the internet. After: etcd listens on a private network, requires client TLS certs signed by a cluster CA, firewall only allows API server IPs to reach 2379–2380, API server requires authenticated clients and RBAC roles with least privilege, and external SSO/OIDC is used for production authentication.
Kubernetes API authentication hardening
WHAT: Avoid using Kubernetes built-in authentication mechanisms (static token files, X.509 client certs without revocation, and service account tokens) for user authentication in production, and treat all API access as privileged requiring MFA.
WHY: Insecure or non-rotatable credentials and lack of revocation enable long-lived compromise of cluster admin/user access, leading to full cluster takeover.
HOW: Use external identity providers (e.g., OIDC with cloud IAM or enterprise IdP) for user auth, enforce short-lived tokens, enable MFA for all user access, and reserve service accounts only for in-cluster workloads with least privilege and rotation.
EXAMPLE: Before (NOT RECOMMENDED): Configure API server with `--token-auth-file=tokens.csv` and long-lived X.509 client certs for users. After (RECOMMENDED): Configure OIDC/IAM integration for kubectl logins with short-lived tokens and mandatory MFA, and use dedicated service accounts only for pods.
Kubernetes RBAC and Kubelet Access Hardening
WHAT: Failing to enable and correctly configure Kubernetes RBAC and Kubelet authentication/authorization allows unauthenticated or over-privileged access to cluster resources and node control APIs.
WHY: Attackers or misconfigured clients can gain powerful control over pods, services, and nodes, leading to data exfiltration, container/node compromise, or full cluster takeover.
HOW: Start the API server with `--authorization-mode` including `RBAC`, define least-privilege Roles/ClusterRoles and RoleBindings, and use the Node and RBAC authorizers with the NodeRestriction admission plugin; for Kubelets, disable anonymous access and enable both authentication and authorization as documented.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): `kube-apiserver --authorization-mode=AlwaysAllow ...` and Kubelet with unauthenticated HTTPS endpoints; After (secure): `kube-apiserver --authorization-mode=Node,RBAC --enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction ...` and Kubelet configured with TLS, client auth, and authorization enabled.
Minimize CI Container Features and Use Distroless/Empty Images
WHAT: Overly feature-rich CI/container images (with shells, package managers, and many OS packages) increase attack surface and make vulnerability scanning noisy and incomplete.
WHY: Extra tools and packages may contain unknown vulnerabilities, be abused by attackers for lateral movement or privilege escalation, and complicate provenance and CVE management.
HOW: Use minimal/distroless or empty images for CI and runtime; avoid including shells and OS package managers; if some OS packages are required, install only what is strictly necessary and then remove the package manager in a later build stage.
EXAMPLE: In Docker, base your CI image on a distroless or `scratch` image and use multi-stage builds to compile in a full image, then copy only the built binary into the minimal final image, omitting shells and package managers.
Kubernetes pod and container security context hardening
WHAT: Containers and pods run with overly privileged security contexts (e.g., root user, broad Linux capabilities, writable root filesystem), enabling attackers to install software or modify the filesystem.
WHY: Excessive privileges increase impact of compromise, allowing privilege escalation, persistence, and tampering with application or host resources.
HOW: In all deployment manifests, define `securityContext`/`podSecurityContext` to run as non-root, drop unnecessary capabilities, and set the root filesystem to read-only; grant only the minimal privileges required for the workload.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): `securityContext: {}`; After (hardened): `securityContext: { runAsNonRoot: true, readOnlyRootFilesystem: true, capabilities: { drop: ["ALL"] } }`.
Kubernetes container and pod security contexts
WHAT: Containers or pods may run with excessive privileges (e.g., root user, broad Linux capabilities, writable root filesystem, privileged securityContext settings), enabling privilege escalation or host compromise.
WHY: Over-privileged containers increase blast radius of a compromise, allowing attackers to escape containers, tamper with workloads, or access sensitive cluster/host resources.
HOW: Configure securityContext and podSecurityContext to set runAsNonRoot: true, use readOnlyRootFilesystem: true where possible, and drop all Linux capabilities by default, only adding specific required ones; enforce least-privilege profiles via Pod Security Standards (Baseline/Restricted) and Pod Security Admission Controller on namespaces, reserving Privileged only for critical system workloads.
EXAMPLE:
Before (over-privileged): securityContext: { privileged: true, runAsUser: 0 }
After (least privilege): securityContext: { runAsNonRoot: true, readOnlyRootFilesystem: true, capabilities: { drop: ["ALL"] } }
Kubernetes Pod and Service Mesh Security Guidelines
WHAT: Misconfigured Kubernetes pods and service-to-service communication can run with excessive privileges (root user, host networking, broad capabilities, API access) and unencrypted traffic, enabling container escape, lateral movement, and data exposure.
WHY: Over-privileged pods and unprotected microservice traffic increase blast radius of compromises, allow bypass of NetworkPolicies, and expose sensitive credentials and data in transit.
HOW: Configure pod security so containers do not run as root, disallow privilege escalation, use a read-only root filesystem, keep /proc masked, avoid hostNetwork/hostPID, drop all unused Linux capabilities, enable SELinux confinement, assign a dedicated ServiceAccount per app, and omit service account token mounts when API access is not needed; deploy a service mesh to enforce mTLS between services, ingress/egress controls, and strong RBAC with least privilege and deny-by-default policies.
EXAMPLE (Kubernetes YAML): Before: `securityContext: { runAsUser: 0, allowPrivilegeEscalation: true, capabilities: { add: ["ALL"] }, readOnlyRootFilesystem: false, hostNetwork: true }` After: `securityContext: { runAsNonRoot: true, allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, capabilities: { drop: ["ALL"] }, readOnlyRootFilesystem: true }` and `hostNetwork: false`, plus `automountServiceAccountToken: false` when the API is not required.
Least-privilege access control
WHAT: Over-privileged accounts and default-permit access controls allow users or services to perform actions beyond what their job or function requires.
WHY: Excessive privileges increase blast radius of account compromise, enable unauthorized data access, and make abuse or misconfiguration far more damaging.
HOW: Define roles with only the minimal permissions needed, set all systems and APIs to “deny all” by default, and explicitly grant access per role based on documented responsibilities.
EXAMPLE: Before: role “admin” has wildcard permissions `*:*` on all resources. After: create separate roles `billing-reader`, `user-support`, `ops-deployer` each with only the specific read/write actions required for their tasks.
Centralized policy enforcement with OPA in Kubernetes and microservices
WHAT: Risk of insecure cluster and microservice configurations (e.g., untrusted images, root containers, unencrypted storage, overly permissive network access, unrestricted lateral movement) when policies are not centrally enforced.
WHY: Misconfigurations can lead to privilege escalation, data exposure, non-compliance, and attackers moving laterally across services and namespaces.
HOW: Use OPA (or equivalent) as a centralized policy engine integrated with Kubernetes admission control, CI/CD, and service mesh; define declarative policies to only allow trusted images, disallow root, require encrypted storage, restrict internet egress, and tightly scope service-to-service access; run policies both at admission time and out-of-band for continuous validation.
EXAMPLE: Before (policy gap): Developers can deploy any image and run pods as root with unrestricted network access. After (with OPA): Admission policy rejects pods using non-allowlisted images, containers with `runAsUser=0`, volumes without encryption flags, or services whose network policies violate defined egress/ingress rules.
Kubernetes secrets handling
WHAT: Storing sensitive data (credentials, keys, tokens) directly in images or as environment variables in Kubernetes can expose secrets to anyone with image/Pod inspection access.
WHY: Exposed secrets enable unauthorized access to services and data, privilege escalation, and lateral movement across applications.
HOW: Store sensitive data only in Kubernetes Secret objects; mount them into containers via read-only volumes; never bake secrets into container images or configuration; avoid using environment variables for secrets; ensure secrets are encrypted at rest using the platform’s encryption mechanisms.
EXAMPLE: Before: `env: [{ name: "DB_PASSWORD", value: "PlainTextPass" }]` baked into image/Pod spec. After: create a Secret, then `volumeMounts: [{ name: "db-secret", mountPath: "/run/secrets", readOnly: true }]` and read the password from the mounted file.
Kubernetes secrets handling and storage
WHAT: Secrets are exposed insecurely when stored in images, environment variables, unencrypted etcd/backups, or overly broad container volumes, allowing anyone with image, filesystem, or backup access to read them.
WHY: Compromise of these locations can leak API tokens, passwords, and keys, giving attackers broad visibility and control over the cluster and dependent systems.
HOW: Mount secrets into read-only volumes (not env vars), keep secrets out of images, enforce least-privilege secret access per pod, enable Kubernetes encryption at rest for Secret resources, encrypt all backups (and use full-disk encryption where possible), and consider using an external secrets manager for centralized storage and rotation.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): store DB_PASSWORD in the container image or as an environment variable and back up etcd without encryption. After (more secure): store DB_PASSWORD in a Kubernetes Secret or external manager, mount it as a read-only volume only to the needing pod, enable encryption at rest for Secrets in etcd, and encrypt etcd and image registry backups.
Kubernetes runtime and pod hardening
WHAT: Failing to monitor container runtime behavior and enforce pod security policies allows risky pods (e.g., with host mounts, shells, or broad syscalls) to run and access sensitive host resources.
WHY: Attackers can escape containers, read sensitive files (/etc/shadow, /proc), abuse network access, and compromise the host or other workloads.
HOW: Enable Pod Security Admission with at least `baseline` (prefer `restricted`) for all pods; deploy runtime security tooling (e.g., Falco) to alert on shells, sensitive mounts, unexpected file reads, and outbound connections; and use sandboxed runtimes (Kata Containers, gVisor, Firecracker) for multi-tenant or untrusted workloads to reduce kernel attack surface.
EXAMPLE: Configure Pod Security Admission to forbid hostPath mounts, privileged pods, and host networking for application pods, and run them on a sandboxed runtime such as gVisor or Kata Containers in shared clusters.
Prevent automatic loading of unwanted kernel modules in containers
WHAT: Unprivileged container processes can trigger automatic loading of vulnerable or unnecessary kernel modules (e.g., by creating specific socket types), expanding the kernel attack surface.
WHY: Automatically loaded modules that admins assume are unused may contain exploitable vulnerabilities, enabling privilege escalation or container escape.
HOW: Uninstall unneeded kernel modules from nodes; explicitly blacklist disallowed modules via modprobe configuration (e.g., /etc/modprobe.d/*.conf); and use a Linux Security Module (e.g., SELinux) to deny module_request permission for containers so they cannot trigger module loads.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): containers can create DCCP/SCTP sockets, causing dccp/sctp modules to auto-load. After (more secure): add `blacklist dccp` and `blacklist sctp` to a modprobe blacklist file and configure SELinux policy to deny module_request for container domains.
Kubernetes API audit logging and monitoring
WHAT: Missing or incomplete Kubernetes API audit logging and alerting can prevent detection of anomalous or unauthorized API calls (e.g., repeated “Forbidden” authorization failures).
WHY: Without detailed, centralized audit logs and alerts, credential abuse, privilege escalation, or other compromises may go unnoticed and hinder incident response and compliance investigations.
HOW: Enable Kubernetes API audit logging, define and apply an audit policy that records security-relevant events (especially authN/authZ failures and sensitive operations), ship logs to a centralized, secure log store, and configure alerts on suspicious patterns such as repeated “Forbidden” responses.
EXAMPLE: Before: Cluster runs without audit logging or audit policy; API calls are not centrally recorded. After: Configure `--audit-log-path` and `--audit-policy-file` on `kube-apiserver`, send logs to a managed logging backend, and set alerts on authorization failures in the logging/monitoring system.
Avoid logging sensitive request/response data
WHAT: Logging full request or response bodies can capture sensitive data (credentials, personal data, secrets) instead of only necessary metadata.
WHY: Exposing sensitive data in logs increases the risk of data leaks, unauthorized access, and regulatory non-compliance.
HOW: Prefer logging only metadata (user ID, timestamp, resource, verb); avoid logging bodies unless strictly required, and then redact or filter sensitive fields before writing to logs.
EXAMPLE: Before: logger.info("Request body: " + requestBody); After: logger.info("Request from user=" + userId + " to resource=" + resource + " verb=" + verb);
Kubernetes audit logging configuration
WHAT: Failing to set the kube-apiserver --audit-policy-file flag or providing an audit policy file without required rules results in no audit events being logged, eliminating security-relevant audit trails.
WHY: Missing or invalid audit logging prevents detection and investigation of security incidents, policy violations, and unauthorized access, and can break compliance requirements that mandate audit trails.
HOW: Always configure kube-apiserver with a valid --audit-policy-file that includes at least one rules entry; validate the file on deployment and during CI/CD, and fail configuration if the flag is omitted or the rules list is empty/invalid.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): kube-apiserver ...               # no --audit-policy-file flag
After (secure): kube-apiserver --audit-policy-file=/etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml ...
Embed security into the container lifecycle early
WHAT: Failing to integrate security checks and policies early in the container and Kubernetes lifecycle leads to insecure builds and deployments.
WHY: Late discovery of vulnerabilities or misconfigurations increases remediation cost and risk of deploying exploitable containers to production.
HOW: Add security scanning, policy checks, and approvals into CI/CD pipelines; align DevOps and security teams on shared security gates for build, test, and deploy stages.
EXAMPLE: Before: CI builds and deploys images without any security scan. After: CI runs image vulnerability scans and Kubernetes manifest policy checks; deployment is blocked if critical issues are found.
Use explicit, minimal, and deterministic Docker base images
WHAT: Using broad or mutable base tags (e.g., `node` or `node:latest`) and large full-OS images introduces non-deterministic builds and an unnecessarily large attack surface with many bundled vulnerabilities.
WHY: Non-deterministic images hinder reproducibility and patch management, while larger images with unused tools and libraries increase the number of potential vulnerabilities and exploit paths.
HOW: Pin Node.js Docker images to a specific minimal variant and immutable digest (e.g., LTS + alpine + SHA256), and avoid generic or latest tags to keep the image small and reproducible.
EXAMPLE: Before: `FROM node` or `FROM node:latest` → After: `FROM node:lts-alpine@sha256:<trusted_digest>`
Secure Node.js Docker Image Configuration
WHAT: Installing all Node.js dependencies (including devDependencies) in production Docker images and omitting NODE_ENV=production leaves unnecessary, potentially vulnerable packages and disables production security optimizations in frameworks.
WHY: Extra devDependencies and non-production configs increase attack surface, risk pulling malicious or unvetted dev tools into runtime, and reduce performance and security hardening.
HOW: In production Docker builds, install only production dependencies deterministically (e.g., via lockfile) and explicitly set NODE_ENV=production so frameworks enable their production security settings.
EXAMPLE:
Before: `RUN npm install`
After:
`ENV NODE_ENV=production`
`RUN npm ci --omit=dev`
Run containers with least privilege
WHAT: Running containerized applications as root, or with application files owned by root while the process runs as a non-root user, allows any compromise (e.g., command injection, path traversal) to execute with excessive privileges inside the container.
WHY: An attacker who gains code execution as root can perform almost any action in the container and attempt container escape or privilege escalation on the host.
HOW: Create and use a dedicated non-root user in the image; ensure all application files and directories are owned by that user (e.g., via COPY --chown); set USER to that account before the final CMD/ENTRYPOINT.
EXAMPLE: In a Dockerfile for Node.js:
Before: `COPY . /usr/src/app` then `USER node`
After: `COPY --chown=node:node . /usr/src/app` then `USER node`
Signal handling and init process behavior in Dockerized Node.js applications
WHAT: Node.js processes running as PID 1 in Docker, or wrapped by a shell as PID 1, may not receive or correctly handle termination signals (e.g., SIGTERM, SIGINT), causing abrupt kills, stuck processes, or ungraceful shutdown of web requests.
WHY: Improper signal handling can prevent containers from stopping cleanly, leave orphaned processes, and abruptly disconnect users during in-flight requests, harming reliability and availability.
HOW: In Docker, avoid shell-form CMD for long-running apps; use exec-form to invoke a minimal init (e.g., dumb-init) as PID 1, which then spawns Node.js and correctly proxies signals. Implement explicit signal handlers (SIGTERM/SIGINT) in Node.js to perform graceful shutdown (e.g., stop accepting new requests, wait for in-flight requests, then exit).
EXAMPLE: Before (PID 1 is Node.js, no init, no handlers):
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
After (PID 1 is init, signals proxied to Node.js, app can handle them):
RUN apk add dumb-init
CMD ["dumb-init", "node", "server.js"]
Avoid leaking build-time secrets in Docker images
WHAT: Storing secrets (e.g., NPM_TOKEN) in Dockerfile ENV or leaving them in image layers (.npmrc) exposes credentials to anyone with image or Dockerfile access.
WHY: Exposed tokens can be used to pull private packages, impersonate services, or access internal resources, leading to data theft or supply-chain compromise.
HOW: Never hardcode secrets in Dockerfile (ENV, RUN, or COPY). Use build-time ARG for tokens, write them to temp files only within a single RUN step, and delete them before the step ends so they are not persisted in any layer; ensure the Dockerfile itself does not contain literal secret values.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): `ENV NPM_TOKEN 1234` then `RUN echo "//registry.npmjs.org/:_authToken=$NPM_TOKEN" > .npmrc && npm ci --omit=dev`. After (safer): `ARG NPM_TOKEN` then `RUN echo "//registry.npmjs.org/:_authToken=$NPM_TOKEN" > .npmrc && npm ci --omit=dev && rm -f .npmrc`.
Leaking secrets via Docker build arguments and image history
WHAT: Secrets (e.g., npm tokens) passed as Docker build arguments or embedded in Dockerfiles are recorded in image history and layers, exposing credentials to anyone with access to the image or build logs.
WHY: Exposed tokens can be used to impersonate your service, exfiltrate packages, or compromise registries and other dependent systems.
HOW: Never hardcode secrets in Dockerfiles or pass them via `--build-arg`; instead, use multi-stage builds and ephemeral secret files or Docker/CI secret management features so secrets exist only in the build stage and are not copied into the final image or history.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): `docker build . --build-arg NPM_TOKEN=1234` and `RUN echo "//registry...:_authToken=$NPM_TOKEN" > .npmrc`. After (safer pattern): use a build stage that reads the token from a secure runtime secret mechanism, writes `.npmrc` only in that stage, installs dependencies, deletes `.npmrc`, and copies only built artifacts (not config files) into the final image.
Protecting secrets and sensitive files in Docker-based builds
WHAT: Risk of copying local node_modules, .env, .npmrc, and other sensitive or modified files into Docker images via broad COPY (e.g., `COPY .`) without a proper .dockerignore or secret-handling strategy.
WHY: Leaks credentials (tokens, AWS keys, config), ships unreviewed/modified dependencies, and increases attack surface of production images.
HOW: Define a strict .dockerignore to exclude node_modules, VCS metadata, logs, and secret/config files; use multi-stage builds so only required artifacts are copied into the final image; mount secrets or use Docker secrets for build-only files like .npmrc instead of baking them into images.
EXAMPLE: Before: `COPY . /usr/src/app` with no .dockerignore, including `.env`, `.npmrc`, `node_modules/`. After: add `.dockerignore` with `node_modules`, `.env`, `.npmrc`, `.git`, logs, etc., and in the final stage use `COPY --from=build /usr/src/app/node_modules /usr/src/app/node_modules` and `COPY . /usr/src/app` (with secrets excluded) while providing .npmrc only via mounted secret in the build stage.
Protecting sensitive config files (e.g., .npmrc) in Docker builds
WHAT: Avoid copying sensitive configuration files (like .npmrc with tokens) into Docker images or build context; instead, mount them as secrets only at build time.
WHY: Including secrets in images or build context exposes tokens/credentials to anyone with access to the image or build artifacts, enabling credential theft and supply-chain attacks.
HOW: Add secret files to .dockerignore so they are excluded from the build context, and use Docker BuildKit’s `RUN --mount=type=secret,...` to mount them only for the specific build step that needs them; never `COPY` these files into any image layer.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): `COPY .npmrc /usr/src/app/.npmrc` in Dockerfile. After (secure): add `.npmrc` to `.dockerignore` and use `RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npmrc,target=/usr/src/app/.npmrc npm ci`.
Injection prevention in Java
WHAT: Untrusted input is directly concatenated into SQL or JPA query strings and executed, allowing attackers to alter queries (SQL/JPA injection).
WHY: Malicious queries can read/modify/delete data, bypass authorization, or compromise the database and underlying system.
HOW: Validate inputs with an allowlist, escape/sanitize outputs, avoid building commands/queries via string concatenation, and always use parameterized queries (PreparedStatement for SQL, named/positional parameters for JPA).
EXAMPLE:
Before (vulnerable): `String q = "select * from color where friendly_name = '" + userInput + "'"; stmt.executeQuery(q);`
After (safe): `String q = "select * from color where friendly_name = ?"; PreparedStatement ps = con.prepareStatement(q); ps.setString(1, userInput); ps.executeQuery();`
XPath Injection in XML Processing
WHAT: Building XPath queries by concatenating or embedding untrusted user input directly into the query string, then executing it.
WHY: Allows attackers to alter the XPath query logic, potentially reading or manipulating unauthorized XML data or bypassing access controls.
HOW: Never concatenate user-controlled data into XPath expressions; instead, use XPathVariableResolver (or equivalent) to bind variables, and validate inputs against strict allowlists before use.
EXAMPLE:
Before (vulnerable): `XPathExpression expr = xpath.compile("//book[@id='" + userId + "']");`
After (safe): Use a variable resolver, add `bookId` via `addVariable(new QName("bookId"), userId);` and compile `"//book[@id=$bookId]"`.
XPATH and NoSQL Injection Prevention
WHAT: Untrusted user input is directly concatenated into HTTP responses or NoSQL/XPath-like query expressions, allowing attackers to inject markup or query operators and alter the intended behavior.
WHY: This can lead to XSS, data exfiltration, unauthorized data modification, or execution of unintended queries against the data store.
HOW: Validate all user-controlled input with an allowlist of permitted characters and length; reject or normalize any value containing characters with special meaning in the target syntax; never build queries or responses via string concatenation—use safe APIs/builders and apply context-appropriate escaping and sanitization on all output.
EXAMPLE: Before (NoSQL): `db.collection.find("{ borough: '" + userInput + "' }");` After: validate `userInput` against an allowlist and use the driver’s query builder, e.g., `Bson expr = eq("borough", userInput); db.collection.find(expr);`.
Log Injection and Cryptography Usage
WHAT: Untrusted data is written directly into logs or handled with custom/incorrect cryptographic code, leading to log injection (e.g., CRLF in log fields) or broken crypto.
WHY: Attackers can forge/alter log entries, enable XSS when logs are viewed in a browser, or compromise confidentiality/integrity of sensitive data if cryptography is misused.
HOW: Use structured logging (e.g., JSON layouts/encoders), avoid string concatenation in log messages (use parameterized logging with constant patterns), limit size of logged user input, apply XSS defenses when rendering logs, never implement your own cryptographic primitives, and prefer vetted secret-management solutions or well-known crypto libraries that support algorithm agility and regular updates.
EXAMPLE: In Java logging, prefer `logger.warn("Login failed for user {}.", username);` over `logger.warn("Failure for user " + username + " and role {}.", role, ex);` and configure Log4j/Logback to use JSON layouts/encoders with maximum string length limits.
Symmetric encryption key and nonce management
WHAT: Incorrect use of symmetric encryption (e.g., reusing nonces with AES-GCM, insecure key storage, or ad‑hoc crypto) can break confidentiality and integrity even if a strong algorithm is used.
WHY: Reused nonces or exposed keys allow attackers to recover plaintexts, forge ciphertexts, or decrypt all protected data.
HOW: Prefer vetted libraries (e.g., Google Tink) and follow OWASP Cryptographic Storage Cheat Sheet; ensure a cryptography expert reviews any direct JCA/JCE use; generate keys with a CSPRNG, store them in a secure key management system, and implement key rotation; for AES-GCM, always use a fresh, unique 96‑bit nonce per encryption and never reuse a nonce with the same key.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): reuse a hard-coded or static IV/nonce for all AES-GCM encryptions; After (secure): for each encryption call, generate a new 12‑byte nonce using SecureRandom and store/transmit it alongside the ciphertext.
AES-GCM nonce uniqueness and size
WHAT: When using AES-GCM, a 12-byte (96-bit) nonce must be generated with a cryptographically secure RNG and must never be reused with the same key; reusing a nonce for multiple encryptions with the same key breaks security.
WHY: Nonce reuse in AES-GCM can allow attackers to recover plaintexts, forge valid ciphertexts, or derive information about the encryption key.
HOW: Always generate a fresh 12-byte nonce using a secure random source (e.g., SecureRandom) for every encryption operation, store/transmit it alongside the ciphertext, and never derive or reuse nonces from predictable or repeated values.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): `byte[] nonce = userSuppliedNonce;` → After (secure): `byte[] nonce = new byte[12]; SecureRandom sr = new SecureRandom(); sr.nextBytes(nonce);`
Cryptographic key rotation and expert review
WHAT: Using long-lived shared secrets derived from ECDH and implementing custom crypto flows with low-level JCA/JCE APIs can lead to weakened encryption if keys are not rotated and design/code are not rigorously validated.
WHY: Stale shared secrets and subtle implementation errors (e.g., misuse of ECDH, AES-GCM, or metadata/AD) increase the impact of key compromise and may allow attackers to decrypt or tamper with data.
HOW: Regularly regenerate ECDH key pairs to derive fresh shared secrets, limit key lifetimes, and prefer well-reviewed crypto libraries; if forced to use raw JCA/JCE, have the complete design and implementation reviewed by a qualified cryptography expert.
EXAMPLE: (Conceptual) Ensure your protocol specifies periodic ECDH keypair regeneration (e.g., per session or per N messages) and mandates external expert review before deployment when using custom JCA/JCE-based crypto.
Ephemeral key, nonce, and authenticity management in hybrid encryption
WHAT: The code derives shared secrets and encrypts data without handling key rotation, secure private-key storage, nonce lifecycle management, public-key validation, or mutual authentication, leading to long‑lived secrets, key compromise, nonce misuse, and spoofed peers.
WHY: Poor key and nonce management or unvalidated public keys can enable decryption of past/future traffic, key theft, ciphertext forgery, and man‑in‑the‑middle attacks.
HOW: Implement periodic key rotation; store private keys in a secure keystore/HSM; treat nonces as required associated data (store/transmit alongside ciphertext and ensure uniqueness per key); validate public keys using certificates or an authenticated key directory; and add peer authentication (e.g., TLS-style certificate verification or signatures over key exchanges).
EXAMPLE: Before (Java): `KeyAgreement.init(keyPair.getPrivate()); keyAgreement.doPhase(partnerPublicKey, true);` with any received `partnerPublicKey`. After: verify `partnerPublicKey` against a trusted certificate chain or pinned key before use, and rotate `keyPair` on a defined schedule while persisting and checking nonces per key.
Threat modeling in the SDLC
WHAT: Failing to perform structured, repeatable threat modeling for your system, especially early in design, leading to unidentified and unmitigated security threats.
WHY: Missing threats or weak mitigations can result in exploitable design flaws, data breaches, and systemic vulnerabilities that are costly or impossible to fix later.
HOW: Integrate threat modeling as a standard SDLC activity; for each feature, systematically model the system from an attacker’s perspective, enumerate what can go wrong, define and implement mitigations, and periodically update the model as the system evolves.
Threat Modeling During Design
WHAT: Failing to perform structured threat modeling during the design phase leads to unrecognized attack surfaces, unprotected trust boundaries, and insecure data flows in the implemented system.
WHY: Undiscovered design-level threats often become costly vulnerabilities in production, enabling data breaches, privilege escalation, or service disruption.
HOW: During design, create and maintain system models (e.g., DFDs) that explicitly document processes, data stores, data flows, external entities, and trust boundaries; use these models to identify and rank threats, define mitigations, and periodically review and update them as the system evolves.
EXAMPLE: Before implementing a new API, first draw a DFD showing the client, API gateway, backend services, databases, and trust boundaries, then use it to identify where authentication, authorization, input validation, and encryption must be enforced.
Threat modeling with STRIDE
WHAT: Failing to systematically identify threats (spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service, elevation of privilege) for each data flow, data store, process, and external entity across trust boundaries can leave concrete attack paths unmitigated.
WHY: Unidentified threats can lead to loss of confidentiality, integrity, availability, authenticity, authorization control, and non-repudiation, resulting in data breaches, account takeover, and service disruption.
HOW: Build or obtain a DFD showing trust boundaries, data flows, data stores, processes, and external entities; then, for each element and interaction, walk through STRIDE categories and document threats, required controls, and priorities before implementation.
EXAMPLE: For each API endpoint in the DFD, explicitly ask: “Spoofing – how could an attacker fake identity here?”, “Tampering – how could request/response or stored data be altered?”, “DoS – how could this call be abused to exhaust resources?”, and record corresponding mitigations (e.g., auth, input validation, rate limiting, logging).
Threat Modeling with STRIDE
WHAT: Failure to systematically identify and respond to threats (e.g., information disclosure, DoS, privilege escalation) during design and implementation leads to unmitigated security flaws in code and architecture.
WHY: Undiscovered threats can result in data breaches, account lockouts, or unauthorized role changes, causing loss of confidentiality, availability, and authorization integrity.
HOW: Incorporate STRIDE-based threat modeling into the development lifecycle: enumerate threats per component, estimate likelihood and impact, prioritize by risk and remediation effort, and define concrete mitigations (code changes, controls, tests) for each identified threat.
EXAMPLE: During design of an authentication service, use STRIDE to identify brute-force login attempts as a DoS threat, then implement rate limiting, account lockout thresholds, and monitoring before writing or deploying the authentication code.
Threat modeling mitigation and validation
WHAT: Failure to define, document, and validate concrete mitigation strategies for identified threats, leading to unimplemented or ineffective security controls.
WHY: Incomplete or untested mitigations allow known threats to persist, increasing the likelihood and impact of successful attacks.
HOW: For each identified threat, document an actionable mitigation requirement (using resources like OWASP ASVS and CWE), ensure it is agreed by stakeholders, stored with “need-to-know” access, and define how it will be tested and measured for effectiveness.
EXAMPLE: Before: Identified threat “data tampering” with no specific mitigation. After: Requirement “All sensitive data in transit must use TLS 1.2+ with certificate validation; add automated tests that fail builds if non-TLS endpoints are introduced.”
Threat modeling integration in the SDLC
WHAT: Development teams may skip or underperform threat modeling, leading to unrecognized design-level security flaws and incomplete risk assessment.
WHY: Missing or incorrect threat models allow systemic vulnerabilities to reach production, increasing the likelihood and impact of successful attacks across the application.
HOW: Make threat modeling a mandatory SDLC activity; involve security specialists in modeling sessions; use standardized methods (e.g., STRIDE, LINDDUN, PASTA) and supporting tools; schedule regular cross-team reviews and keep models updated as the design changes.
EXAMPLE: Before: Design features and APIs without any structured threat analysis or security review gates. After: For each new feature, run a STRIDE-based threat modeling session with developers and security engineers, document identified threats and mitigations, and require all high-risk threats to have implemented controls before release.
Mobile App Authentication and Data Protection
WHAT: Mobile apps that trust client-side logic, hardcode or locally store credentials, use weak passwords/PINs, or store tokens and sensitive data insecurely can be bypassed, impersonated, or have data stolen if the device or app is compromised.
WHY: Attackers can bypass client checks, reuse hardcoded secrets, hijack sessions, or extract sensitive data from storage, logs, caches, or screenshots, leading to account takeover, fraud, and privacy breaches.
HOW: Perform all authentication/authorization and critical checks server-side; never hardcode or persist user credentials; use secure, revocable tokens; enforce strong password/PIN policies; store secrets and tokens only in platform-secure storage (Keychain/Keystore) with encryption at rest and in transit; use platform crypto APIs and hardware-backed key storage; minimize permissions; avoid overly permissive file modes; and prevent leakage via logs, caches, and background snapshots.
EXAMPLE: // Before (insecure): app checks auth locally and stores password in plain text
// After (secure): server validates credentials and issues short-lived token; app stores only the token in Keychain/Keystore, uses HTTPS/TLS for all API calls, and re-prompts for credentials before sensitive actions.
Secure Data Storage and Transmission
WHAT: Sensitive data is exposed if stored unencrypted, logged/cached, transmitted over insecure channels, or kept longer than necessary.
WHY: Exposure can lead to data theft, account compromise, privacy violations, and regulatory non-compliance.
HOW: Encrypt sensitive data at rest and in transit using platform crypto APIs and hardware-backed keystores; avoid custom crypto; store private data only in secure internal storage; prevent sensitive data in logs, caches, UI snapshots, and SMS; always use HTTPS with valid certificates, strong cipher suites, and no disabled validation; keep third-party libraries updated; minimize, anonymize, and expire PII with explicit user consent.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): send plain JSON with full PII over HTTP and log request/response bodies. After (secure): send only required, tokenized fields over HTTPS using system TLS, with no sensitive fields written to logs or persistent caches.
Shortcuts and Siri access control for sensitive app actions
WHAT: Sensitive app functionalities exposed via iOS/iPadOS Shortcuts or Siri can be executed while the device is locked, enabling unauthorized actions if they do not enforce device unlock and user authentication.
WHY: An attacker with physical access to a locked device could trigger shortcuts or Siri intents to access sensitive data or perform privileged operations without the user’s consent.
HOW: For Shortcuts, store secure tokens in Keychain and validate them before executing sensitive actions, and gate execution on UIApplication.shared.isProtectedDataAvailable so actions only run when the device is unlocked. For Siri, set requiresUserAuthentication = true and INIntent.userConfirmationRequired = true on intents that expose sensitive data or operations, ensuring biometric/PIN auth and explicit user approval.
EXAMPLE: Before: A Siri intent or Shortcut directly calls a fundsTransfer() method regardless of device lock state. After: The intent/Shortcut first checks requiresUserAuthentication and userConfirmationRequired, validates a Keychain token, and only then calls fundsTransfer() if UIApplication.shared.isProtectedDataAvailable is true.
Widget and Mobile App Data Protection
WHAT: Widgets and mobile apps may expose sensitive data on the lock screen, in transit, or at rest (e.g., in plists or unsecured storage), and may run without proper integrity or privacy controls.
WHY: Leaking or tampering with sensitive data can lead to privacy violations, unauthorized access, and compromised app integrity.
HOW: Detect lock-screen state (e.g., WidgetInfo.isLocked on iOS 17+) and mask or omit sensitive widget content when locked; restrict background refresh of sensitive data while locked; configure privacy permissions in Info.plist; use App Groups securely for data sharing; enforce ATS for network calls; never store secrets in plist files; use Secure Enclave (SecKeyCreateRandomKey with kSecAttrTokenIDSecureEnclave and appropriate kSecAccessControl* flags) for key storage and biometric-gated operations; and use App Attest + DeviceCheck to validate app integrity server-side.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): store API keys or tokens in Info.plist and always show full account details in a lock-screen widget. After (secure): remove secrets from plist, store keys in Secure Enclave with user presence/biometric access control, and conditionally hide or redact account details in the widget when WidgetInfo.isLocked is true or equivalent custom logic indicates a locked state.
Clickjacking Defense for Framed Content
WHAT: Risk of clickjacking/UI redress if your HTML pages can be embedded in <frame>/<iframe> by untrusted sites, allowing attackers to trick users into clicking hidden or overlaid UI elements.
WHY: Attackers can hijack user actions (e.g., transfers, settings changes) in the context of a valid session, leading to fraud, data modification, or unauthorized operations.
HOW: For all HTML responses, send restrictive framing headers: use `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none';` (or a minimal allowlist such as `'self'` and specific trusted domains), and also set `X-Frame-Options: DENY` or `SAMEORIGIN` for defense in depth; avoid `ALLOW-FROM` as it is obsolete and may fail open.
EXAMPLE: Before (no protection): `HTTP/1.1 200 OK` (no CSP or X-Frame-Options). After:
`HTTP/1.1 200 OK` + `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none';` + `X-Frame-Options: DENY`
Clickjacking Protection for Web Applications
WHAT: Pages that should not be framed can be clickjacked if X-Frame-Options / CSP frame-ancestors headers are missing, misconfigured (e.g., ALLOW-FROM), added via meta tags, or stripped by proxies.
WHY: Attackers can load your pages in hidden/opaque iframes to trick users into performing unintended actions (e.g., fraudulent clicks, state changes) under their authenticated session.
HOW: Set X-Frame-Options (DENY or SAMEORIGIN) or CSP frame-ancestors on all sensitive responses at the server/WAF/filter layer (not via meta tags); avoid ALLOW-FROM; monitor/avoid intermediaries that strip these headers; additionally mark session cookies SameSite=strict or lax as defense-in-depth.
EXAMPLE: (HTTP response headers) Before: no framing protection headers. After: `X-Frame-Options: DENY` and/or `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none';` plus `Set-Cookie: session=...; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict`.
Clickjacking Protection in Frameable Content
WHAT: Risk of clickjacking when your page must be frameable; relying on JavaScript frame-busting (e.g., setting parent.location, onbeforeunload tricks) is insecure and can be bypassed (double-framing, unload/no-content flushing, JS-restricted frames).
WHY: Attackers can overlay your framed page and trick users into performing unintended actions (e.g., transactions, approvals) while believing they interact with a trusted site.
HOW: Prefer server- or header-based defenses (X-Frame-Options, Content-Security-Policy frame-ancestors) and only allow framing from trusted origins; avoid client-side frame-busting scripts as the primary defense, and if framing is required, add in-frame user confirmation (e.g., window.confirm) plus clear origin display.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): `if (top.location != self.location) { parent.location = self.location; }` — relies on frame-busting JS. After (more robust): send `X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN` or `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self' https://trusted.example`.
Django authentication and key management hardening
WHAT: Insecure authentication and key handling occur when custom auth logic replaces Django’s auth framework, weak/unchecked passwords are allowed, plaintext passwords are stored/compared, or SECRET_KEY is short, predictable, or hard-coded.
WHY: These issues enable account takeover, credential stuffing success, offline password cracking, session forgery, and tampering with signed data (cookies, tokens, CSRF).
HOW: Use django.contrib.auth (with contenttypes and sessions) and @login_required for protected views; configure AUTH_PASSWORD_VALIDATORS for length, similarity, common, and numeric checks; always hash passwords with make_password and verify with check_password; generate a ≥50‑char SECRET_KEY via get_random_secret_key(), and load it from environment/secrets manager instead of hard-coding.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): `if request.POST["pwd"] == user.password:` and `SECRET_KEY = "mysecret"`. After (secure): `if check_password(request.POST["pwd"], user.password):` and `SECRET_KEY = os.environ["DJANGO_SECRET_KEY"]`.
Django application security hardening
WHAT: Misconfigured Django settings (weak or exposed SECRET_KEY, missing security middleware/headers, insecure cookies, missing CSRF/XSS/HTTPS protections) can lead to compromised sessions, CSRF/XSS attacks, clickjacking, and insecure transport.
WHY: Attackers can hijack accounts, forge requests, inject scripts, clickjack users, or intercept/modify traffic if these protections are absent or misconfigured.
HOW: Use a strong, randomly generated SECRET_KEY (≥50 chars, letters/digits/symbols) from a cryptographically secure generator; never hard-code it—load from environment variables or a secrets manager, and rotate it regularly, especially after exposure. Enable django.middleware.security.SecurityMiddleware and django.middleware.clickjacking.XFrameOptionsMiddleware; set SECURE_CONTENT_TYPE_NOSNIFF=True, SECURE_HSTS_SECONDS>0, X_FRAME_OPTIONS='DENY' or 'SAMEORIGIN', SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT=True, and SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER when behind a proxy. Configure cookies as secure-only: SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE=True, CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE=True, and always pass secure=True to HttpResponse.set_cookie for custom cookies. Enable django.middleware.csrf.CsrfViewMiddleware, include {% csrf_token %} in forms, and correctly attach the CSRF token to AJAX requests. Use Django’s template system with automatic escaping, avoid safe/mark_safe on untrusted data, and use json_script to safely pass data to JavaScript.
EXAMPLE:
Before (insecure key & cookies):
SECRET_KEY = 'hardcoded-weak-key'
SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE = False
response.set_cookie('my_cookie', 'val')
After (hardened):
import os
SECRET_KEY = os.environ['DJANGO_SECRET_KEY']
SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE = True
CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE = True
response.set_cookie('my_cookie', 'val', secure=True)
Admin panel URL hardening
WHAT: Do not expose the admin interface at the default, well-known path (e.g., "/admin/"); change the URL used for admin.site.urls.
WHY: Default admin URLs are heavily targeted by automated attacks and scanners, increasing the risk of brute-force and exploitation attempts.
HOW: In your top-level URL configuration (e.g., urls.py), update urlpatterns so the route mapped to admin.site.urls uses a non-obvious, project-specific path; avoid disclosing this path in public content or client-side code.
REST API and JWT Security
WHAT: Failing to enforce HTTPS, per-endpoint access control, and proper JWT integrity protection (e.g., accepting `{"alg":"none"}` or shared MAC keys across services) exposes credentials, tokens, and resources to attack.
WHY: Attackers can intercept or modify traffic, replay or forge tokens, impersonate users, and escalate privileges across multiple services if one is compromised.
HOW: Expose REST endpoints only over HTTPS; perform authorization checks on every endpoint; centralize user authentication in an IdP that issues tokens; require signed (or MACed) JWTs and reject `alg:"none"`; prefer signatures over MACs or, if MACs are used, avoid sharing the same key across mutually untrusted services.
EXAMPLE (HTTP vs HTTPS):
Before: `http://api.example.com/login`
After:  `https://api.example.com/login` with server TLS correctly configured and clients rejecting non-HTTPS endpoints.
JWT and API Security Guidelines
WHAT: Improper JWT integrity protection, validation, and claim checking; weak session revocation; overreliance on shared MAC keys; misuse of API keys; missing HTTP method restrictions; and insufficient input and content-type validation can all lead to unauthorized access, token forgery, DoS, or code execution.
WHY: If JWTs are forged or misvalidated, any service (or attacker) with a shared MAC key can impersonate users or services; stale tokens can bypass logout; unthrottled or unauthenticated APIs can be abused; and unvalidated input or content types can enable injection, XXE, or other attacks.
HOW: Prefer asymmetric signatures for JWTs; avoid shared MAC keys across mutually untrusted services; verify JWT integrity and claims (iss, aud, exp, nbf) using server-side configuration, not the JWT header; implement token denylisting on logout; require and manage API keys with rate limiting and revocation but do not treat them as sole protection for sensitive resources; restrict HTTP methods via an allowlist and enforce authorization per method/resource; strictly validate and size-limit all inputs (type, length, range, format) using strong types and validation libraries; use secure parsers (e.g., XXE-safe XML parsers); and validate that request/response bodies conform to documented content types.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure JWT validation, pseudocode): `alg = jwt.header.alg; key = selectKey(alg); verify(jwt, key);` After (secure): `alg = serverConfig.expectedAlg; key = serverConfig.trustedKey; verify(jwt, alg, key); assert(jwt.claims.iss == expectedIssuer && jwt.claims.aud == expectedAudience && now < jwt.claims.exp && now >= jwt.claims.nbf);`
Content Type and Management Endpoint Security
WHAT: Mismatched or uncontrolled content types, exposed management endpoints, verbose errors, and unsanitized logs can lead to code injection, XXE, unauthorized access, information disclosure, and log injection.
WHY: Attackers can execute arbitrary code, exploit XXE, reach privileged admin functions, learn internal details for further attacks, or corrupt/forge logs.
HOW: Strictly validate and document allowed request/response content types; reject unexpected/missing types with 406/415; harden XML parsers against XXE; explicitly set @Consumes/@Produces (or equivalent) and never mirror Accept to Content-Type; ensure response type matches body; keep management endpoints off the public Internet or protect them with strong auth, network segregation, and firewall/ACLs; return generic errors only; sanitize all log data and log before/after security events and token validation failures.
EXAMPLE: (Java, JAX-RS) Before: `@POST public Response api(InputStream body) { ... }` (no @Consumes/@Produces, accepts any type). After: `@POST @Consumes("application/json") @Produces("application/json") public Response api(MyDto dto) { ... }`
HTTP Security Headers for APIs
WHAT: API responses omit or misconfigure security-related HTTP headers, allowing caching of sensitive data, clickjacking, MIME sniffing, or insecure transport.
WHY: Missing/weak headers can lead to exposure of sensitive data, clickjacking attacks, content-type confusion (XSS/MIME sniffing), and downgrade/Man-in-the-Middle attacks.
HOW: For all API responses, set: `Cache-Control: no-store`; accurate `Content-Type` (e.g., `application/json`); `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`; `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none'` or `X-Frame-Options: DENY`; and `Strict-Transport-Security` with appropriate max-age and includeSubDomains.
EXAMPLE: Before: response without security headers. After (HTTP): `Cache-Control: no-store`, `Content-Type: application/json`, `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none'`, `X-Frame-Options: DENY`, `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains`.
CORS configuration for REST APIs
WHAT: Misconfigured CORS headers can allow unauthorized cross-origin JavaScript calls to your REST API.
WHY: Attackers can abuse overly permissive CORS to read sensitive data or perform actions on behalf of users from malicious sites.
HOW: Restrict `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` to a specific allowlist of trusted origins, avoid using `*` for authenticated endpoints, and set appropriate `Access-Control-Allow-Methods` and `Access-Control-Allow-Headers` based on actual needs.
EXAMPLE: Before (overly permissive): `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` on all endpoints; After (restricted): `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com` only on required endpoints and only for needed methods.
Protect sensitive data in HTTP requests
WHAT: Avoid placing credentials (passwords, tokens, API keys) in URLs or other loggable locations; ensure CORS is not overly permissive or enabled when cross-domain calls are not needed.
WHY: URLs and overly broad CORS settings can expose sensitive data via logs, browser history, intermediaries, or unauthorized origins, leading to credential theft and account compromise.
HOW: Disable CORS headers entirely if cross-domain calls are not required; when needed, configure a strict allowlist of trusted origins. Always send sensitive data in POST/PUT request bodies or headers, and in GET requests only in HTTP headers, never in the query string.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure GET): GET /api?token=SECRET_TOKEN. After (safer GET): GET /api with header Authorization: Bearer SECRET_TOKEN and CORS allowed only for https://trusted.example.com.
REST API security: avoid secrets in URLs and use correct HTTP status codes
WHAT: Do not include sensitive data (e.g., API keys) in URLs, and ensure REST endpoints return semantically correct HTTP status codes for both success and error conditions.
WHY: Secrets in URLs are logged, cached, and exposed in referrers; incorrect status codes can hide or misrepresent authentication/authorization and input-validation failures, weakening security controls and monitoring.
HOW: Put credentials and other secrets in headers or secure bodies (e.g., Authorization header), never in query strings; map each outcome to an appropriate HTTP status (e.g., 400 for malformed input, 401/403 for authz failures, 404 for missing resources, 413 for oversized payloads).
EXAMPLE: NOT OK: `GET /controller/123/action?apiKey=a53f435643de32`
OK: `GET /resourceCollection/{id}/action` with `Authorization: Bearer <token>` and use `401` for bad credentials, `403` for insufficient rights, `413` when upload exceeds limits.
Protect internal error details in HTTP 5xx responses
WHAT: Returning HTTP 5xx errors with detailed messages or stack traces exposes internal implementation details to clients.
WHY: Attackers can use internal information (stack traces, file paths, SQL errors) to discover vulnerabilities, system structure, or sensitive data.
HOW: For 5xx responses, log full error details only on the server; return generic error messages to clients and avoid including stack traces, internal paths, or configuration data in the response body or headers.
EXAMPLE: Before: `return Response.status(500).entity(e.toString() + Arrays.toString(e.getStackTrace())).build();` After: `log.error("Unhandled error", e); return Response.status(500).entity("Internal server error").build();`
Microservice privilege and data exposure control
WHAT: Risk of excessive privileges and unintended data exposure when microservices use overly broad scopes/API keys or access unnecessary databases, message queues, or endpoints.
WHY: Over-privileged microservices and uncontrolled data flows increase impact of compromise, enable lateral movement, and cause data leakage of sensitive information.
HOW: For each microservice, explicitly define and enforce minimal scopes/API keys and grants for other services, databases, and queues; inventory where sensitive data is stored and which services read/write it; document and restrict which microservices can call which endpoints and what data they exchange.
EXAMPLE: Before: Service A uses a single admin API key to access all Service B endpoints and all database tables. After: Service A uses a scoped key limited to only the specific B endpoints and tables required for its business function, with separate credentials for read vs. write where applicable.
Microservice architecture security inventory
WHAT: Missing or incomplete documentation of microservices, infrastructure services, data stores, message queues, and sensitive data assets leads to insecure APIs, misconfigured access, and uncontrolled data flows.
WHY: Without a security-focused inventory, it is hard to enforce authentication/authorization, protect sensitive data (e.g., PII, payments), or detect insecure service-to-service and service-to-storage access patterns.
HOW: Maintain an up-to-date catalog of all services, storages, queues, and assets including: IDs, descriptions, source repos, API definitions (with security schemes, scopes, API keys), architecture diagrams, runbooks, data protection levels, and explicit service-to-service and service-to-storage relations with access types.
EXAMPLE: Before: Services call each other and databases ad hoc with no central record of which API requires which scopes or which service can write to which storage. After: A registry lists each microservice with its OpenAPI spec (including auth scopes), linked storage with “Read/Write” flags, and documented data assets marked as “PII” or “confidential,” used as the basis for access-control and monitoring rules.
Use collected architecture information for secure design and testing
WHAT: Failing to use detailed service, storage, and data-flow mappings can lead to missed attack paths and untested exposed endpoints.
WHY: Unidentified service-to-service, service-to-storage, and asset-to-storage relations increase the risk of data exposure, privilege escalation, and unmitigated attack surface.
HOW: Maintain an up-to-date call graph/data-flow diagram of all services, protocols, queues, and storages, and systematically feed this into security requirements, threat modeling, and security test scoping (e.g., enumerate all endpoints and data paths for testing).
EXAMPLE: Before: Perform security testing only on publicly documented APIs. After: Derive the full list of microservice endpoints and data flows from the architecture diagram and test each identified path, including internal and asynchronous communications.
Least-privilege microservice permissions
WHAT: Risk of excessive microservice permissions when APIs and inter-service communications are not explicitly documented and constrained.
WHY: Over-privileged services increase blast radius of compromise, enabling unauthorized data access, lateral movement, and privilege escalation.
HOW: For each microservice, document its API definition and all service-to-storage and service-to-service (sync/async) communications; then grant only the minimal permissions required for those documented operations and revoke any unused or undocumented access.
EXAMPLE: Before: a microservice role with read/write access to all database tables; After: a role limited to SELECT/UPDATE on only the tables and operations referenced in the service’s documented API and data-flow diagram.
OS Command and Argument Injection
