EXAMPLE: Before: All services share one secrets store path with a single read token and no access logs. After: Each service has its own secret path with least‑privilege policies, production and development use separate secret stores, and access logs are fed to an alerting system that flags access from unexpected IP ranges.
Secrets encryption and detection
WHAT: Insecure handling of secrets, including weak/non-quantum-resistant encryption, convergent encryption without safeguards, co-locating keys with ciphertext, and failing to detect secrets in code and configs.
WHY: Leads to disclosure, tampering, or replay of sensitive data (API keys, credentials, tokens), and enables attackers to guess or derive plaintext secrets.
HOW: Use modern, recommended algorithms and key lengths (e.g., AES-256-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305 per current guidance); avoid convergent encryption unless the scheme enforces high resource cost and minimum secret length; never store encryption keys alongside the encrypted secrets unless using envelope encryption with a separate key hierarchy; integrate automated secrets detection (IDE hooks, pre-commit, CI) with regularly reviewed signatures for all relevant secret types.
EXAMPLE: Before: Store DB password in plain text in a config file and commit it to the repo. After: Store an AES-256-GCM–encrypted password in a secure secrets store, keep the key in a dedicated key management system, and enable a pre-commit hook that blocks any accidental password/API key additions to the repository.
Secret lifecycle and incident response for exposed credentials
WHAT: Secrets (API keys, passwords, tokens, private keys, etc.) may be hard‑coded, logged, or otherwise exposed without a defined lifecycle, making them difficult to rotate, revoke, or track after compromise.
WHY: Exposed or long‑lived secrets enable unauthorized access, data exfiltration, and privilege escalation; lack of rotation, revocation, and logging impedes containment and forensics after an incident.
HOW: Implement a secret lifecycle: short-lived secrets, automatic rotation, strict least-privilege access, and guaranteed revocation; never log plaintext secrets (use masking/encryption); define and automate incident response steps for detection, alerting, revocation, rotation, deletion from code/logs, and centralized logging of secret usage (who/when/where).
EXAMPLE: Before (bad): application reads API_KEY from a config file committed to source control and logs "Using API key: <key>". After (better): application reads API_KEY from a managed secret store with automatic rotation, uses it without ever logging the value (only an identifier), and IR playbooks can immediately revoke and rotate the key and remove any accidental exposures from logs.
Secure logging and multi-cloud secrets management
WHAT: Failure to centrally log and monitor secrets usage and access across multiple cloud providers, including missing or inconsistent logs, formats, alerts, and auditing, leading to blind spots in incident response.
WHY: Incomplete or inconsistent logging and access control hinder detection and investigation of breaches, enable undetected misuse of secrets, and prevent enforcement of uniform security policies and key rotation.
HOW: Centralize secrets management and logging; use a standardized logging format/vocabulary; ensure all secret access/usage events are logged to a single IR-accessible location; define uniform policies for access control, key rotation, and auditing across providers; automate key rotation and enforce least-privilege access; aggregate and monitor logs with alerts for suspicious activity.
EXAMPLE: Before (multi-cloud): each service logs secret access locally with ad-hoc fields and no central aggregation or alerts. After: all services use a common log schema (e.g., `timestamp, principal, secret_id, action, result, provider`) and send logs to a central SIEM; access policies and rotation schedules are defined once and applied consistently via a centralized secrets manager.
DOM Clobbering Prevention
WHAT: Avoid relying on window/document named property accesses (e.g., window.x, document.x, or bare x) for security-sensitive data such as URLs, script sources, or configuration, because attacker-injected elements with matching id/name can override these values.
WHY: If user-controlled HTML can be injected, an attacker can clobber these properties to cause unintended redirects, load attacker-controlled scripts, or otherwise execute arbitrary code and exfiltrate data.
HOW: Always access elements via safe DOM APIs (e.g., document.getElementById, querySelector) and store security-sensitive values in local/module-scoped variables or dedicated configuration objects that are not derived from window/document properties; never use global/bare identifiers that can be resolved via named elements.
EXAMPLE: Before (vulnerable): `let redirectTo = window.redirectTo || '/profile/'; location.assign(redirectTo);` After (safer): `const redirectTo = '/profile/'; location.assign(redirectTo);` or use a server-provided constant not influenced by DOM elements.
DOM Clobbering and Unvalidated Redirects in Client-Side Navigation
WHAT: Client-side redirects that read destination URLs from clobberable DOM properties (e.g., window.redirectTo) can be overwritten by attacker-controlled markup, causing redirects to arbitrary locations.
WHY: Attackers can achieve open redirects and arbitrary client-side code execution by navigating victims to malicious pages or loading hostile scripts.
HOW: Never derive redirect targets from DOM properties that can be clobbered (id/name/global variables); instead, use hardcoded or server-provided allowlisted paths, and validate/normalize any user-influenced URL against a strict allowlist before calling location.assign / location.href.
EXAMPLE (JavaScript, before): let redirectTo = window.redirectTo || '/profile/'; location.assign(redirectTo);
EXAMPLE (JavaScript, after): const allowed = new Set(['/profile/','/dashboard/']); const target = allowed.has(userPath) ? userPath : '/profile/'; location.assign(target);
DOM Clobbering Mitigation in Client-Side Code
WHAT: DOM clobbering occurs when attacker-controlled HTML `id`/`name` attributes or named elements overwrite or shadow JavaScript variables, `document`/`window` properties, or built-in APIs, enabling unintended code paths or script injection.
WHY: Clobbered objects can redirect sensitive logic, bypass security checks, or enable XSS/code execution, especially when existing code uses `eval()`-like constructs or trusts `document`/`window` properties.
HOW: Sanitize `id`/`name` before inserting markup; avoid using `document`/`window` for globals; always declare variables with `let`/`const`/`var` and prefer local scope; use strict mode; validate type of `document`/`window` properties (e.g., `instanceof`) before sensitive use; encapsulate state in objects/classes and consider freezing sensitive objects with `Object.freeze`.
EXAMPLE: Before (vulnerable): `var user = document.user; eval(user.code);` and `<form name="user"><input name="code" value="malicious()"></form>`. After (safer): `class Session { constructor(user){ this.user = user; } } const session = new Session(safeUser); if (session.user && typeof session.user.code === 'string') { runSafe(session.user.code); }`
Application Security Event Logging
WHAT: Missing, disabled, or poorly configured application-level security event logging, leading to incomplete or inconsistent records of security-relevant actions.
WHY: Without reliable security logs, attacks, policy violations, and fraud may go undetected, incident investigations are hindered, and compliance/audit requirements may not be met.
HOW: Design and implement consistent security event logging in application code for all critical actions (auth, access control, data changes, policy violations), using standard formats so logs can be correlated and analyzed across systems; keep security logs separate from general process/transaction logs and tune what is logged to the intended security purposes.
EXAMPLE: Before: No logging on login, privilege changes, or data deletion events. After: On each such event, the application records user identity, roles, target resource, action, outcome, timestamp, and source in a structured log entry consumable by central logging/monitoring tools.
Secure logging of untrusted event data
WHAT: Treat all event data from different trust zones as untrusted; it may be missing, modified, forged, replayed, or malicious, and insecure storage or exposure of logs can leak sensitive information or enable tampering.
WHY: Compromised or exposed logs can undermine incident detection, enable privilege escalation, leak sensitive data, or allow attackers to erase or forge audit trails.
HOW: Validate and authenticate event sources, enforce integrity and non-repudiation (e.g., signing), store logs on separate partitions or dedicated databases with least-privilege accounts, restrict filesystem and database permissions, avoid web-accessible log locations or strictly protect them, and use secure protocols and standard formats for log transport.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): application writes logs to a web-accessible directory with default OS permissions and uses the main DB account for log inserts. After (secure): logs are written to a non-web-accessible partition with restrictive ACLs, a dedicated write-only DB account is used for log tables, and remote log shipping uses a standard log format over TLS.
Security event logging for suspicious activities
WHAT: Failure to log security-relevant and suspicious business-logic events (e.g., flow bypass attempts, excessive use, configuration/code changes) with sufficient context (“when, where, who, what”) impedes detection and investigation of attacks and fraud.
WHY: Inadequate logging prevents timely detection of abuse, hinders incident response and forensics, and can allow fraud, data breaches, or configuration tampering to go unnoticed.
HOW: Implement centralized, tamper-resistant logging that records key attributes (timestamps, app/service identifiers, user/source identity, event type/severity, affected object, action, result, reason, HTTP status, and relevant headers) for suspicious, excessive, or out-of-sequence actions, data/config changes, and code/memory modifications.
EXAMPLE: Before: Application only logs generic errors (e.g., “operation failed”) without user, object, or action details. After: For each sensitive action, log: timestamp, app/version, client IP, authenticated user ID, action (“Update profile”), object (user account ID), result (“Fail”), reason (“Incorrect credentials”), HTTP status, and mark it as a security-relevant event.
Secure Logging and Sensitive Data Handling
WHAT: Risk of exposing sensitive or illegal-to-collect data in logs, or disabling/weakening logging needed for security and compliance. Failure modes include logging secrets/PII in cleartext or allowing logging to be fully turned off.
WHY: Leaked log data can enable account takeover, fraud, privacy violations, legal non-compliance, and loss of forensic evidence needed for incident investigation.
HOW: Never log data unless legally permitted; exclude or mask/hash/encrypt secrets and sensitive/PII fields; apply de-identification where identity is not required; ensure logging cannot be fully disabled and that default levels meet business/compliance needs; centralize logging via a tested, reusable log handler that enforces these rules and is controlled via governed configuration.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): `log.info("User {} logged in with password {}", userId, password);`
After (secure): `log.info("User {} logged in", userId);` and, if session tracking is needed, `log.debug("Session {}", hash(sessionId));`
Secure Logging and Event Collection
WHAT: Insecure logging can enable log injection, SQL injection, information leakage, denial of service, and unreliable forensics if event data from other trust zones is not validated, sanitized, correctly encoded, access-controlled, and resilient to failures.
WHY: Attackers can forge or corrupt logs, execute injections via log sinks, exhaust storage or transaction logs, bypass monitoring, or abuse log-driven actions (e.g., lockouts) to cause denial of service or evade detection.
HOW: Use a centralized, application-wide logging module or framework; validate and sanitize all event data from untrusted zones (including CR/LF and delimiters), encode for the log format, and apply SQL injection protections for database writes; ensure logging failures do not break the app or leak data; protect log storage with strict access controls; design log-driven actions to resist DoS; and include logging in code review, security, fuzz, penetration, and performance testing.
EXAMPLE (Java): Before – `logger.info("User=" + request.getParameter("user"));` (no validation/sanitization). After – `String user = validateUserId(request.getParameter("user")); logger.info("User=" + sanitizeForLog(user));`
CWE-117: Improper Output Neutralization for Logs
WHAT: Logs may expose sensitive data (PII, passwords, business data) or be tampered with or deleted if not properly protected at rest and in transit.
WHY: Unauthorized access or modification of logs can leak secrets, enable user-targeted attacks, undermine incident response, and destroy forensic evidence.
HOW: Restrict and periodically review log access privileges; record and monitor all access; use secure transport (e.g., TLS) over untrusted networks; store/copy logs to read-only or append-only media; add tamper detection for modification/deletion; mask, sanitize, hash, or encrypt sensitive fields; verify event origins and perform due diligence before sending logs to third parties.
EXAMPLE: Before: logging full user passwords and sending logs over plain HTTP to a central server with write access for many users. After: log only password reset attempts without the password value, transmit logs via TLS to an append-only store with tightly controlled read access and full access auditing.
Secure Logging Practices
WHAT: Logs must not store PII or secrets (e.g., passwords), must resist tampering, and must not allow log data or volume to degrade system performance or availability.
WHY: Exposed logs enable privacy violations, credential/secret theft, log forgery, data loss, and denial of service via disk exhaustion or slowdowns.
HOW: Redact or avoid logging PII and secrets; enforce strict access control on logs; validate and sanitize all log inputs; isolate logging storage from critical data; rate-limit and size-rotate logs; use append-only or integrity-protected logging with authenticated identities.
EXAMPLE: Before (bad): `logger.info("User {} logged in with pwd {}", user, password);` After (better): `logger.info("User {} logged in", userId);` with passwords never logged and logs written to a protected, rotated, integrity-checked store.
Secure File Upload Validation
WHAT: Unvalidated or weakly validated file uploads (e.g., trusting Content-Type, unsafe extension checks, user-controlled filenames/paths) can allow malicious files, parser exploits, overwrites, and DoS via huge or bomb files.
WHY: Attackers can execute arbitrary code, perform XSS/CSRF, exfiltrate or overwrite data, exhaust storage/CPU, or host illegal content on your system.
HOW: Allowlist only business-critical extensions; validate after decoding filename and against double extensions/null bytes; verify file type via server-side inspection, not headers; rename to server-generated names; restrict filename chars/length and file size; require authorization; store outside webroot or on a separate server; serve via an indirection handler; scan with AV/CDR; keep libraries updated; and protect upload endpoints from CSRF.
EXAMPLE (PHP, extension check):
Before: `if (preg_match('/\.jpg$/i', $_FILES['f']['name'])) move_uploaded_file(...);`
After: `if (pathinfo($safeName, PATHINFO_EXTENSION) === 'jpg' && in_array(mime_content_type($tmp), ['image/jpeg'], true)) move_uploaded_file(...);`
Secure File Upload Handling
WHAT: Unrestricted or weakly validated file uploads (extensions, MIME types, signatures, filenames, and content) can allow attackers to upload and execute malicious files or abuse the file storage system.
WHY: Malicious uploads can lead to remote code execution, XSS/CSRF, data exfiltration, filesystem corruption/overwrite, and storage of illegal or harmful content.
HOW: Use strict allowlists for required extensions and MIME types; validate file signatures; avoid relying solely on blocked extensions or user-supplied Content-Type; generate safe random filenames (or strictly validate user filenames with length and character allowlists and restricted leading characters); and apply content-level validation or rewriting appropriate to the file type.
EXAMPLE (Python):
Before: `f = request.files['file']; f.save(os.path.join(upload_dir, f.filename))`
After: `ext = get_ext(f); assert ext in ALLOWED_EXTS; assert mime_in_allowlist(f); assert sig_matches(ext, f); safe_name = uuid4().hex + '.' + ext; f.save(os.path.join(upload_dir, safe_name))`
Secure File Upload and Storage
WHAT: Unvalidated or improperly handled uploaded files (e.g., images, documents, ZIPs) and insecure storage/permissions can lead to malicious content execution, data leakage, DoS, or SQL injection when stored in databases.
WHY: Attackers can upload malware, exploit parsing libraries, exfiltrate or corrupt data, exhaust storage/CPU, or gain unauthorized access to files or the underlying system.
HOW: Validate file content by type (e.g., image rewriting, Apache POI for MS docs, content-type validation APIs), avoid ZIPs when possible, scan files (e.g., AV/hash services) in a sandbox, store files on a separate host and outside webroot with least-privilege filesystem permissions, enforce authentication/authorization on upload/download, set strict upload/download and post-decompression size limits, and use DB storage only with strong SQLi protections and DBA oversight.
EXAMPLE: Before processing an uploaded image, rewrite/transform it using a safe imaging library and save the rewritten output to a non-executable directory on a separate file server that the web app can write to but not execute from, with read access restricted to authorized users only.
Forgot Password Reset Security
WHAT: Insecure password reset flows can leak which accounts exist, allow brute-forcing or reuse of reset tokens, or change account data without proper proof of identity.
WHY: These flaws enable user enumeration, account takeover, denial of service (reset-email flooding), and unauthorized account changes.
HOW: Use consistent messages and timing for existing/non-existing accounts; rate-limit and add CAPTCHA on reset requests; generate reset tokens with a cryptographically secure RNG, make them long, single-use, securely stored, and short-lived; do not modify the account (e.g., lockout, password change) until a valid token is presented; follow standard input validation and SQL injection prevention.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): `if (!userExists(email)) return "Email not found";` After (secure): `if (requestLooksValid(email)) { enqueueResetFlow(email); } return "If an account exists for this email, you will receive reset instructions.";`
Password reset tokens and PINs
WHAT: Insecure password reset flows (weak or reusable tokens/PINs, guessable security questions, host header trust, HTTP URLs, referrer leakage, or lack of brute‑force protection) can let attackers reset accounts without authorization.
WHY: An attacker who exploits these weaknesses can take over user accounts, deny access to legitimate users, or intercept sensitive reset links.
HOW: Use cryptographically secure random tokens of sufficient length, link them to a specific user in the database, store them securely, and invalidate them after use; avoid JWTs unless you fully understand and mitigate their specific risks; never rely on the Host header when building reset URLs (hard‑code or validate against an allowlist of trusted domains) and always use HTTPS; add a Referrer-Policy with `noreferrer` on reset pages; implement rate limiting or similar controls to prevent brute-forcing of tokens/PINs; for PIN-based resets, create a restricted session that only allows password reset; do not use security questions as the sole reset mechanism and only use well-designed questions as an additional factor; do not lock accounts solely due to forgotten-password attempts.
EXAMPLE (web, pseudo-code): Before: `resetUrl = "https://" + request.headers["Host"] + "/reset?token=" + randomToken();` After: `trustedDomain = "https://accounts.example.com"; resetUrl = trustedDomain + "/reset?token=" + secureRandomToken(); setHeader("Referrer-Policy", "no-referrer"); applyRateLimiting(userIdOrIP);`
Cross-site leaks (XS-Leaks) protections
WHAT: Cross-site leaks occur when cross-origin browser behavior (e.g., cookies, redirects, timing, or residual data) allows an attacker’s site to infer sensitive state (such as login status, user ID, or roles) without directly reading responses.
WHY: Successful XS-Leaks attacks can reveal private account information, deanonymize users, and undermine access control decisions by leaking whether specific sensitive conditions are true.
HOW: Minimize cross-origin observable differences for sensitive actions, avoid exposing user-specific state via cross-site navigations, and configure cookies with appropriate SameSite attributes (Lax or Strict where possible, None only with Secure and when cross-site is required).
EXAMPLE: Before (less safe): `Set-Cookie: session=abc; Path=/; Secure`; After (safer): `Set-Cookie: session=abc; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax`
SameSite cookies and framing protection
WHAT: Missing or misconfigured SameSite cookie attributes and lack of framing protection allow cross-site requests and XS-Leaks (e.g., inferring user state via focus/blur events in iframes).
WHY: Attackers can abuse cross-site cookie sending and iframe embedding to perform CSRF or leak sensitive information about user accounts or actions.
HOW: Explicitly set SameSite and Secure attributes on all session/auth cookies (e.g., SameSite=Lax or Strict as appropriate, always over HTTPS). Block untrusted framing using CSP `frame-ancestors` or `X-Frame-Options` when your app does not need to be embedded by other origins.
EXAMPLE: HTTP header: `Set-Cookie: session=...; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax` and `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self';` or `X-Frame-Options: DENY`.
Clickjacking and XS-Leak Protection for Framed and Cross-Site Requests
WHAT: Failure to restrict framing and cross-site resource loading (e.g., missing CSP frame-ancestors/X-Frame-Options, no Sec-Fetch-* checks, no CORP, no per-resource tokens) allows clickjacking and cross-site leaks via onload/onerror behavior and enumeration of sensitive endpoints.
WHY: Attackers can embed your app in attacker-controlled pages or load your endpoints cross-site to infer user-specific data (e.g., logged-in user ID) without reading response bodies, leading to account deanonymization or targeted attacks.
HOW: Configure CSP frame-ancestors (and X-Frame-Options for legacy browsers) to disallow untrusted framing; use Sec-Fetch-Dest and Sec-Fetch-Site to reject cross-site/iframe requests to sensitive routes; for highly sensitive subresources, require long, unique, server-validated tokens; and set Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy (same-origin or same-site) to prevent your resources from being loaded in other origins.
EXAMPLE: In a Node/Express app, reject iframe and cross-site access to sensitive endpoints:
app.get('/api/users/:id', auth, (req, res) => { if (req.get('Sec-Fetch-Dest') === 'iframe' || req.get('Sec-Fetch-Site') === 'cross-site') return res.sendStatus(403); /* normal handler */ });
postMessage target origin validation
WHAT: Sending messages with window.postMessage using targetOrigin='*' or other overly broad origins allows untrusted origins to receive sensitive data.
WHY: An attacker-controlled window or frame can intercept secrets or internal state, leading to data leakage and cross-origin attacks.
HOW: Always pass an exact, trusted origin string to postMessage; never use '*' for sensitive data, and restrict which origins can be opened or messaged.
EXAMPLE: Before: popup.postMessage('secret message!', '*'); After: popup.postMessage('secret message!', 'https://sub.example.com');
Cross-origin resource and cache leak hardening
WHAT: Resources (e.g., images) can leak sensitive state (such as whether a user is logged in or has access) via cache timing and cross-site interactions if they are publicly guessable or cached across users.
WHY: Attackers can use XS-Leaks techniques to infer user-specific information, leading to privacy breaches, CSRF-like abuse, or account state detection across origins.
HOW: Use unpredictable, per-user tokens in resource URLs that must remain cacheable; disable caching for sensitive resources with `Cache-Control: no-store`; set cookies with appropriate `SameSite` attributes; restrict framing with `frame-ancestors`/X-Frame-Options; and configure CORP/COOP and Fetch Metadata headers to limit cross-origin and cross-site requests.
EXAMPLE: Protect a user avatar: `/avatars/admin.svg?token=<per-user-random-token>` (unguessable per user) and for non-cacheable sensitive content set `Cache-Control: no-store` and `Set-Cookie: session=...; SameSite=Lax`.
Toolchain hardening for C/C++ builds
WHAT: Insecure or weakly configured C/C++ toolchains (compiler/linker/build settings) produce executables without available hardening features, diagnostics, or integration with platform security.
WHY: Misconfigured builds increase the risk of exploitable bugs reaching production and make it difficult or impossible to retrofit security protections after deployment.
HOW: Define and maintain at least Debug and Release build configurations; in Debug, enable full assertions, diagnostics, and runtime checking tools; in Release, enable appropriate optimizations while turning on all available security-hardening flags and platform security integrations at compile and link time.
EXAMPLE: (C/C++ build system) Debug: add flags for full debug info, assertions, and memory guards; Release: add flags for stack protections, control-flow hardening, and secure runtime libraries, and ensure all third-party libraries are built with the same hardening settings.
Secure debug and release build configuration
WHAT: Failing to enable strong diagnostics and security-related compiler options in debug and release builds can leave memory errors, bad parameters, and speculative execution vulnerabilities (e.g., Spectre/Meltdown) undetected and unmitigated.
WHY: Undetected memory and API misuse bugs can become exploitable in production; missing Spectre/Meltdown mitigations can allow data leakage across security boundaries.
HOW: For debug builds, compile with no/low optimization and maximum debug info (e.g., `-O0 -g3 -ggdb`), define `DEBUG` and ensure `NDEBUG` is not defined, enable frame pointers (`-fno-omit-frame-pointer`), and link diagnostic tools such as AddressSanitizer or dmalloc. For release builds, use optimization with debug info (e.g., `-On -g2`) and enable speculative execution mitigations such as `-mfunction-return=thunk` and `-mindirect-branch=thunk`.
EXAMPLE: Before (release): `CFLAGS = -O2`
After (release, hardened): `CFLAGS = -O2 -g2 -mfunction-return=thunk -mindirect-branch=thunk`
Build configuration hardening for release and test builds
WHAT: Misconfigured release/test builds (e.g., leaving debug diagnostics, asserts that abort, or weak compiler/linker flags) can expose sensitive data in dumps/logs and miss important hardening options.
WHY: Insecure builds can leak secrets via crash artifacts and lack exploit mitigations (e.g., PIE, stack protector, RELRO), making successful attacks easier and more damaging.
HOW: For release builds, define NDEBUG, ensure DEBUG is not defined, remove or replace assert+abort() with controlled error handling, and avoid writing sensitive data to dumps or logs; enable appropriate optimizations. For hardened builds with Autotools, explicitly set and verify strong CFLAGS/LDFLAGS (e.g., -fPIE, -pie, -fstack-protector-all, -Wformat-security, -z noexecstack, -z relro, -z now) in m4/Makefile templates when configure ignores command-line flags.
EXAMPLE: (C, GCC/Autotools) Before: CFLAGS="-O2" LDFLAGS="" and production code uses assert(user_input != NULL); abort(); which may generate core dumps with secrets. After: CFLAGS="-O2 -fPIE -fstack-protector-all -Wformat=2 -Wformat-security" LDFLAGS="-pie -z noexecstack -z relro -z now" and replace assert+abort with explicit error handling that logs minimal, non-sensitive context without dumping full process memory.
Build configuration flags not triggering rebuilds
WHAT: Build systems like Make that only track file timestamps can fail to rebuild when security-relevant flags (e.g., CFLAGS/CXXFLAGS toggling DEBUG/NDEBUG, stack protection, RELRO, PIE) change, leaving binaries compiled with unintended debug or insecure settings.
WHY: Mismatched configurations can ship debug builds (e.g., asserts enabled) or omit hardening flags, leading to unexpected aborts (self‑DoS) or reduced resistance to exploitation in production.
HOW: Treat configuration/flag changes as dependencies: encode build modes (debug/release/test) into separate targets or output directories, add phony or stamp files tied to flag sets, or force clean/rebuild when CFLAGS/CXXFLAGS or hardening flags change so that all objects are recompiled under the correct secure configuration.
EXAMPLE: Not provided because the language/tooling is not fully specified.
Build-time security hardening and honoring user security flags
WHAT: Failing to rebuild with updated security-related compiler/linker flags or ignoring user-specified flags (e.g., for PIE/ASLR, DEP, disabling insecure protocols/compression) can leave binaries in insecure debug or weakly protected configurations.
WHY: Insecure builds can cause self‑inflicted DoS (e.g., asserts aborting in production) and enable exploitation via missing ASLR/DEP or legacy/insecure crypto/protocol features, and may cause audit failures.
HOW: Ensure build rules depend on CFLAGS/CXXFLAGS/LDFLAGS so changes trigger rebuilds; honor user-supplied flags; explicitly enable platform protections (PIE/ASLR, DEP, non-executable stack/heap) and disable insecure options (e.g., SSLv2/SSLv3/compression) in third‑party libraries; verify resulting binaries with appropriate tools (e.g., nm, openssl s_client).
EXAMPLE: Before (ignores flags, insecure defaults): `make` with hard-coded flags and OpenSSL built without `-no-ssl2 -no-ssl3 -no-comp -fPIE -pie -z,noexecstack -z,noexecheap`. After (honors and enforces security flags): `make CFLAGS="-fPIE" CXXFLAGS="-fPIE" LDFLAGS="-pie -z,noexecstack -z,noexecheap"` and configure OpenSSL with `Configure ... -no-hw -no-engine -no-comp -no-shared -no-dso -no-ssl2 -no-ssl3`.
Preprocessor configuration and security
WHAT: Inconsistent or ambiguous use of preprocessor macros (e.g., DEBUG, _DEBUG, NDEBUG, _NDEBUG) can cause code to compile with unintended configurations, leading to disabled checks, incorrect logging, or production builds running with debug behavior.
WHY: Misconfigured builds can expose sensitive information, weaken security checks, or behave unpredictably in production, undermining reliability and security guarantees.
HOW: Standardize on explicit Release (NDEBUG) and Debug (DEBUG or _DEBUG) configurations; enforce that both cannot be defined simultaneously and that if neither is defined, the build defaults to Release. Add compile-time checks to fail the build when conflicting macros are set.
EXAMPLE:
Before: (no checks) code may compile with both DEBUG and NDEBUG set.
After: `#if (defined(DEBUG) || defined(_DEBUG)) && (defined(NDEBUG) || defined(_NDEBUG)) #error "DEBUG and NDEBUG cannot both be defined" #endif`
Custom debug assertions and abort behavior
WHAT: Using standard assert() in C/C++ causes abort() on failure when NDEBUG is not defined, which can lead developers to disable or avoid assertions, reducing runtime validation of parameters, return values, and program state.
WHY: Disabling or underusing assertions hides logic and state errors that can become security vulnerabilities (e.g., unchecked inputs, invalid states) in production, making bugs harder to detect and fix.
HOW: Implement and use a custom assertion macro that, in debug builds, logs detailed failure context and triggers a debugger-friendly signal (e.g., SIGTRAP) instead of aborting, and in release builds compiles to a no-op; use assertions alongside explicit if-checks for all critical parameter, return value, and state validations.
EXAMPLE: In C/C++, define a DEBUG-only ASSERT that logs file, line, function, and an optional message, then raises SIGTRAP on failure; in non-DEBUG builds, define ASSERT to evaluate the expression without side effects or to an empty statement.
Assertion and debug trap handling
WHAT: Assertions in debug builds raise SIGTRAP and install a signal handler at startup, potentially altering global process behavior and error handling.
WHY: Misconfigured or globally installed SIGTRAP handlers can interfere with other components’ debugging, mask real faults, or expose internal state in production if left enabled.
HOW: Restrict SIGTRAP-based assertions and handlers to debug builds only, avoid installing global handlers in shared libraries, and ensure production builds either disable these assertions or map them to safe logging without altering signal handling.
EXAMPLE: In production builds, compile with ESAPI_BUILD_DEBUG undefined so that ESAPI_ASSERT1/2 become no-ops or safe logging, and do not register a SIGTRAP handler in the constructor of globally instantiated objects.
Signal handler installation safety
WHAT: Incorrectly overwriting existing signal handlers (e.g., for SIGTRAP) without checking for a prior handler can break other components’ signal handling logic.
WHY: Overwriting another module’s signal handler may disable critical error handling, debugging, or cleanup logic, leading to undefined behavior or security issues.
HOW: Before installing a new signal handler, call `sigaction` to retrieve the old handler; if `old_handler.sa_handler` is non-NULL or not the default/ignored handler, do not replace it. Always check return values of `sigaction`/`sigemptyset` and handle failures safely.
EXAMPLE (C++): Before: `sigaction(SIGTRAP, &new_handler, NULL);` After: `sigaction(SIGTRAP, NULL, &old); if (old.sa_handler == SIG_DFL || old.sa_handler == SIG_IGN) { sigaction(SIGTRAP, &new_handler, NULL); }`
Use compiler warnings and static analysis
WHAT: Failing to enable and act on compiler warnings and static analysis allows defects like incorrect integer promotions, misuse of APIs, and other logic errors to reach production.
WHY: Such unchecked defects can lead to crashes, data corruption, or exploitable vulnerabilities (e.g., unexpected comparison results, tainted data misuse).
HOW: Compile with the highest warning level and treat warnings as errors; enable built-in static analysis (e.g., GCC/Clang analyzers, MSVC /analyze); regularly run dedicated data-flow/taint-analysis tools for issues like SQL injection; fix or justify every reported issue.
EXAMPLE: (C/C++) Build with flags such as `-Wall -Wextra -Werror` and enable the compiler’s static analyzer; integrate a taint-analysis tool in CI to scan for unsafe use of user-controlled input in database queries.
Compiler and linker hardening flags
WHAT: Failing to enable available compiler/linker hardening options (e.g., stack protector, NX, PIE, overflow-preserving flags) can result in binaries that are vulnerable to stack smashing, code injection, and miscompilations due to undefined integer overflow.
WHY: Missing these protections increases exploitability of memory-safety bugs and may cause the compiler to optimize away overflow checks, enabling attacks such as stack-based buffer overflows and integer-overflow-driven memory corruption.
HOW: For supported GCC/Binutils toolchains, enable stack protection (e.g., -fstack-protector-strong or stronger), NX and PIE via linker flags, and overflow-preserving behavior (e.g., -fno-strict-overflow or -fwrapv) where needed; regularly inspect distribution defaults with `gcc -dumpspecs` and verify resulting binaries with tools like checksec.sh.
EXAMPLE: Before (no hardening): `gcc main.c -o app`
After (with hardening): `gcc -fstack-protector-strong -fPIE -fno-strict-overflow -Wl,-z,relro,-z,now -pie main.c -o app`
Compiler warning configuration for safer C/C++/Objective-C code
WHAT: Failure to enable strong compiler warnings and stack protection (e.g., not using -fstack-protector or -fstack-protector-all) can leave stack-based vulnerabilities and other defects undetected.
WHY: Missing these protections increases the risk of exploitable bugs such as stack buffer overflows and logic errors that compilers could otherwise flag.
HOW: Enable stack protection with -fstack-protector or -fstack-protector-all, and turn on aggressive warning sets for your compiler, selectively disabling only clearly noisy warnings (e.g., -Wno-unused-parameter, -Wno-type-limits, -Wno-tautological-compare) instead of disabling broad categories.
EXAMPLE: Before (GCC): g++ main.cpp
After (GCC): g++ -fstack-protector-all -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Wno-unused-parameter main.cpp
Compiler and linker hardening flags for secure builds
WHAT: Builds omit available hardening flags (e.g., stack protector, RELRO, non-executable stack/heap, strict warnings), resulting in binaries compiled without modern exploit mitigations.
WHY: Missing mitigations and diagnostics make memory corruption, format string, integer overflow, and control-flow hijack vulnerabilities easier to introduce and successfully exploit.
HOW: Detect compiler/linker capabilities in your build system and conditionally enable all supported security flags (e.g., -Wall, -Wextra, -Wformat-security, -fstack-protector-all, -fPIE, -pie, -z,noexecstack, -z,relro, -z,now, -Weverything, -fsanitize=integer/shift), making them default for production builds and enforcing them via overridden CFLAGS/CXXFLAGS/LDFLAGS.
EXAMPLE: In a Makefile, probe toolchain and add flags: `GCC_COMPILER=$(shell $(CXX) -v 2>&1 | egrep -ic '^gcc version')`; `ifeq ($(GCC_COMPILER),1) MY_CC_FLAGS+=-Wall -Wextra -Wformat-security -fstack-protector-all endif`; then `override CXXFLAGS := $(MY_CC_FLAGS) $(CXXFLAGS)`.
Safe handling of compiler warnings, signed/unsigned comparisons, and numeric conversions
WHAT: Failing to heed compiler warnings, incorrectly comparing signed and unsigned integers, or using unsafe numeric conversions (e.g., atoi to narrow types) can cause logic errors, overflows, or incorrect security decisions (such as misinterpreting negative values as large positive ones or accepting invalid ports).
WHY: These issues can bypass validation checks, enable out-of-range values, or cause subtle bugs that lead to vulnerabilities like access control failures, memory corruption, or misuse of network resources.
HOW: Enable strict warnings (e.g., -Wconversion) and suppress only specific, understood noise (e.g., via UNUSED_PARAMETER macros), never globally disable warnings; for signed/unsigned comparisons, validate ranges (e.g., assert x ≥ 0) before casting and comparing; for numeric input, avoid atoi and similar silent-fail APIs—use robust parsing (e.g., string streams or strto* functions), check for parse errors, and enforce explicit bounds (such as valid port ranges).
EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe): `int x = GetX(); unsigned y = GetY(); if ((unsigned)x > y) {...}` and `addr.sin_port = htons(atoi(argv[2]));` After (safer): validate `x >= 0` and only then cast and compare, and parse ports with checked conversion and range validation before assigning to `sin_port`.
Avoid silent truncation and ignored return values in bounded output functions
WHAT: Failing to check the return value of bounded output functions (e.g., snprintf) can cause silent string truncation and use of incomplete or attacker-controlled paths or data.
WHY: Silent truncation can lead to incorrect file paths, misrouting, or security checks being bypassed, potentially allowing attackers to influence file operations or other security-sensitive behavior.
HOW: Always capture and validate the return value of snprintf and similar APIs: check for errors (e.g., ret == -1) and for truncation (ret >= buffer_size); on failure, abort the operation or raise an error instead of using the truncated buffer.
EXAMPLE:
Before:
snprintf(path, sizeof(path), "%s/create", selinux_mnt);
fd = open(path, O_RDWR);
After:
int ret = snprintf(path, sizeof(path), "%s/create", selinux_mnt);
if (ret == -1 || ret >= (int)sizeof(path)) { /* handle error, do not use path */ }
else { fd = open(path, O_RDWR); }
Windows runtime exploit mitigations
WHAT: Failure to enable available Windows exploit mitigation features (e.g., Windows Defender Exploit Guard, Process Mitigation Management Tool) leaves applications more vulnerable to memory-corruption and exploit techniques at runtime.
WHY: Missing mitigations can allow successful exploitation of vulnerabilities that would otherwise be blocked or made significantly harder, increasing risk of code execution and data compromise.
HOW: For deployed applications, configure exploit mitigation policies using Windows Defender Exploit Guard and the ProcessMitigations PowerShell module or Group Policy; apply appropriate mitigations (e.g., DEP, ASLR, CFG) per process and verify they are enforced in production environments.
EXAMPLE: Configure process mitigations with PowerShell: `Set-ProcessMitigation -Name MyApp.exe -Enable DEP,ASLR,CFG` and enforce equivalent settings via Group Policy for all production hosts running the application.
Docker daemon exposure and container privilege configuration
WHAT: Misconfiguring Docker by exposing the Docker daemon socket (e.g., /var/run/docker.sock, -H tcp://0.0.0.0) or running containers as root allows attackers to gain unrestricted root access to the host or escalate privileges from within containers.
WHY: Attackers who can access the Docker API or run as root in a container can escape to the host, control other containers, and fully compromise the underlying system.
HOW: Never expose /var/run/docker.sock to the network or mount it into containers; disable or strictly secure any TCP Docker daemon endpoints; always run containers as an unprivileged user (via `docker run -u`, `USER` in Dockerfile, or `--userns-remap=default`) instead of root.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): `docker run -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock myimage` and `docker run myimage` (default root). After (safer): `docker run -u 4000 myimage` and avoid any `-v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock` or `-H tcp://0.0.0.0:2375` usage.
Limit container privileges and capabilities
WHAT: Containers running as root, with unrestricted Linux capabilities, allowed privilege escalation, open inter-container networking, or disabled security modules expose the host and other workloads to compromise.
WHY: An attacker who breaks out of an over-privileged container can escalate to host root, move laterally to other containers, exfiltrate data, or disrupt cluster operations.
HOW: Run containers as non-root users (e.g., Kubernetes `securityContext.runAsUser`), drop all capabilities and add back only required ones (`--cap-drop all --cap-add ...` or `securityContext.capabilities`), forbid privileged/`--privileged` containers, set `--security-opt=no-new-privileges` or `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`, restrict pod-to-pod traffic with Docker custom networks or Kubernetes NetworkPolicies, and keep/enable seccomp/AppArmor/SELinux profiles rather than disabling them.
EXAMPLE: Docker: `docker run --user 4000 --cap-drop all --cap-add CHOWN --security-opt=no-new-privileges alpine`; Kubernetes Pod spec: `securityContext: { runAsUser: 4000, allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, capabilities: { drop: ["ALL"], add: ["CHOWN"] } }` combined with restrictive NetworkPolicies and enabled seccomp/AppArmor/SELinux profiles.
Container security hardening for Linux-based deployments
WHAT: Containers may run with weak isolation, excessive resource access, writable filesystems, and unscanned images, leading to privilege abuse, DoS, and persistence by attackers.
WHY: Missing LSM profiles, resource limits, read-only mounts, and image scanning can allow container escape, resource exhaustion, data tampering, and deployment of vulnerable or malicious images.
HOW: Keep default Linux Security Module profiles enabled and, where possible, apply seccomp/AppArmor/SELinux profiles; configure strict CPU/memory/FD/process limits (ulimits, Kubernetes resource limits/quotas); run containers with read-only root filesystems and mount volumes as read-only unless writes are strictly required; and integrate container/Dockerfile security linters and scanners into CI/CD pipelines.
EXAMPLE: In Kubernetes Pod specs, set `securityContext: { seccompProfile: {...}, readOnlyRootFilesystem: true }` and define `resources: { requests: {...}, limits: {...} }`; in Docker, run with `--read-only --ulimit nofile=1024 --ulimit nproc=256 -v data:/data:ro` and add an image scanning step (e.g., `docker scan` or similar) in the build pipeline.
Docker rootless mode for daemon and containers
WHAT: Running the Docker daemon and containers with root privileges increases the impact of a container escape or daemon compromise.
WHY: If an attacker breaks out of a rootful container or exploits the daemon, they may gain root access on the host, leading to full system compromise.
HOW: Enable and run Docker in rootless mode (or use an alternative like Podman) so the daemon and containers run as an unprivileged user, after verifying that rootless limitations are acceptable for your environment.
EXAMPLE: Configure and start Docker using rootless installation and startup commands so that `dockerd` runs under a non-root user account instead of as root.
Use secure secret management for containers and supply chain security
WHAT: Storing sensitive data (passwords, tokens, SSH keys) in images, environment variables, or runtime commands, and using unsigned/untracked images from untrusted registries, exposes secrets and enables supply-chain attacks.
WHY: Leaked secrets and tampered images can lead to unauthorized access, data breaches, and execution of malicious code in your environment.
HOW: For Docker, store sensitive data only in Docker Secrets; never bake secrets into images or pass them via CLI/env; restrict access to secrets and rotate them. For Kubernetes, enable etcd encryption and/or use dedicated secret-management tools instead of relying on default plaintext storage. Enforce image provenance, generate SBOMs, sign images, use a trusted registry with strict access control, and validate/signature-check images at deployment with continuous runtime monitoring.
EXAMPLE: (Docker) Before: `docker run -e DB_PASSWORD=supersecret myapp:latest` After: `docker secret create db_password ./db_password.txt` and reference `db_password` as a secret in your service/Compose configuration.
Secure communication and access control for drone software
WHAT: Insecure communication (unencrypted links, weak Wi‑Fi auth, spoofable GPS/telemetry) and exposed services (open SSH/FTP ports, weak webserver configs) allow interception, command injection, replay, and unauthorized control of drones and peripherals.
WHY: Attackers can hijack control, exfiltrate telemetry or sensor data, manipulate flight behavior, or pivot into attached systems, causing safety, privacy, and operational impacts.
HOW: Encrypt all control/telemetry channels with modern, mutually authenticated protocols; enable 802.11w MFP and strong Wi‑Fi auth; disable or firewall unused ports; harden SSH/FTP/webserver configs; enforce strong credentials and least-privilege access on companion computers and cameras.
EXAMPLE: Before (Python, unencrypted TCP): `sock = socket.create_connection((host, 5760)); sock.send(cmd)`; After: `ctx = ssl.create_default_context(purpose=ssl.Purpose.SERVER_AUTH); sock = ctx.wrap_socket(socket.create_connection((host, 5760)), server_hostname=host); sock.send(cmd)`
Secure drone communication protocols
WHAT: Insecure configuration or use of drone communication protocols (MAVLink, CAN, ZigBee, Bluetooth, Wi‑Fi) can allow spoofing, replay, command injection, eavesdropping, and deauthentication attacks.
WHY: Successful attacks can lead to loss of control, data theft, unauthorized commands, or physical compromise of the drone and its subsystems.
HOW: Enable protocol-specific security features: MAVLink 2.0 message signing and secured heartbeat handling; secure CAN variants (e.g., DroneCAN) where possible; AES‑128 and rotating network keys for ZigBee; Bluetooth LE Secure Connections (avoid “Just Works”); WPA3 and 802.11w MFP for Wi‑Fi, plus SSID hiding and MAC filtering where feasible.
EXAMPLE: When configuring MAVLink 2.0, require message signing for all control messages and validate heartbeat frequency and source before acting on any received commands.
Secure drone Wi-Fi configuration
WHAT: Insecure wireless configuration (e.g., using WEP, no management frame protection, broadcasting SSID, no MAC filtering) allows attackers to intercept, deauthenticate, or gain unauthorized access to drone control and video streams.
WHY: Compromise of the Wi-Fi link can lead to loss of control, data theft, command injection, or complete takeover of the UAV.
HOW: Configure the access point and drone to use WPA3 (or at least WPA2 with strong passphrases), enable 802.11w Management Frame Protection, disable SSID broadcast, and restrict connections via MAC address filtering where feasible.
EXAMPLE: Before: Wi-Fi security set to “WEP/Open”, SSID broadcast enabled, no MFP. After: Wi-Fi security set to “WPA3-Personal”, 802.11w MFP required, SSID broadcast disabled, and only whitelisted MAC addresses allowed to connect.
Database configuration and credential handling for applications
WHAT: Risk of database compromise due to exposed network access, unencrypted connections, weak/auth-less accounts, or credentials hard-coded in source or broadly readable config files.
WHY: Attackers can intercept data, steal or modify credentials, gain unauthorized access, escalate privileges, and exfiltrate or corrupt sensitive information.
HOW: Isolate the DB (local socket/localhost, firewall/DMZ), require TLSv1.2+ with certificate validation, enforce authentication with strong per-app accounts using least privilege, store credentials only in non-webroot config files with restricted permissions (and encrypt where supported), and never connect directly from untrusted thick clients—use a controlled backend API.
EXAMPLE (config pattern): Store DB credentials in a protected config file outside the web root with OS-level read access limited to the application user, and configure the DB listener to bind only to localhost with TLS required for all client connections.
Database permission and configuration hardening
WHAT: Risk of privilege escalation, data exposure, or remote code execution due to over-privileged database accounts, default accounts/databases, insecure services/features, and unprotected credentials/backups.
WHY: Excessive privileges or misconfigured services let attackers access or modify sensitive data, execute OS commands, pivot to other systems, or recover data from stolen backups.
HOW: Use least privilege for DB accounts (no root/sa/SYS, no admin rights, restricted hosts, only required DBs and minimal CRUD permissions, no ownership, minimal use of links/linked servers); apply granular table/column/row permissions and views; encrypt/protect stored credentials and backups; harden OS and DB per vendor baselines; remove default accounts/databases; run DB services under low-privilege users; install security patches; separate transaction logs from data files; disable unneeded features (e.g., xp_cmdshell/xp_dirtree, CLR, SQL Browser, Mixed Mode, FILE privilege, sample DBs); run mysql_secure_installation and follow vendor hardening guides.
EXAMPLE: Before: application connects as `sa` with full instance admin, Mixed Mode enabled, xp_cmdshell allowed, backups world-readable on shared disk. After: application connects as dedicated user `app_user` with only SELECT/UPDATE/DELETE on required schemas from app host only; xp_cmdshell/CLR/SQL Browser/Mixed Mode disabled; default/sample DBs removed; backups stored on restricted, encrypted storage.
Virtual patching for web applications
WHAT: Relying only on source-code fixes can leave known vulnerabilities exploitable during long remediation windows; failing to add a security enforcement layer allows attacks to reach the application in the meantime.
WHY: Exploits against known but unpatched vulnerabilities can lead to data exposure, compromise, or service disruption before development teams can deploy code fixes.
HOW: Deploy a virtual patching layer (e.g., WAF/IPS/web server plugin) to inspect and filter traffic for known vulnerability patterns, reduce exposed attack surface (e.g., enforce input validation or block XSS payloads), and maintain this in parallel with, not instead of, permanent code fixes.
EXAMPLE: Before: Application is directly exposed while developers schedule a future release to fix an input-validation bug. After: A WAF rule is immediately added to block or strictly validate requests to the vulnerable endpoint, and the rule stays in place until the secure code version is deployed and verified.
SQL Injection in User-Controlled Parameters
WHAT: Failing to sanitize and validate user-supplied input (e.g., the `reqID` parameter) before using it in SQL queries allows attackers to inject or modify SQL commands.
WHY: SQL injection can expose, modify, or delete arbitrary data, compromise authentication, and potentially lead to full system compromise.
HOW: Use parameterized queries/prepared statements for all database access, strictly validate and type-check user inputs, and avoid concatenating user data into SQL strings.
EXAMPLE (PHP, vulnerable):
$sql = "SELECT * FROM subscribers WHERE id = " . $_GET['reqID'];
$result = $db->query($sql);
EXAMPLE (PHP, fixed with prepared statement):
$stmt = $db->prepare("SELECT * FROM subscribers WHERE id = ?");
$stmt->execute([(int)$_GET['reqID']]);
Virtual patching and allowlist-based input validation
WHAT: Failing to apply virtual patches and strict allowlist-based input validation leaves web applications exposed to known vulnerabilities and injection-type flaws even after they are identified.
WHY: Unpatched or loosely filtered inputs can be exploited using public PoC payloads, leading to data leakage, injection attacks, or active security incidents.
HOW: For each identified vulnerability, determine if a virtual patch is applicable, record it in a tracking system with a unique identifier and impact level, specify affected versions/configurations, collect PoC payloads, and implement a positive security (allowlist) model that defines valid input characteristics (e.g., type, length, charset) per parameter and blocks all non-conforming input.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): `reqID = request.getParameter("reqID"); // used directly without checks` After (secure): `reqID = request.getParameter("reqID"); if (!reqID.matches("^[0-9]+$")) { return errorResponse(); }`
Virtual patching for input validation of request parameters
WHAT: Validate and constrain request parameters (e.g., `reqID`) so that only one instance is accepted and its value strictly matches the expected format (e.g., digits only), rejecting duplicate parameters and malformed input.
WHY: Prevents injection attacks (such as SQL injection) and evasion techniques that rely on duplicate parameters, unexpected characters, or exploit-specific payload variations.
HOW: For each parameter on vulnerable endpoints, enforce a positive security model: ensure exactly one occurrence of the parameter, validate it against a strict allowlist pattern (e.g., `^[0-9]+$` for numeric IDs), and avoid rules that only block a single known exploit string; instead, define generic validation rules and track rule IDs in your bug-tracking system.
EXAMPLE: Before (vulnerable): `exportsubscribers.php?reqID=1' or 1='1` accepted without checks. After (patched): WAF rule rejects requests where `&ARGS:/reqID/` count is not `1` or where `ARGS:/reqID/` does not match `^[0-9]+$`, blocking any non-numeric or duplicate `reqID` values.
Virtual patch testing and deployment for WAF rules
WHAT: Misconfigured or untested virtual patches in a WAF can block legitimate user traffic (false positives) or fail to block real attacks (false negatives), leaving vulnerabilities exploitable.
WHY: Incorrect virtual patching can cause outages, degrade user experience, and create a false sense of security while real vulnerabilities remain exposed.
HOW: Deploy new virtual patches in “log only” mode first; test them using multiple clients (browser, curl/wget, local proxy, audit log replay); request retests from the originating assessment tool/team; refine rules to handle evasions; track rule IDs in the ticket/patch system; periodically reassess and remove virtual patches once the underlying code is fixed; monitor alerts to confirm effectiveness.
EXAMPLE: Before: Enable a new ModSecurity rule in blocking mode directly on production. After: Enable the rule with SecRuleEngine DetectionOnly, validate logs and retest, then switch to blocking mode once false positives are resolved and tracking is in place.
Session ID Name Fingerprinting
WHAT: Using default, framework-specific session ID names (e.g., PHPSESSID, JSESSIONID) exposes implementation details and makes session identifiers easier to fingerprint and target.
WHY: Revealing underlying technologies can aid attackers in selecting framework-specific exploits and tooling, increasing the risk of successful session hijacking.
HOW: Configure the application/framework to override the default session cookie name with a generic, non-descriptive name that does not reveal technology or purpose (e.g., “id”), and keep this consistent across the app.
EXAMPLE: Before (PHP): `session_name("PHPSESSID");` → After: `session_name("id");`
Session ID Naming and Entropy for Web Applications
WHAT: Default, framework-specific session ID names and low-entropy or predictable session identifiers allow attackers to fingerprint the tech stack and brute-force or predict valid sessions.
WHY: Technology disclosure aids targeted attacks, and weak or predictable session IDs enable session hijacking and account compromise.
HOW: Rename default framework session cookie names to a generic, non-identifying name (e.g., "id"), and generate session IDs using a strong CSPRNG with at least 64 bits of entropy; avoid custom or predictable schemes.
EXAMPLE (PHP): Before: `session_start(); // uses "PHPSESSID"`; After: `session_name('id'); session_start(); ini_set('session.sid_length', 32); ini_set('session.sid_bits_per_character', 6);`
Session ID Entropy and Length for Brute-Force Resistance
WHAT: Session IDs with insufficient effective entropy (e.g., fixed or predictable portions, or too few random bits) can be brute-forced, allowing attackers to guess valid sessions.
WHY: Successful guessing of session IDs lets attackers hijack user sessions, impersonate users, and access protected data or actions.
HOW: Generate session IDs using a cryptographically secure random source with at least 64 bits of effective entropy; ensure all bits are unpredictable or increase length to compensate for any fixed/predictable parts; choose an encoding (hex, Base64, etc.) that preserves the required entropy (e.g., ≥16 hex characters for 64 bits).
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): sessionId = timestamp + userId; // predictable parts. After (secure): sessionId = SecureRandomBytes(8); // 64 bits from CSPRNG, then encode (e.g., hex) for storage/transport.
Session ID Content and Exchange
WHAT: Session IDs that contain meaningful or sensitive data, are predictable, or are accepted via insecure channels (e.g., URL parameters) can be disclosed, guessed, or fixed, leading to account/session compromise.
WHY: An attacker who obtains or predicts a session ID can hijack user sessions, access PII, or infer internal application logic; leaked IDs in logs, history, or referrers increase exposure.
HOW: Generate session IDs with a framework’s built-in session management or a CSPRNG of ≥128 bits; ensure IDs are opaque and never embed PII or business logic; store all session-related data server-side in a protected repository (encrypt if sensitive); use cookies as the only accepted transport for session IDs and reject IDs supplied via URLs, POST bodies, or custom headers; keep frameworks updated and harden default configs; secure any storage of session IDs against unauthorized access.
EXAMPLE (Java): BEFORE: `String sid = userId + "-" + System.currentTimeMillis(); response.addHeader("Location", "/home?sid=" + sid);` AFTER: `String sid = new BigInteger(130, SecureRandom.getInstanceStrong()).toString(32); HttpSession session = request.getSession(true); session.setAttribute("sid", sid); Cookie c = new Cookie("SESSIONID", sid); c.setHttpOnly(true); c.setSecure(true); response.addCookie(c);`
Secure session ID transport and cookie usage
WHAT: Session IDs are exposed or hijacked when applications accept non-cookie tracking mechanisms (e.g., URL parameters) or mix HTTP/HTTPS, causing IDs to be sent in cleartext or via insecure channels.
WHY: Attackers can eavesdrop, steal, or fix session IDs, leading to account compromise, data exposure, and session hijacking.
HOW: Restrict session tracking to cookies only; enforce HTTPS for the entire session; set Secure on session cookies; enable HSTS; do not switch a live session between HTTP and HTTPS; regenerate/set cookies only after HTTPS redirects; avoid mixed content and separate insecure/public content onto a different domain.
EXAMPLE (HTTP): Before: app accepts session IDs via URL parameters over HTTP and HTTPS. After: app rejects URL-based session IDs, uses only Secure cookies over HTTPS with HSTS enabled and no HTTP endpoints on the same host.
Secure use of session cookies
WHAT: Session cookies can be exposed or abused if cookie attributes (Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite, Domain, Path) are missing or overly permissive, enabling MitM theft, XSS-based stealing, CSRF, cross-subdomain attacks, or session fixation.
WHY: Attackers who obtain or control session IDs can hijack user sessions, impersonate users, or pivot between applications on the same domain.
HOW: Always set Secure on session cookies and serve them only over HTTPS; set HttpOnly to block script access; set SameSite (e.g., Lax/Strict) to limit cross-site sending; avoid setting Domain so cookies are restricted to the origin host; set Path as narrowly as possible to only the application paths that need the session; do not host apps of different trust levels on the same domain or share broad Domain cookies.
EXAMPLE (HTTP):
Before: `Set-Cookie: SID=abc123`
After:  `Set-Cookie: SID=abc123; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax; Path=/app;`
Session Cookie Domain, Path, and Lifetime Hardening
WHAT: Session IDs in cookies can be fixed, stolen, or shared across applications if cookies use overly broad Domain/Path attributes, are shared by apps of different security levels on the same host, or are made persistent unnecessarily.
WHY: Attackers can perform session fixation, cross-app session hijacking, or steal session IDs via DNS spoofing/hijacking/poisoning or other cross-application access, leading to full account compromise.
HOW: Use the narrowest possible Domain and Path for session cookies (avoid domain-wide cookies like `example.com` when not required), avoid hosting apps of different trust/security levels on the same domain/host, and use non-persistent (session) cookies for authentication sessions by omitting `Expires` and `Max-Age` so the browser deletes them on close.
EXAMPLE (HTTP header):
BEFORE: `Set-Cookie: SID=abc; Domain=example.com; Path=/; Expires=Wed, 21 Oct 2025 07:28:00 GMT`
AFTER:  `Set-Cookie: SID=abc; Domain=app.example.com; Path=/app; Secure; HttpOnly`
Secure handling of cookies and Web Storage data
WHAT: Sensitive data is improperly persisted in cookies or Web Storage (localStorage/sessionStorage), or cookies lack security attributes, allowing unauthorized access or manipulation.
WHY: Attackers or other system users may read or tamper with state, perform unauthorized actions, or steal confidential data from disk, memory, or over insecure connections.
HOW: Store sensitive data only when strictly necessary and for the minimum duration; encrypt sensitive values before persisting; set Secure and appropriate flags on cookies; validate all state transitions against expected cookies; avoid storing sensitive data in localStorage/sessionStorage unless encrypted and justified; document each cookie’s name, purpose, and necessity.
EXAMPLE (HTTP cookie, pseudocode): Before: `Set-Cookie: sessionId=123; Path=/` After: `Set-Cookie: sessionId=<encrypted-token>; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict`
Session ID Management and Web Worker Secret Handling
WHAT: Improper session ID handling (accepting attacker-supplied IDs, not regenerating on privilege changes) and leaking secrets from Web Workers to the main window can lead to session fixation and secret exposure.
WHY: Attackers can hijack or fix user sessions, exploit stored session IDs for SQLi/XSS, or misuse Web Workers to perform sensitive operations with stolen secrets.
HOW: Only accept session IDs generated by the application; treat session IDs as untrusted input and validate them; regenerate session IDs on authentication and any privilege change; destroy old IDs; keep secrets and all code that uses them inside Web Workers and never postMessage secrets to the main window.
EXAMPLE (PHP): Before: `session_start(); // uses existing ID from user, no regeneration on login`. After: `session_start(); if ($login_ok) { session_regenerate_id(true); }`
Session ID Regeneration and Separation
WHAT: Failure to regenerate the session ID on authentication or privilege changes allows session fixation, where an attacker forces a victim to use an attacker-chosen session ID.
WHY: Successful session fixation lets attackers hijack authenticated sessions, potentially gaining full access to the victim’s account and data.
HOW: Always regenerate the session ID on login, logout, and privilege changes using the framework’s session-renewal APIs, and use distinct session IDs or token names for pre-authentication (anonymous) and post-authentication (authenticated) states.
EXAMPLE (Java, J2EE): Before: `HttpSession s = request.getSession(); // reuse existing ID on login`. After: `request.getSession().invalidate(); HttpSession s = request.getSession(true); // new ID on login`.
Reauthentication after sensitive account events
WHAT: Failing to require secure reauthentication after high‑risk account events (e.g., password/email changes, logins from new/suspicious devices, or account recovery flows) can let attackers persist or escalate access once they gain a foothold.
WHY: Without reauthentication at these points, session hijacking or partial compromise can turn into full, long‑term account takeover and data exposure.
HOW: After critical changes or risky signals, invalidate or step‑up existing sessions and require the user to reenter strong credentials or perform MFA, using well‑vetted patterns such as those in the “Reauthentication After Risk Events” guidance of the Authentication Cheat Sheet.
Session cookie binding and expiration
WHAT: Failure to validate and bind all session-related cookies (e.g., pre-auth HTTP cookie and post-auth HTTPS cookie) and to enforce proper idle/absolute server-side session timeouts allows reuse of stale or weaker cookies to access active authenticated sessions.
WHY: Attackers can hijack user sessions by reusing unprotected cookies or long-lived session IDs, gaining unauthorized access to authenticated accounts and sensitive data.
HOW: For each authenticated request, verify all expected cookies and their relationships (e.g., pre-/post-auth IDs, scopes) before granting access; avoid reusing the same cookie name across paths/domains; configure short, risk-based idle and absolute timeouts; on timeout or logout, actively invalidate the session on the server (e.g., HttpSession.invalidate(), Session.Abandon(), session_destroy()) and clear the client cookie with an expired Expires/Max-Age.
EXAMPLE: Before (server-side): accept access if secure_session_cookie is valid, ignoring any pre_auth cookie; no timeout, or timeout checked only via client timestamp. After: require both pre_auth and secure_session_cookie to match a bound server-side session record, enforce server-side idle and absolute timeouts on each request, and on expiry call the platform’s session invalidation API and send Set-Cookie: id=; Expires=<past date>.
Session Timeout and Caching Controls
WHAT: Failure to enforce session timeouts and expiration on the server side, and improper caching of session identifiers and sensitive content, allows attackers to extend or reuse sessions and access private data after logout.
WHY: Leads to session hijacking, prolonged impersonation, and exposure of sensitive information via browser or intermediary caches.
HOW: Enforce idle and absolute timeouts server-side; regenerate session IDs on a renewal timeout and invalidate old IDs; provide a global logout that invalidates the server-side session; send restrictive cache headers (e.g., Cache-Control: no-store, no-cache, must-revalidate, Pragma: no-cache) on all sensitive pages and any response containing session IDs.
EXAMPLE: Before (HTTP): `Cache-Control: public` and client-side JS tracking login time for timeout; After: server checks session age on each request, invalidates on timeout, regenerates IDs periodically, and returns `Cache-Control: no-store, no-cache, must-revalidate` on authenticated responses.
Reauthentication After High-Risk Events
WHAT: Missing or weak reauthentication after high-risk events (e.g., password change, suspicious login, account recovery completion) allows existing sessions to remain trusted without renewed proof of identity.
WHY: Attackers who hijack or reuse long-lived sessions can change credentials or take over accounts without being challenged, leading to account compromise and data exposure.
HOW: Detect high-risk events (password changes, new/suspicious IP or device, completion of recovery/challenge flows) and require the user to reauthenticate with primary credentials or MFA before allowing sensitive actions to proceed.
EXAMPLE: (Web app) After a user initiates a password change or logs in from a new device, invalidate the current session for sensitive operations and redirect to a reauthentication page that requires password or MFA before continuing.
Client-Side Session Management and Anomaly Detection
WHAT: Risk of session fixation, unauthorized session reuse, and undetected session ID attacks if sessions are not time-limited, properly closed, or monitored for anomalies on the client and server side.
WHY: Attackers can hijack or guess valid sessions, reuse old session IDs, or manipulate cookies to impersonate users, leading to account compromise and data exposure.
HOW: Enforce pre-login timeouts and renew session IDs on stale login pages; trigger logout on browser/tab close and after idle time via client code; optionally prevent cross-tab session sharing; implement server-side detection of excessive session ID attempts and anomalies (modified/added cookies, reused IDs, sudden User-Agent/location changes) and alert/block offending sources.
EXAMPLE: Before: Accept any existing session ID on login and keep it active until server idle timeout, without anomaly checks. After: On login page load, start a timer and, after N minutes, force reload and issue a new session ID; on each page, run a client timer that redirects to /logout after idle; on the server, log and rate-limit requests with changing session IDs per IP and invalidate sessions when cookie or User-Agent changes unexpectedly.
Session ID Binding, Logging, and Concurrent Session Control
WHAT: Failure to bind session IDs to client properties, to log session lifecycle events safely, and to control simultaneous logons can allow undetected session hijacking, misuse, and unauthorized account access.
WHY: Attackers can reuse or steal session IDs to impersonate users; without binding, safe logging, and session controls, attacks are hard to detect, investigate, or automatically block.
HOW: Bind each session ID to stable client properties (e.g., IP, User-Agent, client certificate) and invalidate or flag the session if they change; log session lifecycle events (creation, renewal, destruction, privilege changes, invalid activity) with a salted hash of the session ID instead of the raw value; protect administrative session-management interfaces; and, if simultaneous logons are disallowed, terminate older sessions or require the user to choose which session remains active while exposing UI to view and remotely terminate active sessions.
EXAMPLE: Before: `log.info("user=" + userId + " sid=" + session.getId());`
After: `String sidHash = hashWithSalt(session.getId(), serverSalt); log.info("user=" + userId + " sidHash=" + sidHash);`
Session management hardening with a Web Application Firewall (WAF)
WHAT: Rely on a WAF to enforce secure session management when application code cannot be modified, including missing cookie security attributes and weak session handling.
WHY: Insecure cookies and session handling enable session hijacking, fixation, and unauthorized use of active sessions.
HOW: Configure the WAF to rewrite Set-Cookie headers to always add Secure and HttpOnly flags, track session IDs, renew client-side session IDs on privilege changes, bind sessions to client properties (IP/User-Agent), and enforce session expiration.
EXAMPLE: Before (HTTP response header): `Set-Cookie: SID=abc123; Path=/` → After (rewritten by WAF): `Set-Cookie: SID=abc123; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly`.
Legacy Application Risk Management
WHAT: Legacy applications may be unpatched, unsupported, and use obsolete technologies or protocols, leaving known vulnerabilities exploitable and hindering monitoring/logging.
WHY: Unmitigated legacy risks can lead to remote compromise, data breaches, and blind spots in detection and response due to incompatible formats and interfaces.
HOW: Maintain an up-to-date inventory (including versions, configs, hosts, services, SBOMs), perform formal or informal threat modeling and risk assessments, and apply compensating controls (network isolation, strict access control, monitoring integration) based on identified risks.
EXAMPLE: Before: Running an EoL app directly on a flat corporate network with default configs and no documented dependencies. After: Document the app and its dependencies (SBOM), place it in a segmented network, restrict access to specific hosts/ports, and feed its logs into a SIEM via a compatible proxy or converter.
Legacy application access control and least privilege
WHAT: Legacy applications often expose overly broad network and feature access, allowing unauthenticated or over-privileged users to reach sensitive functionality or data.
WHY: Excessive access increases the risk of data exfiltration, lateral movement to privileged networks, business disruption, and regulatory impact if the application is compromised.
HOW: Enforce least privilege by restricting network access (subnets, IP allowlists, VPN), requiring strong authentication (app-level or via IdP), disabling high-risk/administrative features, closing all non-essential ports, and, where possible, placing an intermediary service/API in front of the legacy app so only controlled data flows are allowed.
EXAMPLE: Before: Legacy app is directly exposed on the public internet with all features enabled and no authentication. After: App is moved to a restricted subnet behind a VPN, protected by an IdP login, admin features are disabled for normal users, unused ports are firewalled, and external clients interact only via a new API that mediates and validates all requests to the legacy app.
Legacy Application Security Maintenance
WHAT: Legacy applications may contain unpatched code vulnerabilities and outdated dependencies that remain exploitable if not regularly identified and addressed.
WHY: Unmanaged vulnerabilities can lead to remote code execution, data breaches, or service compromise, especially when public exploits or CVEs exist.
HOW: Schedule automated vulnerability scans (SAST/SCA and host scans) where possible; review results and apply security patches or upgrades prioritized by severity and exploitability; when patching is not feasible, restrict network and access permissions around the affected components.
EXAMPLE: Before: Legacy service runs with outdated libraries and no regular scanning or patching. After: CI pipeline runs SAST/SCA on each release, security team reviews findings weekly, applies critical patches within defined SLAs, and isolates components that cannot be patched with strict firewall and access controls.
Legacy application monitoring and incident response
WHAT: Legacy applications may produce logs in incompatible formats and lack modern monitoring hooks, leading to missed or delayed detection of security incidents affecting these systems.
WHY: Undetected or slowly detected compromises of critical legacy systems can result in prolonged attacker presence, data breaches, and extended downtime, impacting confidentiality, integrity, and availability.
HOW: Implement enhanced monitoring for legacy apps by normalizing their logs (via custom APIs or converters) into formats your security tools can ingest, or by using automation scripts to regularly scan for indicators of compromise; monitor for anomalous network traffic to and from legacy environments; and define, document, and prioritize incident response procedures for these systems within your business continuity plan.
EXAMPLE: N/A
PHP configuration hardening for secure deployments
WHAT: Misconfigured php.ini and server settings (e.g., exposing errors, allowing remote file access, weak session settings, dangerous functions enabled) can leak sensitive data, enable RFI/LFI, or allow code execution.
WHY: Attackers can use these misconfigurations to read arbitrary files, execute system commands, hijack sessions, or gain detailed insight into your environment for further exploitation.
HOW: In production, set `display_errors=Off`, `log_errors=On` with a non-web-accessible `error_log`; restrict file access with `doc_root`/`open_basedir`; disable remote URLs (`allow_url_fopen=Off`, `allow_url_include=Off`); disable unused dangerous functions via `disable_functions`; harden sessions with strict cookies (`session.use_strict_mode=1`, `session.use_only_cookies=1`, `session.cookie_secure=1`, `session.cookie_httponly=1`, `session.cookie_samesite=Strict`), strong IDs (`session.sid_length`, `session.sid_bits_per_character`), and appropriate paths/domains; turn `file_uploads=Off` if unused and otherwise isolate `upload_tmp_dir`; keep `expose_php=Off` and resource limits (memory, execution time) conservative.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): `display_errors=On`, `allow_url_fopen=On`, `allow_url_include=On`, `session.use_only_cookies=0`, `session.cookie_secure=0`, `disable_functions=`. After (hardened): `display_errors=Off`, `log_errors=On`, `allow_url_fopen=Off`, `allow_url_include=Off`, `session.use_only_cookies=1`, `session.cookie_secure=1`, `session.cookie_httponly=1`, `session.cookie_samesite=Strict`, `disable_functions=system,exec,shell_exec,passthru,phpinfo,show_source,highlight_file,popen,proc_open,...`.
Web service transport and message security
