WHAT: Web services that handle sensitive data or authenticated sessions without proper TLS, authentication, authorization, integrity, and confidentiality controls are vulnerable to eavesdropping, tampering, impersonation, and unauthorized access.
WHY: Missing or weak controls can lead to credential theft, data disclosure, data modification, account takeover, and abuse of administrative functions.
HOW: Enforce well-configured TLS for all sensitive web service traffic; verify server certificates (issuer, expiry, revocation, hostname, key possession); avoid Basic Auth or use it only over TLS; use mutual TLS where appropriate; require per-request authorization checks for every sensitive operation and restrict admin functions to separate, admin-only interfaces; use XML digital signatures for XML message integrity and strong encryption (in transit and at rest) for sensitive data.
EXAMPLE: Before: Expose `/api/payments` over HTTP with Basic Auth and no per-request authorization checks. After: Expose `/api/payments` only over HTTPS with strict TLS config and certificate validation, replace Basic Auth with token or mTLS, enforce role-based checks on each payment request, sign XML payloads with XML digital signatures, and encrypt stored sensitive fields with strong keys.
Web service admin access control and schema/content validation
WHAT: Administrative and management functions in a web service must be accessible only to authorized web service administrators, and all SOAP payloads must be strictly validated against their XML Schema Definitions (XSD) with length, character set, and allow-list patterns for fixed-format parameters.
WHY: Missing access control or weak input/schema validation can let attackers invoke sensitive admin operations or inject malicious data, leading to data exposure, corruption, or full system compromise.
HOW: Isolate admin capabilities into a separate application or endpoint protected by strong authentication/authorization; enforce schema validation on every SOAP request/response; in XSDs, define maximum lengths, allowed character sets, and allow-list regex patterns for all parameters, especially fixed formats (e.g., zip codes, phone numbers).
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): a single SOAP endpoint exposes admin operations and parses incoming XML without schema validation. After (secure): admin operations are moved to a separate, admin-only endpoint, and every SOAP message is validated against a strict XSD that constrains field lengths, characters, and formats before processing.
Web service security hardening
WHAT: Web services may be vulnerable to XML-based DoS (e.g., entity expansion, recursive/oversized payloads, overlong element names), XEE/XML bombs, XSS via unencoded output, malware in attachments, and resource exhaustion (CPU, memory, files, connections, message size/throughput).
WHY: Exploitation can lead to denial of service, remote code execution, data theft, XSS in clients, and compromise of the host system.
HOW: Use hardened XML parsers with entity expansion disabled and limits on depth, size, and element name length; validate XML and inputs with strict allowlists; enable protection against external entities and XML bombs; HTML/JS-encode all output rendered in browsers; scan all attachments with up-to-date antivirus inline before saving; enforce limits on SOAP message size, throughput, CPU, memory, open files, connections, and processes; configure services to comply with WS-I Basic Profile.
EXAMPLE: Before (XML parsing): parser = new XmlParser(); parser.load(requestBody); // default settings, XXE + DoS possible. After: parser = new SecureXmlParser(); parser.disableExternalEntities(); parser.setMaxDepth(50); parser.setMaxSize(1_000_000); parser.setMaxNameLength(256); parser.load(validatedInput);
DOM-based XSS prevention for HTML subcontexts
WHAT: Untrusted data written into HTML subcontexts via DOM APIs (e.g., innerHTML, outerHTML, document.write) can lead to DOM-based XSS if it is interpreted as markup or script.
WHY: Attackers can inject and execute arbitrary JavaScript in the victim’s browser, enabling session theft, data exfiltration, or full UI compromise.
HOW: Do not pass raw user-controlled data to HTML-rendering DOM APIs; first HTML-encode and then JavaScript-encode all untrusted input before insertion, or use safer APIs that treat data as text (e.g., textContent) instead of HTML.
EXAMPLE: Before (vulnerable): element.innerHTML = userInput; After (safer): element.textContent = userInput; or element.innerHTML = jsEncode(htmlEncode(userInput));
JavaScript encoding and HTML attribute contexts
WHAT: Incorrectly encoding untrusted data in JavaScript execution contexts (e.g., event handlers, script blocks) or double-encoding HTML attributes can either break functionality or still allow DOM-based XSS (e.g., JavaScript-encoded strings in onclick still execute).
WHY: Attackers can inject or execute arbitrary JavaScript, leading to XSS, data theft, session hijacking, or full account compromise.
HOW: Avoid placing untrusted data in JavaScript code or event-handler attributes; if unavoidable, strictly validate/allowlist values and treat them as data, not code. For non-executing HTML attributes set via the DOM (e.g., element.setAttribute("value", ...)), apply only JavaScript encoding when the attribute value is embedded in a JS string literal, and do not additionally HTML-attribute encode to avoid double-encoding.
EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe/broken): x.setAttribute("value", '<%=ESAPI.encoder().encodeForJavascript(ESAPI.encoder().encodeForHTMLAttribute(companyName))%>'); After (safer): x.setAttribute("value", '<%=ESAPI.encoder().encodeForJavascript(companyName)%>'); Avoid: x.setAttribute("onclick", encodedUserData);
Avoid string-based DOM event handlers and code-evaluating APIs
WHAT: Using setAttribute with JavaScript event handler attributes (e.g., "onclick") or APIs that take code as strings (setTimeout, setInterval, new Function) causes the string to be interpreted and executed as code, enabling DOM-based XSS.
WHY: If any part of the attribute value or code string is influenced by user input, an attacker can inject arbitrary JavaScript that runs in the victim’s browser.
HOW: Do not use setAttribute for event handlers or pass code as strings; instead, bind events with addEventListener and pass real functions, and ensure no user-controlled data is ever treated as executable code.
EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe, string code): x.setAttribute("onclick", "alert(22)"); After (safer): x.addEventListener("click", function () { alert(22); });
JavaScript and CSS/URL Encoding for Untrusted Data in Execution Contexts
WHAT: Inserting untrusted data directly into JavaScript execution contexts (event handlers, CSS url(), URL attributes) can lead to DOM-based XSS if the data is interpreted as code.
WHY: Attackers can inject JavaScript that executes in the victim’s browser, enabling session theft, data exfiltration, or arbitrary actions as the user.
HOW: Never place raw untrusted data into JavaScript-executed strings, event handlers, CSS url(), or URL attributes; instead, first URL-encode data used in CSS url() or URL attributes, then JavaScript-escape it before insertion, and prefer assigning function references instead of code strings for event handlers.
EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe): `document.body.style.backgroundImage = "url(" + userInput + ")";` After (safer, Node ESAPI): `document.body.style.backgroundImage = "url(" + ESAPI.encoder().encodeForJavascript(ESAPI.encoder().encodeForURL(userInput)) + ")";`
URL and JavaScript escaping for untrusted data in URL attributes
WHAT: Inserting untrusted data directly into URL-related attributes or JavaScript string contexts can lead to XSS, especially when building URLs in DOM attributes (e.g., href, backgroundImage).
WHY: Attackers can inject script or malicious URLs, resulting in arbitrary script execution in the user’s browser.
HOW: When untrusted data is used inside a URL attribute that is also in a JavaScript string context, first URL-encode it, then JavaScript-encode it (e.g., encodeForURL → encodeForJavascript). Avoid this double-encoding for fully qualified URLs where encoding the colon would break the protocol.
EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe): `x.setAttribute("href", userRelativePath);` After (safer): `x.setAttribute("href", ESAPI.encoder().encodeForJavascript(ESAPI.encoder().encodeForURL(userRelativePath)));`
DOM-based Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) Prevention in JavaScript
WHAT: DOM-based XSS occurs when untrusted data is treated as HTML, code, or markup in the browser (e.g., using innerHTML, outerHTML, eval, or event-handler attributes) instead of as plain text.
WHY: Attackers can inject and execute arbitrary JavaScript in the victim’s browser, leading to session theft, data exfiltration, UI redress, or full account compromise.
HOW: Treat untrusted data only as displayable text; avoid eval and APIs that interpret strings as code/HTML; prefer textContent/innerText and safe DOM APIs (createElement, setAttribute for non-event attributes, appendChild); JavaScript-encode and quote untrusted data when building JS templates; never place untrusted data into event-handler attributes or HTML-rendering sinks.
EXAMPLE: Vulnerable: `div.innerHTML = location.hash;` and `eval(userInput);`
Secure: `div.textContent = location.hash;` and avoid eval by using explicit logic or safe parsing of expected data types.
Use untrusted data only on the right side of expressions
WHAT: Using untrusted data on the left side of an expression (e.g., as an object property name like window[userData]) allows attackers to modify internal or external object attributes.
WHY: This can lead to privilege escalation, data tampering, or takeover of critical objects such as window, enabling XSS or other injection attacks.
HOW: Never use user-controlled values as object keys, variable names, or other left-hand-side targets; restrict untrusted data to right-hand-side values and validate/encode it according to its output context.
EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe): window[userDataOnLeftSide] = "userDataOnRightSide"; After (safer): const key = "fixedKey"; window[key] = userDataOnRightSide;
Limit untrusted input in dynamic object property accessors
WHAT: Using untrusted data as object keys (e.g., object[userInput]) can let attackers read or overwrite internal or sensitive properties on window or other objects.
WHY: Attackers may subvert application logic, change security-relevant attributes, or access data they should not control.
HOW: Do not use raw user input on the left side of property assignments or lookups; instead, map or validate user input against a strict allowlist and use fixed property names (e.g., if/else or lookup tables) for actual object access.
EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe): `myMapType[userInput] = value;` After (safer): `if (userInput === 'location') { myMapType.location = value; }`
Don't eval() JSON to convert it to native JavaScript objects
WHAT: Using eval() on JSON or other untrusted strings to create JavaScript objects allows arbitrary code execution instead of just data parsing.
WHY: Attackers can inject malicious JavaScript into JSON or string data; eval() will execute it, leading to DOM XSS, data theft, or full script compromise.
HOW: Never use eval() for JSON; instead, ensure the input is valid JSON and parse it with safe JSON APIs such as JSON.parse() (and stringify with JSON.stringify() when needed).
EXAMPLE:
Before: const obj = eval(untrustedJsonString);
After:  const obj = JSON.parse(untrustedJsonString);
